definition: The game keeps a threat budget recomputed before each hostile event as a function of one or more proxies for player strength, multiplied by a difficulty scalar, and spends that budget on enemy count and composition. RimWorld computes raid points as (wealth points + pawn points) x threat scale x starting factor x adaptation factor, capped at 10,000: wealth points rise from 0 at 14,000 storyteller wealth to 4,200 at 1,000,000, each healthy colonist adds 15 to 200 points, a 0.7 starting factor applies through day 10, and an adaptation factor drops after colonist deaths or downings. Factorio's enemy evolution factor rises with elapsed time, pollution produced, and spawners destroyed, unlocking larger biters. Oblivion scaled enemy level to the player's level. Inputs: player state proxies and recent losses. Output: a scalar budget or tier consumed by the event or spawn system.
design_levers: which proxies define strength (wealth, population, time, kills, player level, recent damage taken)
the curve from proxy to budget, including dead zones, piecewise slopes, and the hard cap
difficulty multiplier presets and whether players can set them freely
adaptation or mercy terms that lower the budget after losses and raise it after easy wins
grace period length before scaling starts
how budget maps to enemy composition, such as tiers unlocked at thresholds versus more of the same unit
dynamics: Players optimize the ratio of combat value to counted value, producing lean, militarized bases.
Run length and difficulty converge across skill levels because the system rubber-bands toward a target challenge.
Coupled with permadeath, the adaptation term creates recovery arcs after a massacre instead of an immediate death spiral.
Coupled with pollution or expansion (Factorio), the threat becomes a cost of growth that players trade against output.
failure_modes: Scaling on wealth punishes building: RimWorld players practice wealth management, avoiding valuable furniture or art so raids stay small.
Scaling on player level makes progression feel null when every enemy keeps pace, a common criticism of The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion.
Proxies that ignore defensive investment let a cheap killbox beat budgets tuned for open combat, or let an undefended rich colony be overwhelmed.
Opaque formulas read as the game cheating when a large attack follows a burst of growth.
name: Adaptive threat scaling
open_questions: Can a learned estimate of actual defensive capability, such as a fast simulated raid against the current base, replace wealth proxies and remove the incentive to stay poor?
What adaptation rate keeps tension stable without players perceiving rubber-banding?
player_experience: Success is answered by stronger opposition, so the player never fully escapes danger. Players learn to read what the game counts as strength and manage it: converting wealth into combat power instead of decoration, or holding back expansion. After a disaster, mercy terms give a breathing window that feels like the world easing off.
summary: Threat intensity is computed from a measure of the player's strength, such as wealth, population, time survived, or recent performance.

synergy.note: The director spends a threat budget that scales with wealth, keeping pressure proportional to success.
Raids grow with the colony, so defenses must scale.

tension.note: One rewards growth, the other punishes it; tuning both sets the game's attitude to expansion.

definition: Each placeable type has a table of signed effects from neighbor types within a footprint, ring, or radius. When an object is placed (and in some games when a neighbor later changes), its value is recomputed as a base plus the sum of qualifying neighbor contributions, sometimes capped or with diminishing returns. The value feeds score, production yield, or desirability. Islanders (2019) previews the points a building will earn from nearby buildings before it is placed, and points unlock new building packs. Civilization VI (2016) gives districts adjacency yields from neighboring terrain and districts, such as science for a Campus next to mountains and gold for a Commercial Hub next to a river. Tile-laying builders such as Dorfromantik score matching edges between neighboring tiles. The state is the placement map plus the effect table; the update is a local sum.
design_levers: neighborhood shape: touching tiles, ring, or radius, and whether diagonals count
size and asymmetry of the effect table, including negative pairs that force separation
stacking rule for multiple neighbors: linear, capped, or diminishing
whether values freeze at placement or recompute when neighbors change later
how much of the calculation the preview shows before commitment
dynamics: Clusters of mutually reinforcing types form districts, and nuisance types get pushed to edges or buffers.
Scarce space turns adjacency into a packing problem in which early placements constrain later ones.
When adjacency feeds unlocks or income, early good clusters compound into a lead.
failure_modes: Once players find the best repeating cluster, every settlement uses the same stamp and the spatial puzzle ends.
Positive-only tables make maximum density always optimal, removing any reason to spread out.
Hidden or partly shown effect tables push players to wikis and calculators to plan placements.
Retroactive recomputation changes the value of old placements in ways players did not intend and cannot trace.
name: Adjacency scoring
open_questions: Can a learned model of layout quality replace hand-written pairwise tables while staying predictable enough to plan against?
What table size and asymmetry keep a solved cluster template from appearing within a few hours of play?
player_experience: Every placement is a small search problem with a visible answer. Players hover candidates to read preview numbers, reserve tiles for pieces they expect later, and feel clever when one placement lights up several neighbors. Penalties make them keep nuisances apart, so layouts acquire districts and buffers.
summary: A placement's value is computed from a table of bonuses and penalties for the placements around it.

claims.text: Lemonade Stand's daily inputs are glasses made, advertising signs, and price per glass, set against a weather report.
In Two Point Hospital assistants run marketing.

definition: Owns an awareness, brand, or hype stock per business, product, or venue and the rule that maps it onto customer traffic. Each period paid campaigns add to the stock with diminishing returns, and the stock decays toward a baseline when spending stops; its current level multiplies arrivals, the share of customers who consider the offering, or launch sales. Lemonade Stand (1973) reduces it to a daily input with no carryover: advertising signs bought before the day resolves raise sales alongside price and the weather. Two Point Hospital has assistants run marketing campaigns that bring in more patients. Capitalism and Game Dev Tycoon use advertising or marketing spend to build brand or pre-release hype. It differs from customer-value-choice, which owns how a customer who is already present chooses among offerings by price and value; this mechanic owns how many customers show up or consider the offering at all.
design_levers: cost per campaign unit and campaign duration
decay rate of awareness after spending stops
saturation curve, or diminishing returns per unit spent
targeting by customer segment, product, or condition
whether awareness raises arrivals, conversion, or willingness to pay
whether advertising can sell a poor product or only amplifies quality
dynamics: Advertising raises traffic and revenue that fund more advertising, a reinforcing loop limited by saturation.
Pre-release hype front-loads sales, so campaign timing and release timing couple.
Extra arrivals load service capacity, so a campaign can create queues that lower satisfaction.
failure_modes: Linear returns make maximum advertising always correct and remove the decision.
Effects too small to see in the statistics teach players to skip advertising entirely.
Without decay, one early campaign buys permanent demand.
Advertising that overrides quality lets poor products sell and undermines the product-quality systems.
name: Advertising and awareness
open_questions: Could simulated customers with stated tastes respond to generated ad copy, making campaign content rather than only spend a lever?
Which decay and saturation curves keep advertising a recurring decision instead of a one-time setting?
player_experience: Buying customers. The player decides how much to spend before the demand exists, watches arrivals rise and fall with each campaign, and learns that awareness fades: a store or game the market has forgotten needs fresh spending, while a strong brand lets prices rise.
summary: Spending on advertising raises a demand or awareness stock that decays without upkeep and scales how many customers arrive or buy.

claims.text: The Super NES version of SimCity added Dr. Wright, an advisor character who appears to report problems in the city.

definition: An advisor layer watches a set of indicators (budget balance, unemployment, crime, service coverage, happiness, military strength) and maps threshold crossings or rule matches to authored messages spoken by a named character, usually with a recommended action. It owns no simulation state: only trigger conditions, a priority per message, cooldowns, and an optional persona per department. Each evaluation interval it tests its conditions, ranks firing messages by severity, suppresses those still on cooldown, and presents the top one as a pop-up, voiced line, or entry in an advisor panel the player opens on demand. Inputs are aggregate state variables; outputs are text and, in some games, a one-click link to the relevant tool. Canonical forms: the department advisors of SimCity 2000 and SimCity 4, the Super NES SimCity advisor Dr. Wright who appears to report city problems, the advisor screens of the Civilization series, and Tropico's Penultimo.
design_levers: which indicators each advisor watches and the threshold or trend that triggers a message
diagnosis only versus a concrete recommendation or a one-click fix
one generalist advisor versus a council of department advisors with conflicting priorities
delivery mode: interrupting pop-up, voiced line, or passive panel opened on demand
cooldown and repetition rules per message
accuracy: whether advisors read true state, a lagged view, or a view biased toward their department
dynamics: Advisors act as an embedded tutorial whose value fades as the player's own causal model improves.
Department advisors arguing for opposite policies externalize tradeoffs such as tax revenue versus satisfaction.
When advice is trusted, player builds converge on what the advisor recommends, narrowing strategic variety.
failure_modes: A message keeps firing while the player cannot act on it, so players mute or ignore the advisor entirely.
Advice derived from a single indicator recommends the wrong fix when the cause is an interaction, such as more police when crime is driven by unemployment.
Advisors that are always right reduce the player to following instructions; advisors that are often wrong teach players to ignore all advice.
Lines written for early-game states become irrelevant or wrong at late-game scale.
name: Advisors
open_questions: Can a language-model advisor grounded in live state queries answer arbitrary why-questions accurately enough to be trusted, and how should it express uncertainty?
Does advice deliberately biased by an advisor's department or personality produce better decisions than neutral advice?
player_experience: The player gets a running diagnosis without reading every graph. Early on advisors teach which variables matter and what usually fixes them; later the player weighs advice against their own model, and conflicting advisors make tradeoffs explicit. Bad or repetitive advice is felt as nagging.
summary: In-world advisor characters monitor simulation indicators, summarize problems, and recommend actions.

definition: Selecting an individual agent opens a live panel that reads that agent's internal state: need levels, mood and its itemized contributors, current action and its target, queued actions, skills, traits, relationships, health by body part, inventory, and sometimes a log of recent thoughts or events. The mechanic owns only the selection and which fields are exposed; it reads state owned by other mechanics and refreshes each tick or on change. Its key design property is whether it shows reasons (why the agent is doing this) or only values. Canonical forms: The Sims need bars and visible action queue, RimWorld's needs, health, and social tabs with each mood thought listed with its source and expiry, Dwarf Fortress unit thoughts and preferences sheets, and RollerCoaster Tycoon guest windows listing a guest's thoughts, cash, hunger, and nausea.
design_levers: depth of exposure: raw meters, itemized reasons, or a full decision trace
whether each reason lists its source, magnitude, and remaining duration
live updating versus snapshot on open
which variables stay hidden (true personality, latent potential) to preserve uncertainty
whether every agent is inspectable or only a representative sample at large populations
supporting affordances such as follow camera, thought bubbles, and pinned favorites
dynamics: Players trace aggregate problems to individual causes, such as following one hauler to find a pathing bottleneck.
Named, inspectable agents raise the emotional cost of loss, which strengthens permadeath and injury systems.
Exposed reasons create pressure on designers to make the underlying model truthful, since players test it against what the panel says.
failure_modes: Panels with dozens of unranked numbers overwhelm players without telling them what matters.
The panel shows state but not the decision rule, so behavior still looks random even after inspection.

Inspection exposes shortcuts in the agent model; following citizens in SimCity (2013) revealed that agents took the nearest free home and job rather than keeping their own, undermining belief in individual citizens.
At city scale inspecting one agent is unrepresentative, so players cannot diagnose aggregate problems from it.
name: Agent inspection
open_questions: For agents driven by language models, what inspection format (plans, memories, rationales) lets players predict behavior rather than just read it?
How much reason exposure maximizes attachment before it turns agents into transparent spreadsheets?
player_experience: A crowd becomes individuals. When an agent misbehaves the player clicks it to find out why, reads the cause, and fixes the environment rather than the agent. Reading named thoughts and histories builds attachment and supplies the raw material for player stories.
summary: Selecting an agent opens a panel that reveals its needs, mood contributors, current job, and the reasons behind its behavior.

synergy.note: Inspection panels expose the thought list, converting hidden state into narrative.

definition: Owns a traversal representation (tile grid, navmesh, or waypoint graph) with per-cell or per-edge movement costs and permissions, plus each agent's current path or a shared direction field. On request a search returns a least-cost route from position to goal; A* (Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael, 1968) expands nodes by cost so far plus an admissible heuristic. Paths are invalidated and recomputed when the map changes or agents block each other. Scale variants trade exactness for speed: Factorio (2019) abstracts each 32x32 chunk into terrain components and runs a reverse resumable A* over them to supply the heuristic for tile-level A*; Supreme Commander 2 searches a portal graph between 10x10 m sectors and shares flow fields so many units read one direction field instead of each searching. Inputs: terrain and floor costs, doors and allowed areas, other agents. Outputs: routes, travel times, and occupancy along routes that feed hauling, traffic, and defense.
design_levers: movement cost per terrain, floor, road, or door type
search method and hierarchy (grid A*, navmesh, hierarchical abstraction, flow fields) and per-tick search budget
repath triggers and frequency when the map or obstacles change
local avoidance between agents (none, steering, reservation) versus passing through each other
agent map knowledge and permissions (full map, explored only, allowed areas, locked doors)
dynamics: Shortest-path choices concentrate trips on a few links, producing congestion that lowers throughput without any explicit traffic rule.
Defenders shape attacker routes with walls and gaps, so layout itself becomes the defense mechanic.
Travel time silently becomes the largest work cost, so compact bases and well-placed stockpiles dominate efficiency.
failure_modes: Agents take absurd detours or get stuck because the cost model or permissions disagree with what the player sees on screen.
Repathing storms after map edits become a late-game slowdown on large colony and factory maps.
Per-unit paths ignore other units and stall at chokepoints; Emerson describes Supreme Commander 2's earlier single-path system compounding collisions into stops.
Deterministic pathing invites exploits such as mazes and wall-hugging layouts that trivialize threats.
name: Agent pathfinding
open_questions: Can learned crowd models or mean-field approximations replace per-agent search at city scale while preserving individual route choices?
How much should paths reflect imperfect knowledge and preferences such as scenery or safety rather than shortest cost?
player_experience: The player notices pathfinding mostly through layout: where doors, stockpiles, and roads go decides how far agents walk. In defense play the player builds mazes that lengthen enemy routes; in colony sims the player winces as a colonist crosses the map for one item. Failures are visible and comic, so players learn the cost model by watching.
summary: Agents compute routes through space using movement costs, and the routes they choose shape congestion, travel time, and access.

definition: Each agent holds an experience stock and level per skill. Doing a task adds experience at a rate scaled by learning modifiers; crossing thresholds raises the level, and some games decay unused high levels. Level feeds work speed, success or botch chance, output quality, and minimum-level gates. RimWorld uses levels 0-20; experience to the next level rises from 1,000 at level 0 to 30,000 at level 19; passion sets learning to 35% (none), 100%, or 150%; skills above 9 decay by 30 to 3,600 XP per day; a daily cap of 4,000 XP per skill cuts further gains to 20%; construction speed is 50% plus 15% per level; some backstories make pawns incapable of a work type. The Sims raises skills through objects such as bookshelves and easels and gates promotions on them; Dwarf Fortress dwarves improve by repeating labors. Inputs: task time, learning modifiers. Outputs: speed, quality, eligibility for tasks.
design_levers: experience curve shape and level cap
learning-rate modifiers such as passions, traits, age, and teachers
decay of unused skills and daily learning caps
effect curves per level on speed, quality, and failure chance
hard gates (minimum level, incapable) versus soft penalties
dynamics: Specialization snowballs: the best agent at a job gets assigned it, which raises that skill further and widens gaps.
Losing a specialist opens a capability hole that forces retraining or recruitment; with permadeath this is a common crisis.
Coupled with quality tiers, item value depends on who made it, so assignment becomes an economic decision.
failure_modes: Uncapped or linear growth turns every long-lived agent into a master, flattening differences between characters.
Grinding: players set agents to repeat cheap tasks to farm experience, which RimWorld counters with a daily learning cap.
Steep effect curves make low-skill recruits useless, so new agents are dead weight rather than trainees.
Decay without clear feedback reads as random loss of competence.
name: Agent skills
open_questions: Can skills be represented as learned competence (policies that actually improve) rather than numeric multipliers, and does that change player attachment?
Which decay and cap settings keep specialization meaningful without rewarding grinding?
player_experience: Agents become individuals with track records. The player assigns specialists, trains newcomers on low-stakes work, and feels the loss when a master crafter dies. Skill growth gives each character a slow progression arc that runs alongside the base's growth.
summary: Agents gain skill through practice or training, and skill sets work speed, quality, and access to tasks.

synergy.note: Hiring trades wage cost against skill, and skills grow with time on the roster.
Priorities route skilled agents to the jobs they do best.
Skilled workers produce higher-quality goods.

definition: The feed subscribes to simulation events (raid arrived, agent died, contract completed) and to condition predicates over state (food below a threshold, building unpowered, storage full, entity damaged). It owns a list of active alerts, each with type, severity, timestamp, a deduplication key, a location or entity link, and a lifetime. Each tick it adds an alert on the rising edge of a predicate or on an event, merges alerts with the same key, removes condition alerts when the condition clears, and expires event alerts after a timeout or dismissal. Optional rules pause the game or drop speed on chosen types. Canonical forms: RimWorld's severity-colored event letters plus a persistent condition list (low food, colonist needs rescue), Factorio alerts for entities under attack or destroyed, trains out of fuel, and ghosts lacking construction materials, problem icons over buildings and the Chirper feed in Cities: Skylines, Dwarf Fortress announcements, and the Football Manager inbox.
design_levers: event alerts versus persistent condition alerts that clear themselves
severity tiers, color, and sound per alert type
auto-pause or speed-drop rules per alert type
aggregation: one alert for many identical problems versus one per entity
persistence until dismissed versus until the condition clears
click-through to location and player-side filtering
in-fiction framing (social posts, letters) versus neutral system text
dynamics: The alert set encodes what the designer considers a problem, so players optimize to keep icons off rather than toward their own goals.
With auto-pause, alert density sets the effective pacing of a real-time game.
Paired with an event director, alerts announcing incident arrival create a recognizable beat structure of calm, alarm, and response.
failure_modes: Alert fatigue: frequent low-value alerts bury the one that matters, and players miss a fatal problem.
In-fiction feeds read as noise; many Cities: Skylines players hid the Chirper feed with mods.
Predicates near a threshold, such as power just at capacity, flicker and spam add and remove cycles.
Alerts that report symptoms (no goods) rather than causes send players to fix the wrong thing.
name: Alerts feed
open_questions: Can a learned salience model rank and merge alerts by predicted consequence so the feed stays useful at megabase or metropolis scale?
Do natural-language digests of many alerts help players more than icons, or do they slow reaction time?
player_experience: In a system too large to watch, the feed decides where the player looks. The player triages, jumps the camera to the alert, and learns to dread specific alert types. Auto-pause on alerts turns real-time play into a series of decision points.
summary: A notification layer surfaces discrete events and threshold crossings with severity and a link to their location.

definition: Owns a herd of individual animals or a count per species, each with growth stage, food state, often affection or mood, and sometimes pregnancy and genes. Each day animals eat from grazing or stored fodder, grow toward maturity, and roll for products such as milk, eggs, or wool and for births; care actions raise affection or mood, which scales yield and quality. Stardew Valley tracks friendship from 0 to 1000 and mood from 0 to 255: unfed animals stop producing but do not die, mood under 70 can skip production, quality products need mood 150, and a nightly birth check governs pregnancies. RimWorld and Dwarf Fortress breed animals that must be fed, sheltered, trained, or slaughtered; Farming Simulator ties livestock productivity to feed. Inputs are feed, housing, and care; outputs are products, meat, and offspring.
design_levers: feed requirement per animal and the balance between grazing and stored fodder
time to maturity and product cycle per species
how care, mood, and affection scale yield and quality
breeding rate and population caps from housing size
losses: disease, predators, exposure, slaughter decisions
dynamics: Feed demand links husbandry to crop fields and storage, especially before winter.
Herds become targets for predators and raids, requiring fences and defense.
Breeding for traits ties husbandry to inheritance and long-term planning.
failure_modes: Unchecked breeding produces runaway herds that eat all fodder and then starve, a recurring colony-sim problem.
Daily care actions with no decisions become chores players automate away or abandon.
Animals that can never die or fall ill turn husbandry into passive income.
name: Animal husbandry
open_questions: Can learned animal behavior and animation make individually simulated livestock expressive enough to deepen attachment without bespoke animation per species?
player_experience: Routine care with compounding returns. The player builds pens and barns, keeps feed stocked through winter, and turns daily tending into reliable income. Animals can become personal: named, petted, and missed when lost to a predator or a hard winter.
summary: Domestic animals are housed, fed, tended, and bred, and they yield products whose quantity and quality depend on their care.

claims.text: The Sims 2 gives each Sim an aspiration with wants and fears, and an elder's remaining lifespan depends on the aspiration meter; The Sims 3 replaced wants and fears with wishes that pay Lifetime Happiness.
The Sims 4 adults take a bonus trait from their chosen aspiration.

definition: Owns, per agent, a long-term aspiration (a goal type such as family, knowledge, or fortune), a few open want slots, sometimes paired with fear slots, and a reward stock. A generator refills empty slots by sampling wants from a pool weighted by aspiration, traits, life stage, needs, and recent events; each want is a predicate over simulation state (make a friend, gain a skill level, get promoted) with a point value. When a predicate becomes true the want pays its points and leaves its slot, and a realized fear subtracts. Points feed a meter that shifts mood or behavior and usually a currency for rewards. The Sims 2 set the form: the aspiration biases which wants and fears appear, fulfilled wants fill the aspiration meter, and an elder's remaining lifespan depends on that meter. The Sims 3 replaced it with wishes that pay Lifetime Happiness, and The Sims 4 ties a bonus trait and a goal track to the chosen aspiration. Wants do not decay like needs; unlike a career ladder they are generated from state rather than authored as a fixed sequence, and unlike villager requests they are the agent's own goals.
design_levers: number of open slots and whether fears exist alongside wants
reroll, lock, and dismiss rules for slots
generator weights by aspiration, traits, life stage, and recent events
point value per want and what points buy (meter effects, reward objects, traits)
difficulty and time horizon of individual wants relative to play pace
whether unmet wants cost anything or simply expire
dynamics: Players chase wants that line up across household members, so generated goals couple separate characters' days.
Wants seeded by recent events (a promotion, a new baby) create follow-on arcs, an informal story chain driven by state.
Points buy rewards that make later wants easier to meet, a reinforcing loop toward a comfortable late game.
failure_modes: Wants that need unavailable or off-lot actions clutter the slots and teach players to ignore the panel.
Cheap repeatable wants let players farm points, so the reward store empties early and the meter stops mattering.
Generators that ignore context produce incoherent wants, such as wanting a first date the day after a spouse dies, which breaks the illusion of a mind.
Too many slots turn the panel into a checklist with no choice in it.
name: Aspirations and wants
open_questions: Can a language model write wants from an agent's memories and relationships while keeping each want checkable as a predicate over game state?
Do fears add enough drama to justify goals the player cannot fully prevent from failing?
player_experience: A stream of small, personal goals. The player reads what each character wants right now, plans the day around one or two of them, and collects a payout when they land, so an open sandbox gains a to-do list that comes from the character rather than the designer. Fears add dread: the player steers away from events the character would hate.
summary: An agent's long-term aspiration and current state generate short-horizon wants, and sometimes fears, whose fulfillment pays into a reward meter or currency.

definition: Each player runs a local simulation that publishes a small exported state to a server, such as surplus resources, service capacity, pollution, or a snapshot of a town, and periodically imports neighbors' exported state as boundary conditions. Exchanges resolve with delay, so play does not require both players online at once. In SimCity (2013), cities in a region connect by highways, rail, and waterways, trade resources, share services such as garbage collection or health care, see traffic and pollution cross borders, and pool wealth into Great Works such as an arcology; the connection was asynchronous, with brief disruptions tolerated. Animal Crossing island visits and Death Stranding's shared structures are related forms. Inputs: local surpluses and needs. Outputs: imported flows and shared projects.
design_levers: which variables are exported and imported (goods, services, pollution, visitors)
synchronization interval and conflict resolution
region size and how neighbors are matched (friends, public, random)
shared projects that require pooled contributions
fallback behavior when the server or a neighbor is offline
dynamics: Specialization emerges: one city goes industrial or hosts the hospital and the others import those services.
Externalities such as pollution and traffic cross borders, creating friction between players who never speak.
Shared projects create focal points that coordinate otherwise independent players.
failure_modes: Server dependence makes single-player play fragile; SimCity (2013) launched with outages and save problems, and an offline mode came later.
Abandoned neighbor cities leave dependent players short of the services they relied on.
Small play areas forced by the region design made specialization a necessity rather than a choice, which players criticized.
name: Asynchronous shared regions
open_questions: Can AI-controlled stand-in neighbors, trained on real player cities, keep regions alive when players leave?
What exchange latency preserves the feeling of a shared region while keeping each player's simulation independent?
player_experience: The player is part of a neighborhood without coordinating schedules. They specialize, relying on neighbors for what they lack, and notice others' choices arrive as traffic, pollution, or help. Cooperation feels light because commitments are small and delayed.
summary: Separate players' simulations affect each other asynchronously through shared regions, visits, or exchanges of goods and services.

definition: Owns the state of a contest in progress (score, clock, possession or positions, fatigue, morale) and each participant's attribute vector and tactical instructions. Each step the engine selects the next event (pass, shot, pitch, overtake) and resolves it by sampling probabilities computed from the involved participants' attributes, the tactics in force, fatigue, and context, then updates state and emits commentary or animation. Football Manager, which continues the Championship Manager series begun in 1992, renders its engine as text, as a 2D pitch from Football Manager 2005, and in 3D from Football Manager 2009; Out of the Park Baseball reports simulated games as text play-by-play; Motorsport Manager resolves races from driver and car ratings with player pit and pace calls. Inputs: lineups, attributes, tactics, in-match interventions. Outputs: results, per-participant statistics, injuries, and form that feed rosters, morale, and finances.
design_levers: event granularity (per possession, per pitch, per lap) and how many events are rendered to the player
mapping from attributes to event probabilities and the weight of randomness relative to ratings
tactical instruction set and how strongly each instruction shifts event probabilities
fatigue, morale, and home-advantage modifiers
in-match interventions such as substitutions, touchline shouts, and pit calls
dynamics: Results feed morale, form, finances, and transfers, so streaks compound into dynasties or collapses.
Communities reverse-engineer engine weights into a tactical meta, which yearly engine revisions then disrupt.
Simulated statistics become scouting data, coupling the engine to player valuation and transfer markets.
failure_modes: One tactic or formation dominates because the engine overweights a parameter, and the player community converges on it.
Low-variance engines make results feel predetermined by ratings; high-variance engines make tactics feel irrelevant.
Rendered visuals that disagree with the underlying event logic undermine trust in the simulation.
Players cannot tell bad luck from bad decisions because the attribute-to-outcome mapping is opaque.
name: Attribute-driven match engine
open_questions: Can event models trained on real tracking or event data replace hand-tuned probabilities while keeping tactics legible to players?
Can generated commentary explain why an event happened in terms of attributes and tactics, so players can separate luck from decisions?
player_experience: The player is the coach in the stands: setting lineups and tactics, watching a sampled stream of events, and reading results as evidence about whether decisions worked. Upsets feel earned or cruel; across a season noisy results become stories about form, slumps, and tactical identity.
summary: Contest outcomes are simulated play by play from participant attributes, tactics, and randomness instead of being played directly.

synergy.note: Hidden attributes make scouting valuable because they drive simulated outcomes (Football Manager).

definition: Owns a lot (item, quantity, optional reserve price), the standing bids, and a clock. Bidders submit or raise bids under a format: ascending open outcry, sealed bid, descending price, or a timed listing with a buyout price. When the clock ends or no bidder will go higher, the rule assigns the lot to the winner, transfers money, and settles fees. AI bidders bid up to a valuation computed from their needs and cash. M.U.L.E. (1983) runs real-time auctions for each resource, breaks ties in favor of the trailing player, and lets players who withhold supply raise prices on later turns; its designers replaced land auctions with one free plot per turn because auctioning land fed a runaway loop. MMO auction houses such as World of Warcraft's use timed listings with a minimum bid and an optional buyout price.
design_levers: auction format (ascending, sealed-bid first or second price, descending, timed listing with buyout)
tie-breaking and catch-up rules, such as awarding ties to the trailing player
reserve prices, minimum increments, and listing fees or deposits that act as money sinks
auction duration and whether bidding happens in real time or between turns
AI bidder valuation function and how much cash it holds back
which goods are auctioned versus sold at fixed prices or granted for free
dynamics: Withholding supply from an auction raises clearing prices on later rounds, enabling deliberate shortage play.
Bidding wars between two rivals let a third party buy cheaply elsewhere.
Reserve prices and fees act as money sinks that slow inflation in persistent economies.
failure_modes: Auctioning productive assets such as land lets the richest player buy more production, the snowball M.U.L.E.'s designers removed by granting free plots.
AI bidders with simple valuation rules can be baited into overpaying or never compete, so auctions become trivial.
Long timed auctions in MMOs reward bots and last-second sniping over judgment.
Collusion between human bidders suppresses prices when the rules cannot detect it.
name: Auctions
open_questions: Can LLM bidders with private valuations and bluffing make single-player auctions as tense as multiplayer ones?
Which catch-up rules (tie-breaks, budget caps) prevent auction snowballs without feeling arbitrary?
player_experience: Reading rivals. The player estimates what a lot is worth to each competitor, decides how far to push the price, and feels the sting of overpaying or the relief of a bargain. In real-time formats such as M.U.L.E. bidding is a test of nerve and timing; in timed listings it becomes patient sniping and undercutting.
summary: Goods, land, or rights are allocated by bidding procedures in which players or agents compete on price under rules for timing, ties, and reserves.

definition: Owns a global, per-agent, or per-category autonomy setting that gates which actions an agent may select for itself. Each decision cycle the setting filters or reweights the candidate set before action selection: at full autonomy the agent chooses among all actions; at reduced levels only urgent self-care or specific categories remain; at zero the agent idles until ordered. Player orders always take precedence while queued. The Sims (2000) exposes free will as an option, and even with it on, Sims need orders to pay bills, find jobs, exercise, or conceive. RimWorld's drafting switches a colonist from self-assigned work to direct control for combat or emergencies. Inputs: the setting, the order queue, urgency of needs. Outputs: the share of agent time under player versus agent control.
design_levers: number of levels and whether the setting is global, per agent, or per action category
which actions stay autonomous at each level (survival needs, social, self-care)
override rules when player orders conflict with urgent needs
quality of autonomous choices (competent versus deliberately flawed agents)
dynamics: Players run mixed teams of puppets and free agents, adjusting per character and per crisis.
Low-autonomy play exposes needs systems as chores, while high-autonomy play exposes utility-scoring quirks as personality.
With permadeath, the choice to delegate during danger (drafting colonists for a raid) becomes a risk decision.
failure_modes: Autonomous choices are worse than the player's, so players turn autonomy off and drown in micromanagement.
Autonomy that is too competent removes the player's role and turns the game into a screensaver.
Agents override intent at bad moments, such as wandering off mid-task, which reads as disobedience rather than personality.
Unclear boundaries between autonomous and ordered actions make failures hard to attribute.
name: Autonomy levels
open_questions: Can language-model agents accept intent-level delegation (keep the house running during the party) as a richer replacement for discrete autonomy levels?
Do players attach more strongly to agents they control or to agents they watch, and which autonomy setting maximizes attachment?
player_experience: Lets the player choose how much to micromanage. High autonomy turns play into arranging and watching; low autonomy turns it into puppetry with responsibility for every need. Players switch per situation: autonomy for routine life, manual control for crises and set pieces.
summary: The degree to which agents act on their own is adjustable, from full free will to explicit commands only.

tension.note: Agents with strong free will resist direct commands; designers must decide who is in charge.

claims.text: Factorio's blueprint library keeps a player's blueprints across saves, shares them with other players in multiplayer, and separately holds save-specific game blueprints.

definition: A blueprint is a saved snapshot of a region's entities with relative positions, rotations, and configuration (recipes, filters, circuit settings, sometimes tiles). State owned: a library of blueprints plus placed ghosts awaiting construction. Capture copies selected entities into a blueprint; stamping projects its entities at a cursor with rotation or mirroring, checks placement validity, and creates ghost build orders that construction agents or the player fulfill. Export serializes a blueprint to a string or file that other players can import. Canonical form: Factorio blueprints, blueprint books, a personal library that persists across saves and is visible to other players in multiplayer, and exchange strings used by community sites. Others: Dyson Sphere Program and Satisfactory blueprints, Mindustry schematics shared as text, and Space Engineers ship blueprints rebuilt through projectors.
design_levers: unlock timing: available from the start or gated behind progression such as construction robots
what is captured: entities only or also configuration, tiles, and logic
parameterized blueprints that substitute items or values at placement
sharing scope: within a save, across saves, or exported strings and workshop integration
who fulfills placed ghosts: the player by hand or automated builders
validity rules when stamping over obstacles or partial resources
dynamics: Modular, tileable designs become dominant because they stamp cleanly, shaping the visual language of player bases.
Shared blueprint strings create a design culture of named, versioned community layouts.
Stamping lowers the marginal cost of expansion, so growth becomes limited by resources and logistics rather than player time.
failure_modes: Imported meta designs replace the core puzzle, and players report feeling they are executing other people's solutions.
Late unlock makes the repetitive early game tedious and drives players to mods.
Blueprints that break when stamped into slightly different terrain or orientation cost more time than rebuilding by hand.
name: Blueprints
open_questions: Can generative models produce valid blueprints from a goal such as a 45 per second green circuit block, and does that remove or relocate the design puzzle?
How should parameterized blueprints be represented so designs adapt to terrain and recipes without becoming full programming?
player_experience: Solving a layout once is enough. The player designs a module carefully, then scales it by stamping, which moves attention from placing pieces to designing systems. Imported community designs let newcomers skip solved problems; some players feel that copying removes the puzzle.
summary: Player-made layouts can be saved, stamped as build orders, copied, and shared as text or files.

synergy.note: Stamping solved belt layouts lets players scale proven designs instead of re-solving them.
Shareable blueprint strings created whole communities of design exchange.

claims.text: In Football Manager the board judges the manager's performance.

definition: Owns a set of expectations (league finish, cup progress, budget balance, profit, playing style, youth development) imposed or agreed at the start of a season or term, and a confidence stock held by an evaluator such as a board, owner, chairman, or fan base. After each match, report, or period the stock moves by the gap between results and expectations, weighted by importance and recency; crossing warning levels triggers meetings, ultimatums, or budget cuts, and falling below the floor ends the job. Expectations are re-set from the organization's reputation and resources, so success raises the bar. Football Manager has the board judge the manager's performance and, with fan confidence, decide whether the manager is sacked; other sports management games set owner or chairman goals for each season. It differs from elections, where an electorate decides tenure at fixed dates, and from scenario-objectives, which test a fixed goal at a deadline; here a continuously updated stock can end the job at any time.
design_levers: how expectations are set: imposed from reputation or negotiated with the player
weight per result and how fast older results fade
warning thresholds and the events they trigger (meetings, ultimatums, budget cuts)
firing threshold and whether the player continues in a new job
separate evaluators (board, owner, fans) and how they combine
grace period after hiring
dynamics: Players manage expectations as well as results, for example by accepting modest targets to buy safety.
High-variance match engines produce sudden sackings that become career stories.
Being fired and hired by another club turns failure into a career path instead of a game over.
failure_modes: Expectations re-set too aggressively after success make long tenures impossible, punishing good play.
Sackings driven by short streaks feel arbitrary when simulated results have high variance.
Confidence that forgives too easily makes the threat vanish after one good season.
Hidden weights leave players unsure which goal actually matters.
name: Board confidence
open_questions: Can language-model board members with distinct priorities negotiate expectations with the player in conversation and remember broken promises?
What weighting of recent results makes sackings feel deserved under a high-variance match simulation?
player_experience: A clock on the player's job. Every result moves a meter the player does not fully control, so a run of bad form becomes existential and a promised top-four finish hangs over every match. Success raises expectations, so security never fully arrives.
summary: An evaluator such as a board, owner, or chairman sets expectations, updates a confidence stock from results against them, and fires the player below a threshold.

definition: Owns one money stock and a ledger of flow categories. Each accounting period income (taxes, fees, sales, trade) is added and expenses (upkeep, wages, service funding, interest) are subtracted. Players often set a funding fraction per department, and service effectiveness scales with it. In Micropolis, the open-source SimCity engine, the collection every 48 city-time steps computes revenue = population x average land value / 120 x tax rate x a difficulty factor, sets required police and fire funds at 100 per station and road funds per road and rail tile, and converts the fraction actually paid into RoadEffect (0-32) and PoliceEffect and FireEffect (0-1000), so underfunded roads decay and coverage shrinks. A negative balance leads to loans, bonds, bankruptcy, or game over; SimCity 2000 ends the game after extreme deficit spending.
design_levers: accounting period length and whether flows post continuously or at fixed ticks
which expense categories are player-adjustable and how effectiveness scales with the funding fraction
upkeep per building relative to the revenue it enables
consequence of a negative balance (borrowing, forced cuts, bankruptcy, or game over)
how much ledger detail and forecasting the interface shows
dynamics: Surpluses fund expansion that raises both revenue and upkeep, so cash pressure returns at each growth stage.
Underfunding one service degrades a dependent system (roads, crime, fires), which later lowers the revenue base.
Periodic settlement creates sawtooth cash curves and end-of-period scrambles.
failure_modes: Upkeep that scales slower than revenue makes money irrelevant by mid-game, a common complaint about Cities: Skylines.
Funding sliders whose effects are delayed or hidden teach players to cut services without visible cost until a collapse.
Fixed upkeep with no link to growth produces an early cash trap with no recovery path.
name: Treasury and budget
open_questions: Can an LLM advisor explain a deficit as a causal chain through the ledger well enough to replace spreadsheet-style budget panels?
What upkeep-to-revenue curve keeps money a meaningful constraint into the late game?
player_experience: Periodic reckoning. The player watches a running balance and a monthly or yearly ledger, trims service budgets to stay solvent, and decides when a surplus should become new construction. Shortfalls show up as visible decay: crumbling roads, slower fire response, unpaid staff.
summary: A money stock with income and expense flows such as taxes, upkeep, wages, and service funding; a negative balance leads to debt or failure.

synergy.note: Debt extends the treasury in time, trading future flexibility for present growth.

definition: A recipe or activity emits one or more secondary outputs alongside its primary product, at a fixed ratio per cycle or per capita. The byproduct accumulates in a local output buffer or tile stock; when that stock hits a cap, the producer stalls, degrades, or releases it into the environment. The player must route it to a consumer, a sink (incinerator, landfill, vent), or a converter. In Oxygen Not Included a Natural Gas Generator burning 90 g/s of natural gas yields 800 W plus 67.5 g/s of polluted water and 22.5 g/s of carbon dioxide that must be piped away or vented into the base. In Factorio oil processing yields heavy oil, light oil, and petroleum gas together, so an unconsumed output backs up and halts the refinery. In Cities: Skylines buildings generate garbage that trucks must collect or it accumulates and flags the building as a problem. Inputs: production cycles or population. Outputs: a waste stock and an impairment signal (stall, pollution, illness, abandonment).
design_levers: byproduct ratio per cycle and whether it scales with efficiency upgrades
buffer size before the producer stalls or starts releasing waste into the environment
whether the byproduct is pure waste, a sellable good, or an input to another chain
available sinks and their costs, such as incinerators, landfills, vents, or voiding
the impairment when unhandled: production stall, pollution, disease, morale loss, or abandonment
dynamics: Waste outputs become inputs elsewhere, so industrial clusters form around reuse loops (polluted water to a water sieve in Oxygen Not Included, heavy oil cracked to light oil in Factorio).
Disposal capacity becomes a hidden ceiling on growth, separate from input supply.
Coupled with pollution spread, unhandled byproducts shift cost onto neighbors and land value.
Players overbuild storage for byproducts as a buffer, trading space for time before the next fix.
failure_modes: A cheap sink that destroys anything removes the problem and turns the mechanic into a one-time build tax.
Byproducts with no use and no penalty become clutter that players ignore.
Fixed-ratio multi-output recipes deadlock silently when one output has no consumer, and the stall appears far from its cause.
Waste that only matters late, such as a full landfill or spent nuclear fuel, surprises players who built for hours without a disposal plan.
name: Byproducts and waste
open_questions: Can a generative chemistry model produce byproduct sets for new recipes that stay balanced without hand tuning?
What ratio of waste to useful output keeps disposal a design problem rather than a chore?
player_experience: Every new building arrives with a cleanup problem attached. The player learns to ask where the waste goes before placing a producer, and designs sinks, reuse loops, or disposal districts. A full output buffer stopping a whole line teaches that the unwanted product sets the pace of the wanted one.
summary: Production emits secondary outputs such as sludge, garbage, heat, or spent fuel that must be handled or they impair the system.

synergy.note: Waste outputs are the sources that pollution diffusion spreads.

claims.text: Tamagotchi (1996) has Hunger, Happy, and Training meters, life stages, and an adult form that depends on care.
Princess Maker 2 covers the daughter's life from age 10 to 18 and has 74 endings.

definition: Owns, per raised creature or character, a running history of care and attributes (tallies of neglect and discipline, stat values, behavior counts) and a developmental table that maps ranges of that history to next-stage forms or final outcomes. Between stages the history accumulates from care actions and scheduled activities; at each stage boundary the table is evaluated, by first matching branch or best score, and the chosen form replaces the old one, setting appearance, stats, behavior, lifespan, or an ending. Tamagotchi (1996) chooses its adult character from the quality of care it received, so neglect yields a different creature rather than only a sick one. Princess Maker 2 (1993) develops the daughter's attributes from age 10 to 18 and then selects one of 74 career endings from her attributes and history. It differs from creature-care, which owns need meters and care actions; from lifecycle-aging, whose stages advance without branching; and from trait-inheritance, where form comes from the parents' genes rather than the individual's own history.
design_levers: which history variables are tracked and how they are weighted
number of stage boundaries and branches per boundary
threshold placement and whether ties resolve by priority or chance
visibility of the table (hidden, hinted, or shown)
whether later care can redeem an early bad branch
how different branches are mechanically, from cosmetic to changes in stats, lifespan, or ending
dynamics: Players compare outcomes socially (which character did yours become), turning private care into shared stories.
Replays to collect branches convert one raising loop into a collection game.
Players reverse-engineer the tables, and community guides become part of the game's culture.
failure_modes: Hidden tables push optimization to wikis and walkthroughs, after which players follow a recipe instead of raising.
Branches that differ only cosmetically make care history feel irrelevant.
Early branches that cannot be recovered punish new players for mistakes they could not understand.
A single best branch turns the table into a target and removes variety.
name: Care-dependent development
open_questions: Can generative models produce a distinct form or ending for every care history, and do players value that over a small set of collectible authored branches?
How much of the table should be visible so that care feels intentional without becoming a recipe?
player_experience: Raising with consequences. Every feeding, scolding, lesson, or missed call writes into a history the player cannot fully see, and the reveal at the next stage passes judgment on it. Players replay to see other branches, compare results with friends, and look up the tables to aim for a particular form or ending.
summary: A creature's or character's accumulated care or attribute history selects which form or outcome it develops into at each stage boundary, from a fixed branching table.

claims.text: In The Sims 2 adult careers have ten levels and teen careers three; promotion requires advancing three skills, enough household friends, and high mood, and missing work two days in a row causes firing.

definition: A career is an ordered list of levels, each with a title, pay, schedule, and promotion requirements. State owned: per character, current career and level, and a job performance meter. Update rule: each work period, performance changes based on attendance and inputs such as mood, skills, or task completion; when performance and the next level's requirements are met, the character is promoted; very low performance or missed shifts cause demotion or firing. Inputs come from other mechanics (skills, relationships, needs); outputs are income, schedule, and status. Canonical form: The Sims 2, where adult careers have ten levels, teen careers three, promotion requires advances in three skills, a number of household friends, and high mood, and missing work two days in a row gets a Sim fired; The Sims 4 adds daily career tasks and branching tracks.
design_levers: number of levels and spacing of requirements
requirement types: skills, relationships, mood, or task completion
performance meter rate and decay
branching tracks at upper levels
random work events with choices, such as The Sims chance cards
pay and schedule curve across levels
dynamics: Career requirements route characters' free time into skill and friend grinding, coupling work to social and needs systems.
Schedule conflicts between household members' careers create household logistics problems.
Promotions raise income and enable home upgrades, a reinforcing loop toward comfort.
failure_modes: Requirements become a checklist that drains spontaneity from life simulation.
Rabbit-hole careers where the Sim leaves the lot make the career invisible to play.
Pay grows faster than costs, so money stops mattering by mid-career.
name: Career ladder
open_questions: Can generated workplaces with colleagues, tasks, and politics replace authored rabbit-hole careers without large writing costs?
Does requirement opacity, like a real workplace, make careers more engaging than explicit checklists?
player_experience: A long-term arc for one character. The player schedules skill-building and socializing around work, watches the performance bar before a promotion, and feels the status jump of a new title and pay. It gives sandbox life a direction.
summary: Characters advance through ranked job levels by meeting skill, relationship, and performance requirements.

claims.text: Victoria 3 uses a nested tooltip system in which highlighted terms inside a tooltip open further tooltips, a system introduced by Crusader Kings III.
Victoria 3 UX work repositioned tooltips so players can move into a nested tooltip without opening another, and added military tooltips that break down battle calculations.

definition: Any displayed derived value (mood, stability, price, income, work speed, battle strength) can be hovered to list its contributing terms, each with a label, source, sign, and magnitude, usually as base plus additive modifiers times multiplicative modifiers. Terms that are themselves derived or that name a game concept can be hovered again, opening a nested tooltip. The mechanic owns no simulation state but requires the simulation to compute values as explicit lists of labeled modifiers rather than opaque formulas. Update rule: on hover, read the modifier list for the value, sort and render it, and attach hover targets to sub-terms. Canonical forms: Paradox grand strategy (Europa Universalis IV, Stellaris), Crusader Kings III, which introduced nested tooltips on highlighted terms that Victoria 3 adopted, Victoria 3 tooltips breaking down battle calculations, RimWorld info-card stat breakdowns (skill and capacity factors behind work speed), and Civilization yield breakdowns.
design_levers: recursion depth: one level of breakdown versus nested tooltips on every term
whether tooltips can be pinned or locked so the player can move into them
which modifiers are hidden from the breakdown, if any
presentation of additive versus multiplicative terms, ordering, and rounding
whether each modifier shows its remaining duration
glossary links from terms to concept explanations
dynamics: Full transparency speeds up optimization and exploit discovery, pushing play toward spreadsheet min-maxing.
Because each new effect appears in breakdowns automatically, modifier architectures are easy for modders to extend legibly.
Players learn the simulation's causal graph by walking tooltips, which lowers the need for external wikis.
failure_modes: Late-game modifier stacks grow into walls of numbers that no longer explain anything.
Rounded or partial terms that do not sum to the displayed value erode trust in the whole interface.
Values with clamps, caps, or nonlinear interactions are presented as simple sums and mislead.
Hover-dependent design moves essential information off the main screen and works poorly with controllers and touch.
name: Causal breakdown tooltips
open_questions: When values come from a learned simulator instead of modifier lists, can attribution methods produce breakdowns players trust?
Do counterfactual tooltips (what single change would flip this outcome) teach faster than additive breakdowns?
player_experience: The player can interrogate any number until the lever appears. Opaque systems become debuggable: why is stability falling, which modifier expires next, what would fix it. Players who enjoy optimization dig through several levels; others glance at the top line.
summary: Hovering a derived value shows the named modifiers that produce it, and terms inside the tooltip can be hovered in turn.

synergy.note: Itemized modifiers are only legible when tooltips decompose them (Paradox titles).

definition: Owns one aggregate score (or one per district or class) computed each evaluation period from service levels, problems, and events, usually smoothed toward its previous value. Downstream systems read it: growth and migration, productivity, tax tolerance, election odds, and unrest. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, a yearly evaluation sums seven problem values (crime, pollution, housing cost as 0.7 x average land value, taxes as rate x 10, traffic, unemployment, fires), maps the sum to a 0-1000 score, multiplies it by penalties for missing stadium, airport, or seaport (0.85 each), underfunded roads, police, and fire, and the share of unpowered zones, adjusts for population growth, and averages it with last year's score; an approval poll then gives 100 citizens a yes with probability score / 1000. Frostpunk (2018) splits the score into Hope and Discontent, and the game ends in revolt if hope stays too low or discontent too high for too long.
design_levers: which inputs enter the score and their weights
smoothing or averaging period, which sets how quickly fixes show up
thresholds where satisfaction triggers growth, emigration, strikes, or game over
single score versus separate scores per class, district, or faction
how causes are explained (complaint lists, thoughts, polls, advisors)
dynamics: Low satisfaction drives emigration, which lowers demand for services and can partly restore satisfaction for those who stay.
Satisfaction tied to productivity creates spirals where unhappy workers produce less and services decline further.
Scores averaged over time let a short crisis pass without punishment but punish sustained neglect.
failure_modes: A single number hides which problem matters, so players chase the wrong fix without a breakdown view.
Easy maximization by stacking one cheap amenity makes satisfaction irrelevant.
Long smoothing makes improvements feel unrewarded and pushes players to over-correct.
name: Citizen satisfaction
open_questions: Can LLM-voiced citizens explain their dissatisfaction in specific, accurate terms that point to real causes in the simulation?
Is one aggregate score better or worse for play than many per-group scores when citizens can explain themselves?
player_experience: A report card on the whole system. The player watches one number rise and fall, digs into the complaint list or overlays to find the cause, and fixes the top problem. In crisis games like Frostpunk it becomes the meter the player is always defending.
summary: An aggregate satisfaction score computed from services, conditions, and events modulates growth, productivity, and unrest.

synergy.note: Low satisfaction accumulates into unrest; unrest further lowers satisfaction.
Satisfaction becomes votes, tying tenure to welfare (Tropico).
Satisfied populations attract migrants; dissatisfied ones leave.

claims.text: Stardew Valley's Community Center has six rooms and thirty bundles; completing rooms repairs the quarry bridge, greenhouse, minecarts, and bus, and a Joja membership replaces bundles with payments.

definition: The game defines named sets of collectibles (items, fish, insects, fossils, species, recipes) and tracks which members the player has obtained, donated, or observed. State owned: per set, a membership checklist and completion state. Update rule: when the player acquires or submits a qualifying item, mark it; when a set is complete, grant a reward or unlock. Collection drives engagement with other systems because members are spread across seasons, locations, and rarities. Canonical forms: Stardew Valley's Community Center, with six rooms and thirty bundles whose rewards repair the quarry bridge, greenhouse, minecarts, and bus, Animal Crossing: New Horizons' museum and Critterpedia, and Viva Pinata's species journal with per-species visit, resident, and romance requirements.
design_levers: set size and rarity distribution of members
seasonal, weather, or location gating of members
reward type: functional unlocks, cosmetics, or none
fixed versus randomized set contents, such as Stardew Valley remixed bundles
whether items are consumed by submission
visibility of missing members as silhouettes or hints
dynamics: Collection targets route player attention through seasons, weather, and locations they would otherwise skip.
Players share calendars and spreadsheets of where and when members appear.
Alternative completion routes, such as the Joja membership in Stardew Valley, frame collection as a moral choice.
failure_modes: The last few rare members take far longer than the rest, turning completion into a grind.
Members missable for a season or year punish players who fall behind.
Functional rewards locked behind collection force players who dislike collecting through it.
name: Collection goals
open_questions: Can generated collectible sets tied to world state, such as species that evolved in this run, keep collection goals meaningful in procedural worlds?
What rarity curve keeps the final members exciting rather than grinding?
player_experience: A gentle, open checklist. The player plans around a missing fish that appears only in rain in autumn, feels a click when a set completes, and has a reason to explore every corner of the simulation.
summary: Catalogs of items, species, or bundles give the player sets to complete for rewards or recognition.

claims.text: Infinite Craft starts from water, fire, wind, and earth; a new pair is generated by Llama 2 or Llama 3.1 with an emoji under a twenty-token cap and stored so all players get the same result, and new results earn a First Discovery label.

definition: Owns a recipe graph that maps combinations of elements, usually unordered pairs, to results, the set of elements the player has found, and per-recipe discovery records. A combine action looks up the chosen inputs: if a recipe exists the result joins the player's set, first-time results are announced, and the new element becomes an input for further combinations; if none exists nothing happens or a small cost is paid. The graph is hidden, so the loop is experimentation, and progress is counted in elements found rather than items used. Infinite Craft (2024) starts from water, fire, wind, and earth and has no fixed graph: on a cache miss a language model (Llama 2, later Llama 3.1) names the result, capped at twenty tokens, with an emoji; the result is stored so every player gets the same answer, and the player who triggered it earns a First Discovery label. Little Alchemy and Doodle God use authored graphs. It differs from hand-crafting, where known recipes turn carried components into useful items at workstations, and from generative-content, which owns the model call rather than the discovery loop.
design_levers: graph size and depth, authored or generated
number of inputs per combination and whether order matters
cost of a failed combination
hint systems and whether the count of remaining recipes is shown
shared first-discovery records and leaderboards
whether elements have any use beyond further combination
dynamics: Each discovery enlarges the input set, so the number of untried pairs grows roughly with the square of elements found.
A shared cache turns discovery into a race for First Discoveries and produces community lists of paths to rare results.
Players form folk theories about how the graph or the model reasons and test them systematically.
failure_modes: Without hints, players brute-force every pair or consult a list, which ends the discovery loop.
Authored results that do not follow from their inputs feel arbitrary.
Generated graphs drift into nonsense or offensive results and need moderation.
Elements with no use beyond combining make the collection feel hollow once novelty fades.
name: Combination discovery
open_questions: Can generated combination results carry mechanical properties that make them useful inside a simulation, rather than only names?
What hint density keeps experimentation fun without turning it into lookup?
player_experience: Curiosity as the whole loop. The player tries pairs on a hunch, laughs at or argues with the result, and chases rare elements by reasoning about what the designer or the model would think. Each find opens new combinations, so the field of untried ideas keeps growing.
summary: The player combines owned elements to discover the products of a hidden recipe graph, and finding recipes is itself the goal.

claims.text: Zach Barth designed SpaceChem's global histograms so players could check their solutions without feeling overwhelmed by the top players a leaderboard would list.
Opus Magnum ranks solutions on cycles, cost, and area, and players combine them in an unofficial sum statistic.
Zachtronics deliberately offers no in-game rewards for optimization in Opus Magnum, so players who optimize do so for intrinsic reasons.

definition: After a solution passes validation, the game computes several independent metrics that trade off against each other and shows the player's value on each as a marker on a histogram of all players' (or friends') values for that puzzle. State owned: per-puzzle score distributions aggregated on a server, plus the player's best per metric. Update rule: on completion, simulate the solution, compute metrics, upload them, and fetch the current distributions. The metrics come from a design-evaluation mechanic; this mechanic owns only the population comparison. Canonical forms are Zachtronics games: SpaceChem ranks instructions, cycles, and reactors, and Zach Barth designed its global histograms so players could check a solution without being overwhelmed by the top players a leaderboard lists; Opus Magnum compares cost, cycles, and area; TIS-100, Shenzhen I/O, Infinifactory, and Exapunks use the same pattern.
design_levers: number of metrics and how strongly they trade off against each other
global distribution versus friends-only comparison
bin width and handling of outliers or exploit scores
per-metric personal bests versus recognition of Pareto-optimal combinations
whether any reward is attached to good scores (Zachtronics deliberately attaches none)
dynamics: Players replay solved puzzles to move their marker, extending content life without new content.
Communities build external record trackers for Pareto frontiers that the in-game histograms do not show.
Friend comparison produces asynchronous rivalry without direct competition.
failure_modes: Metrics that do not trade off collapse into one dominant solution, and the histograms show a single spike.
Exploit or bugged solutions create impossible scores that distort the left tail.
Late puzzles are attempted only by skilled survivors, so average players appear below median on every metric.
Independent per-metric bars ignore balanced solutions; Opus Magnum players invented an unofficial sum metric to score them.
name: Comparative histograms
open_questions: Can distributions seeded by automated solvers before launch give useful comparison targets without discouraging human players?
Does showing a Pareto frontier instead of per-metric histograms change which tradeoffs players explore?
player_experience: Instead of a rank, the player sees where they sit in a crowd on each axis. A solution that is slow but cheap still feels good, and a visible tail of better scores invites returning to a solved puzzle to shave cycles. Comparison is social but low in intimidation.
summary: A player's solution is plotted against distributions of other players' scores on several metrics.

synergy.note: Multi-metric ratings become social when plotted against everyone else's solutions (Opus Magnum).
Open-ended programming puzzles gain replay value from optimization histograms.

tension.note: Directed randomness makes scores incomparable across players.

definition: Each host (agent, building, settlement, or country) carries a disease state from a small compartment set, usually susceptible, infected, recovered or immune, and dead. Each tick infected hosts transmit to susceptible contacts with a probability per contact (agent-based) or at a rate proportional to infected times susceptible (aggregate), and leave infection at a recovery or death rate. Inputs are contact structure (adjacency, shared rooms, trade and travel links), host resistance, and interventions such as quarantine, vaccination, or medicine; outputs are cases, deaths, and lost labor. Kermack and McKendrick showed that an epidemic occurs only above a threshold set by infectivity and recovery rates. Plague Inc. spreads a player-evolved pathogen between countries until a cure completes; Theme Hospital has contagious patients who infect others inside the hospital; World of Warcraft's 2005 Corrupted Blood debuff spread by proximity and escaped its raid through suspended pets and fast travel to cities.
design_levers: transmission probability per contact or aggregate rate, and which contacts count (adjacency, shared rooms, trade routes, flights)
infectious period, incubation length, and whether carriers can be asymptomatic
recovery, death, and immunity rules, including whether recovery confers lasting immunity
intervention set and costs: quarantine, closing borders or ports, vaccination, treatment
spatial resolution: per agent, per building, per settlement, or per country
how much disease state is shown: case counts, overlays, or only visible symptoms
dynamics: Hubs such as cities, hospitals, and transport nodes become superspreaders, so network topology matters more than total population.
Sick workers leave jobs, cutting production of the food, medicine, or care that would end the outbreak.
Agents or players bypass quarantine for convenience, so enforcement becomes its own problem, as in the Corrupted Blood outbreak.
Depletion of susceptible hosts ends waves on its own, producing boom-and-bust waves that can look like successful policy.
failure_modes: A reproduction number far above any real pathogen makes spread unstoppable and interventions pointless; Lofgren and Fefferman noted Corrupted Blood's exceeded any observed real disease.
Contact channels the designer did not model, such as Corrupted Blood's suspended pets and fast travel, carry infection past intended boundaries.
Hidden infection with no leading indicator reads as a random wipeout rather than a failed response.
Aggregate compartments with no spatial structure give every outbreak the same curve, so the player learns one fixed response.
name: Contagion
open_questions: Can LLM-driven agents produce plausible behavioral responses to outbreaks (compliance, panic, rumor) that change the effective contact rate in play?
What is the minimum contact structure that still makes intervention placement a meaningful spatial decision?
player_experience: Watching an invisible quantity become visible too late. Early cases look harmless, then counts climb faster than responses can be built, so the player learns to act on leading indicators: isolating carriers, closing links, stockpiling medicine, or, in Plague Inc., keeping symptoms mild so the disease spreads widely before lethality alerts the world. Most responses trade economic activity against spread.
summary: Disease spreads between agents or regions via contact rates and moves hosts through compartments such as susceptible, infected, and recovered.

synergy.note: Health coverage determines whether outbreaks are contained.

definition: A creation is serialized to a compact format, uploaded to a shared catalog with metadata, and ranked by downloads, ratings, or curation; other players browse and import it, or the game pulls catalog items into their worlds automatically. Spore uploaded every creature, vehicle, and building to the Sporepedia, ranked items by downloads, and redistributed them to populate other players' galaxies, with only a few kilobytes per item because the game rebuilds each creation procedurally from its template; it passed 100 million creations by May 2009, and players could filter or ban user content. Steam Workshop for Cities: Skylines, Planet Coaster blueprints, and Factorio blueprint strings are other forms. Inputs: serialized creations. Outputs: imported content and creator reputation.
design_levers: serialization format and size, such as procedural templates versus full assets
ranking and discovery signals (downloads, ratings, curation, subscriptions)
automatic versus opt-in import into other players' worlds
moderation tools and content filters
attribution and feedback to creators
dynamics: A small share of creators produce most of the popular content.
Shared blueprints spread optimal designs quickly, which compresses the discovery phase for later players.
Communities form around creator challenges and showcases.
failure_modes: Offensive or infringing uploads spread fast without moderation; Spore needed filters and in-game bans.
Popularity rankings concentrate attention on a few creators and bury new work.
Imported content that breaks balance or performance degrades the importer's game.
name: Content sharing
open_questions: Can models classify and moderate uploaded creations at scale with fewer false positives than keyword or report systems?
How should catalogs recommend shared content without concentrating attention on a few top creators?
player_experience: Creators build for an audience and check how their work spreads; browsers get far more variety than the developer shipped. Seeing another player's creature walk through your world, or importing a polished city block, makes the game feel populated.
summary: Player creations such as buildings, creatures, or blueprints are uploaded, browsed, rated, and imported into other players' games.

synergy.note: Shared first discoveries give generated content social value (Infinite Craft).
Mods need distribution; sharing platforms need mods.

definition: Owns a pool of offers, each with a requirement (cargo type and quantity, a service, or an object meeting a spec), an origin and destination or a client, a deadline, a payout, and often a penalty and a reputation gate. Offers are generated from templates and current simulation state, sit on a board until they expire, and are accepted by the player. On completion the rule checks the requirement, pays out (often scaled by distance, cargo value, or speed), and updates reputation; lateness or abandonment forfeits pay or charges a penalty.
