Euro Truck Simulator 2's freight market, Elite Dangerous mission boards, Farming Simulator contracts, Car Mechanic Simulator repair orders, and Transport Tycoon's time-limited subsidies are common forms.
design_levers: payout formula (distance, cargo value, urgency, risk) relative to running costs
deadline tightness and the penalty for lateness or abandonment
offer generation: random templates versus real shortages in the simulation
reputation or rank gates that unlock higher-paying work
number of simultaneous contracts allowed and board refresh rate
dynamics: Players chain contracts into loops that minimize empty legs, producing self-discovered trade circuits.
Reputation gating creates a ladder where risky early work buys access to lucrative later work.
When contracts are generated from real shortages, completing them dampens the shortage that created them.
failure_modes: Templated contracts detached from simulation state feel like grind, since taking the best payout per minute is the only decision.
Abandon-and-refresh exploits let players cherry-pick outliers when boards regenerate too freely.
Payouts that outscale costs make every contract profitable and remove route planning.
name: Contracts and orders
open_questions: Do contracts generated by a language model from live simulation state (a town short of grain, a rival's broken supply line) feel less like grind than templated ones?
Can open-ended commissions be judged by learned evaluators, such as a model scoring whether a built structure meets a client's brief?
player_experience: A steady menu of concrete goals. The player scans offers, weighs payout against distance, risk, and time, chains jobs so trips are never empty, and races deadlines. Contracts turn an open sandbox into a sequence of short, legible tasks.
summary: Discrete jobs with requirements, deadlines, and payouts, such as deliveries or commissions, drive income and planning.

synergy.note: Contracts give routes a purpose and a deadline.

definition: Belts form directed chains of tiles; each tile holds a fixed number of item slots per lane and moves items forward at a tier-dependent speed. Items enter from inserters, machines, or side-loading and exit at the end, onto another belt, or into a machine. Splitters divide and merge flows, often with priority and filter settings; undergrounds and bridges cross other belts. Factorio holds 4 items per lane per tile and carries 15, 30, 45, or 60 items per second across both lanes for transport, fast, express, and turbo belts. Internally it groups adjacent belts into transport lines and stores the gaps between items, so a free-flowing line updates only its end gaps each tick. Satisfactory, Dyson Sphere Program, and Mindustry use similar belt tiers, and Shapez raises belt speed through upgrades. Inputs: items placed on belts. Outputs: items delivered at a throughput capped by the slowest segment.
design_levers: throughput per tier and number of lanes
splitter, merger, and priority or filter options
crossing options such as undergrounds, bridges, or vertical lifts
item density and whether mixed items share a lane
belt cost and unlock schedule
dynamics: Main-bus and ratio-block conventions emerge from throughput caps, and players share them as blueprints.
Belt saturation sets factory module sizes, so each tier upgrade reshapes layouts.
Mixed-item belts create sushi designs and clogging failure modes.
failure_modes: Spaghetti layouts become unreadable and players stop understanding their own factory.
Lane imbalance and side-loading rules are opaque without wikis.
Belt counts at large scale cost simulation time; Factorio's transport-line rewrite was made to cut this cost.
name: Conveyor transport
open_questions: Could layout assistants that propose belt routing under player constraints keep the puzzle while removing tedium?
What is the smallest set of belt primitives that still supports deep layout optimization?
player_experience: Layout as the main puzzle. Players route belts around each other, balance lanes, and design compact buses, and they can see throughput problems as gaps or backed-up lines. A compressed belt feeding a full row of machines is a visible proof of a correct design.
summary: Items move continuously on belts or lanes with throughput limits, splitters, merges, and priorities.

synergy.note: Belts make recipe chains spatial, turning ratios into a layout puzzle (Factorio, Satisfactory).

claims.text: In Rebel Inc. the more initiatives the player funds from the monthly budget, the more corruption and inflation rise, and a governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.

definition: Owns a corruption level per polity, region, or city and the rule that turns it into losses. Each period the level rises with drivers such as the volume of spending or programs, distance from the seat of government, the number of administered territories, or weak institutions, and falls with countermeasures such as anti-corruption policies, courthouses, audits, or dedicated spending; some games accumulate it as a stock with slow decay, others recompute it each turn from current conditions. A share that grows with the level is then removed from tax revenue, trade, production, or program effectiveness, or added to costs. Rebel Inc. (2018) makes corruption a side effect of governing: the more civilian initiatives the player funds, the more corruption and inflation rise, and a governance tab offers anti-corruption measures. Civilization (1991) and Europa Universalis IV use other forms. It differs from taxation, which sets the rate of collection, and from stability-unrest, which owns grievance; corruption owns the leak between what the state raises and what it gets to use.
design_levers: drivers of corruption (spending volume, distance, territory count, institution quality)
what leaks and how much: revenue, output, program effectiveness, or costs
countermeasures and their price (policies, buildings, dedicated spending)
accumulated stock with decay versus a level recomputed each period
visibility, from a shown meter to losses visible only in the ledger
dynamics: Corruption caps efficient size, since each additional city, territory, or program returns less, a balancing loop on expansion.
Spending to win support raises corruption that erodes the budget for further spending, as in Rebel Inc.
Players invest in countermeasures first in regions far from the center, which shapes expansion order.
failure_modes: One cheap countermeasure, a single building or policy, zeroes corruption and removes the mechanic from play.
A flat percentage loss with no driver the player can influence feels like an arbitrary tax rather than a decision.
Distance-based corruption punishes spread-out realms so hard that one empire shape dominates.
Leaks without a breakdown make budgets feel randomly short.
name: Corruption leakage
open_questions: Can corruption be modeled as agents (officials, contractors) who skim and can be investigated, rather than as a percentage, while staying readable?
Which drivers make corruption a strategic constraint rather than a flat tax?
player_experience: Growth carries a hidden tax. The player watches part of every budget vanish, weighs how much to spend fighting it, and learns that expanding programs or territory faster than institutions can follow makes each new unit of spending worth less.
summary: A corruption level driven by spending, administrative reach, or size removes a share of revenue or output until countermeasures bring it down.

definition: Owns one or a few creatures, each with need meters (hunger, happiness, hygiene, health, discipline), a life stage, and often an affection or obedience value. Meters decay in game or real time, and the player restores them with direct care actions: feeding, cleaning, playing, giving medicine, or scolding. Neglect accumulates into sickness, a worse adult form, running away, or death. Tamagotchi (1996) shows hunger and happy meters and a discipline meter, leaves droppings that cause sickness if not cleaned, cures illness with medicine, and ages the pet through life stages in real time; Nintendogs adds stylus petting and voice-recognized commands; Seaman responds to the player's speech. Inputs are care actions and elapsed time; outputs are the creature's condition, form, and behavior.
design_levers: number of needs and their decay rates in game or real time
severity of neglect consequences: mood, sickness, altered growth, death, leaving
care actions available and whether they are menu choices or direct manipulation
whether care quality shapes the adult form or personality
pause or vacation options that suspend decay
dynamics: Check-in frequency becomes the main loop, coupling the game to the player's daily schedule.
Care quality branching into different adult forms motivates replays and comparison between players.
Shared or shown-off pets turn care quality into social status.
failure_modes: Real-time decay with no pause punishes absence; the first Tamagotchi units could stop time only through the clock-setting mode.
Once the optimal care routine is known, interactions become a checklist and attachment fades.
Creatures with too few reactions repeat the same animations, breaking the illusion of a living pet.
name: Creature care
open_questions: Can language models give pets memory and open-ended conversational responses while keeping their needs legible?
Does generated animation or behavior reduce the repetition that ends attachment?
player_experience: Responsibility and attachment. The player checks in often, notices small changes, and feels guilt when the creature gets sick from being forgotten. Care is direct and tactile rather than managerial, and the creature's growth or decline mirrors the player's attention.
summary: The player directly feeds, cleans, and plays with a creature whose needs decay; neglect causes sickness, stunted growth, or death.

synergy.note: Wall-clock decay makes care a daily ritual and absence meaningful (Tamagotchi).

definition: Owns a creature's learned decision parameters: weights linking perceived situations or objects to actions. After the creature acts, a reward or punishment signal (a player stroke or slap, or a change in an internal drive) adjusts the weights for that situation-action pair, so its future selection probability rises or falls and generalizes to similar situations. Creatures (1996) uses about 1,000 neurons in 9 lobes; a 16-cell decision layer picks the strongest-firing action; drive reduction releases a reward chemical and drive increase a punishment chemical, which reinforce excitatory or inhibitory synapses, so norns learn to eat when hungry but not when full. In Black & White (2001) the creature follows a belief-desire-intention model with desires as simplified perceptrons and opinions as decision trees; the player strokes or slaps it after actions and uses leashes to direct its attention. Inputs: player feedback, drives, perceived objects. Outputs: changed action probabilities.
design_levers: learning rate and how quickly old associations fade
credit assignment window that decides which recent action receives the feedback
granularity of the situation representation (object types, desires, contexts), which decides what generalizes
feedback channels such as stroke and slap, food, demonstration, and attention leashes
innate drives and biases the learning starts from
dynamics: Creatures from the same start diverge into distinct personalities, which drives players to share and compare them.
Learned behavior acts on the world, so training choices reshape villages, alignment, and appearance in Black & White.
Learning from internal drives without player input produces self-taught habits and odd local optima.
failure_modes: Credit assignment errors attach feedback to the wrong action or object, and players cannot tell why the creature learned something.
Learning too slowly makes training feel ignored; too quickly lets one slap erase hours of shaping.
Generalization surprises, such as a creature learning to eat villagers, read as bugs rather than lessons.
Emergent learned behavior varies by player, which makes testing and balancing expensive; Black & White was later called overrated for underusing its creature.
name: Creature learning
open_questions: Can modern reinforcement learning or language-conditioned policies give creatures learning that generalizes the way players intend, with explainable credit assignment?
Does exposing a creature's learned associations improve attachment or destroy the illusion of a mind?
player_experience: The player becomes a parent or trainer. Each reward is a bet about what the creature will generalize, and personality emerges from the history of training. Success feels like understanding; failure feels like a stubborn pet, and players blame themselves for bad habits.
summary: A creature's behavior is learned from player reward and punishment or from neural adaptation over its life.

synergy.note: The creature learns from how the god acts, making the player's own behavior a training signal (Black & White).

definition: Each map cell, district, or agent holds a crime level derived from a propensity function over conditions, minus a suppression term from policing. In the open-sourced SimCity engine (Micropolis), crimeScan sets each cell to 128 - land value + population density (capped at 300), subtracts a police-influence map smoothed three times from station positions and funding, and clamps to 0-250; the city average drives a high-crime warning above 100 and crime feeds back into land value. Agent-based variants such as Cities: Skylines 2 spawn criminals and crime events that police units respond to, with arrests flowing into jails and prisons of limited capacity. Tropico and SimCity 2000 use similar aggregate fields, and Prison Architect models the justice end, where reform and labour programmes lower recidivism and the prison is graded on recidivism, happiness, and violence. Inputs: land value, density, education, employment, happiness, police coverage and funding. Outputs: crime map, satisfaction and value penalties, incidents, and incarcerated population.
design_levers: inputs and weights of the crime propensity function (land value, density, unemployment, education, happiness)
police coverage radius, capacity, and the funding-to-effect curve
justice pipeline capacity: jail and prison slots and what happens when they fill
strength of crime's feedback into land value, migration, and satisfaction
aggregate field versus discrete crime events with agents
dynamics: Coverage creates safe islands around stations and crime pockets in gaps, so station placement becomes a covering problem.
Coupling with land value and zoning makes crime track inequality across the map.
Budget cuts to policing show up with a lag, producing oscillation when players react late.
failure_modes: When suppression is just coverage, the optimal play is blanketing the map with stations, and the social causes the model encodes stop mattering.
Crime lowers land value, which raises crime, so poor districts can lock into a spiral the player cannot read as a loop.
Hidden justice capacity limits make crime rise for no visible reason once jails fill.
name: Crime and policing
open_questions: Can agent-level motives (need, opportunity, social ties) produce crime patterns that reward social policy over coverage, without becoming illegible?
Would generated investigations or court cases make the justice side of the loop a playable system rather than a capacity number?
player_experience: The player reads a crime overlay, spots hot districts, and decides between adding stations, raising police funding, or fixing root causes such as low land value or unemployment. Crime is a visible symptom of neglected neighborhoods and a running cost of growth.
summary: Crime levels arise from local conditions such as land value, density, or unemployment, and police coverage, prisons, and justice reduce them.

definition: Owns a countdown to a scheduled crisis (in days, turns, or progress percent), the crisis's nature, and sometimes its expected severity. Each tick the counter falls; at zero the crisis applies a large state change such as extreme cold, an attack, a flood, or a scenario loss, which the player's preparation mitigates. The timer may be fixed, randomized within a known window, or driven by a rival process the player can slow. Frostpunk's main scenario builds toward the Great Storm, and its Last Autumn scenario races to finish an outpost before a storm; Plague Inc. runs a cure-research percentage that ends the game when it completes; Don't Starve's winter arrives on a fixed schedule; The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask frames play around a three-day falling moon. Inputs are elapsed time and actions that shift the clock; outputs are the crisis and its severity.
design_levers: warning lead time and whether the exact date is known
crisis severity and whether it is shown in advance
whether player actions can delay, accelerate, or weaken the crisis
single climactic crisis versus recurring crises of rising strength
failure handling: scenario loss, heavy damage, or partial survival
dynamics: Players shift from expansion to stockpiling as the counter runs down, creating distinct phases within a run.
Countdowns reward forecasting tools that project resource runways to the deadline.
Recurring crises such as winters or droughts escalate into a cycle of preparation and recovery.
failure_modes: A crisis with a fixed required preparation becomes a build order that players replay rather than a plan.
Too much lead time removes tension; too little makes the crisis an unavoidable random event.
A single climactic crisis gives a scenario a hard end and little reason to replay.
name: Crisis countdown
open_questions: Can a director model choose crises that target the player's actual weak points while keeping the warning fair?
player_experience: Dread and focus. Knowing what is coming and when, the player turns the remaining days into a plan: stockpile coal, insulate homes, finish the walls. The final days narrow choices to triage, and surviving feels earned because the preparation was the player's own.
summary: A known future crisis such as a storm, winter, cure, or deadline is announced in advance, and the remaining time structures preparation.

synergy.note: A known winter or storm turns the season calendar into a preparation deadline.
Forecasts let the player plan against the countdown rather than be ambushed by it (Frostpunk).

definition: Each planted cell or field holds a crop type, a growth progress value, and condition flags such as watered, fertilized, or diseased. Each tick or day, progress advances at a base rate multiplied by modifiers for soil fertility, water, light, temperature, and season; outside allowed conditions growth stops or the plant dies. At maturity the crop is harvested for a yield, sometimes scaled by care or skill, and the cell resets, regrows, or loses fertility. Harvest Moon and Stardew Valley require daily watering and tie crops to seasons of a fixed calendar; RimWorld scales growth by soil fertility and light and halts it outside a temperature band; Farming Simulator turns field preparation, sowing, fertilizing, and harvesting into vehicle operations; Manor Lords and Farthest Frontier track soil fertility per field and reward crop rotation. Inputs: seeds, labor or player actions, environmental conditions. Outputs: harvested goods and an updated field state.
design_levers: growth duration per crop and number of visible stages
which conditions gate growth (water, light, temperature, season, fertility) and whether violating them pauses or kills the crop
single-harvest versus regrowing crops
yield and quality modifiers from fertilizer, skill, or care
soil fertility depletion and recovery rules, including rotation or fallow
labor or action cost of planting, tending, and harvesting
dynamics: Harvests arrive in pulses, creating labor peaks that compete with construction and hauling.
Seasonal growth windows couple farming to storage and spoilage, turning winter into a stockpiling test.
Soil depletion pushes expansion onto new land or forces rotation schedules.
Weather events and blights can wipe out a season and cascade into famine.
failure_modes: Daily manual tending scales poorly, so large farms become rote clicking until automation such as sprinklers arrives.
One crop with the best value per day dominates and planting choice disappears.
Season-change crop deaths feel arbitrary when the calendar is not prominent.
Growth too fast relative to consumption makes food trivial; growth too slow with harsh winters makes early runs unwinnable.
name: Crop cultivation
open_questions: Can learned plant growth models give crops plausible responses to microclimate that players can still reason about?
How much automation can farming absorb before cultivation stops being a decision?
player_experience: Planning around a delayed payoff. The player commits land and time now for a harvest days or a season later, then guards the field against weather, pests, and neglect. In avatar farming games the daily watering round becomes a ritual; in colony sims the growing season becomes a deadline that sets how much must be stored for winter.
summary: Planted crops progress through growth stages over days or seasons depending on water, soil, and season, then are harvested.

synergy.note: Watering and harvesting consume the daily energy budget, forcing farm sizing tradeoffs.
Season-locked crops create a calendar of planting decisions.

definition: Owns a large population of visitor agents, each with preference parameters sampled at spawn (intensity range, nausea tolerance, tastes), a cash budget, and mood stocks such as happiness, energy, hunger, thirst, and toilet. When choosing what to do, a visitor filters attractions by preference and budget, picks among the acceptable ones, and on rejection or experience emits a named thought that changes happiness. In RollerCoaster Tycoon, per the OpenRCT2 reimplementation, a guest rejects a ride whose intensity rating is below its minimum or above its maximum preferred intensity (both widened by happiness), whose nausea rating exceeds its tolerance (300, 600, 800, or 1000 plus happiness), or whose price exceeds twice the ride's value (value quartered when the park charges entry); rejections lower happiness and create thoughts such as bad value, and guests with nothing left to ride head home. Outputs: attendance, spending, park rating, crowding.
design_levers: preference distributions sampled at spawn (intensity, nausea, tastes, budget)
acceptance rule (hard thresholds versus scored choice) and the price-to-value tolerance multiplier
thought vocabulary and how thoughts aggregate into a park or facility rating
mood decay rates and leave-the-park thresholds
crowd size and spawn rate tied to rating, marketing, or price of entry
dynamics: Preferences spread over intensity create demand for a portfolio of gentle and intense attractions rather than one best ride.
Rating raises attendance, and the larger crowd congests queues and paths until mood falls, a balancing loop on growth.
Players learn the value threshold and price every attraction just below it, a stable arbitrage the rule invites.
failure_modes: Price-value rules that ignore context let players overcharge a few attractions with no penalty, or punish small price changes too harshly.
Thought spam: hundreds of identical thoughts bury the actionable signal.
Narrow preference sampling makes the crowd behave like one average agent, removing segmentation decisions.
Large crowds cost pathfinding and update time, capping park size.
name: Crowd preferences
open_questions: Can visitor preference models fitted to real attendance or survey data make tycoon crowds more segmentable without losing legibility?
How should thousands of thoughts be summarized so the player sees causes rather than noise?
player_experience: The player reads the crowd as a distribution: thought feeds and aggregate complaints reveal what is missing, and the fix is a layout or pricing change rather than an order. Individual guests are funny and disposable; the crowd's mood is the scoreboard, and pricing becomes a dial between revenue and goodwill.
summary: Large visitor populations with individual preferences, budgets, and tolerances choose attractions and react with visible thoughts.

synergy.note: Individual tastes and budgets make pricing and attraction mix matter.
Visible queues and complaints let crowds express capacity problems.

claims.text: Victoria 3 pops share profession, culture, religion, state, and workplace.
Crusader Kings III applies faith hostility opinion modifiers from 0 to -30 between characters.

definition: Owns categorical identity attributes (culture, faith, and in some games ideology or ethics) per province, county, or population group, plus conversion progress or a per-period conversion share. Each period progress accrues from sources such as assigned missionaries or court officials, state religion and laws, assimilation into the majority culture, buildings, and the ruler's or government's alignment, against resistance from population size, development, or fervor; when progress completes the attribute flips, or in population-group models a fraction of each group switches. Other systems read the identities: a mismatch with the ruler or state adds unrest and opinion penalties, a match or accepted status grants bonuses, and shared or hostile identities shape alliances and wars. Victoria 3 stores its population as pops that share profession, culture, religion, and state. Crusader Kings III applies opinion penalties between faiths by hostility and lets rulers convert counties' faith and culture. Europa Universalis IV converts province religion with missionaries. It differs from population-strata, which owns class tiers and promotion; identity is orthogonal to class.
design_levers: conversion speed and the resistance factors (population size, development, fervor)
which agents or policies can convert (missionaries, court officials, laws, buildings)
binary flip per province versus a share of each population group per period
penalties and bonuses attached to matching or mismatched identities
tolerance and acceptance rules that let mixed identities coexist
whether players can found, reform, or hybridize faiths and cultures
dynamics: Majority identities grow by assimilation, a reinforcing loop toward homogeneous heartlands with contested borderlands.
Identity mismatch feeds unrest and revolt, coupling conversion to stability and military occupation.
Shared faiths and cultures become alliance lines, so identity maps shape diplomacy.
failure_modes: Cheap, certain conversion homogenizes every realm and erases the identity layer by mid-game.
Severe unrest from mismatched identity turns conquering other cultures into a trap and narrows play to one strategy.
Faiths and cultures that differ only in numeric modifiers feel interchangeable.
Treating the conversion of real faiths and peoples as a pure optimization can read as endorsing forced conversion.
name: Culture and religion conversion
open_questions: Can language models generate new faiths and cultures whose doctrines produce consistent mechanical effects and believable schisms?
Can conversion run as diffusion through social networks of individual agents rather than as a per-province progress bar?
player_experience: The map has a second layer of identity beneath its borders. The player conquers land that will not accept them, then spends missionaries, officials, or decades of policy converting it, choosing between tolerating diversity and its unrest or homogenizing at a cost. Faiths and cultures spreading, splitting, and reforming become the long arcs of a campaign.
summary: Provinces or population groups carry culture and faith identities that drift or are converted by missionaries, policies, and rulers, changing unrest, opinion, and bonuses.

definition: Owns each customer's (or segment's) preference weights and budget, and each offering's price and value attributes. When a customer wants a good or service, the rule scores every reachable offering, typically utility = perceived value x preference match - price - distance or wait, then buys the best one, samples in proportion to scores, or buys nothing when every price exceeds willingness to pay. Lemonade Stand (1973) reduces it to three daily inputs (glasses made, advertising signs, price per glass) whose sales vary with the weather report. RollerCoaster Tycoon guests refuse rides and stalls they judge too expensive for what they offer and say so in their thoughts. Capitalism weighs price, quality, and brand by product category to split demand among competing stores.
design_levers: shape of the utility function and which attributes (quality, brand, novelty, distance, wait) enter it
price sensitivity per customer segment, income class, or trait
heterogeneity: one representative customer versus sampled individual preferences
deterministic best choice versus probabilistic (logit) choice
whether customers explain rejections through thoughts, reviews, or complaints
dynamics: Competing sellers undercut each other until quality or brand differentiation ends the price war.
Choices propagate congestion: the best-value stall attracts queues that lower its effective value.
Segmented preferences reward a portfolio of offerings over one best product.
failure_modes: A single representative customer yields one optimal price that players find once and never revisit.
Hidden value thresholds read as random rejection unless thoughts or reviews explain them.
Weak price sensitivity lets players charge extreme prices with little loss, so gouging dominates.
name: Customer value choice
open_questions: Can LLM-driven customers with stated tastes and budgets haggle or complain in language while staying consistent with a calibrated demand curve?
How much preference heterogeneity is needed before players stop finding a single dominant price?
player_experience: Finding the price people will bear. The player probes prices, watches thoughts or sales drop when they overreach, and invests in quality or marketing to justify charging more. Small numbers become visible crowds walking past or lining up.
summary: Customers choose among offerings by comparing price to perceived value and personal preference.

definition: Owns a budget that refills at the start of each in-game day (energy points, stamina, clock hours, or a fixed number of time slots) and a cost per action. Actions spend from the budget; at zero the player is penalized or the day ends, and sleep restores the budget, sometimes less after staying up late. Stardew Valley gives 270 base energy, raised by Stardrops, charges energy for tool use, exhausts the farmer at 0, and makes them pass out at -15 energy or at 2 a.m.; passing out away from home costs 10% of gold up to 1,000g, and going to bed after midnight restores less. Harvest Moon set the stamina-and-clock farm day that Stardew Valley follows; Persona allocates a fixed number of time slots per day to activities. Inputs are action costs and restoration items; outputs are the actions completed per day.
design_levers: budget size and whether it grows with progression
cost per action and which actions are free
penalties at or past zero and for staying up late
restoration sources within the day, such as food
time slots versus a continuous pool
dynamics: Players batch tasks spatially to save time, which shapes farm and base layout.
Budget-expanding items become top priorities, forming an upgrade path.
Automation such as sprinklers frees the budget from chores for new activities, marking progression.
failure_modes: A budget that is too tight early makes the opening a grind; one that grows too fast stops mattering by midgame.
When one activity has the best return per point, every day becomes the same routine.
Harsh pass-out penalties push players to reload rather than accept a bad day.
name: Daily action budget
open_questions: Can generated daily events or requests keep each day's allocation decision fresh without hand-authored content?
player_experience: Every morning is a planning puzzle. The player picks which crops to water, whom to visit, or which job to take, knowing the rest must wait. The end of each day gives a natural stopping point and a sense of steady progress, and upgrades that stretch the budget feel substantial.
summary: A per-day pool of energy, stamina, or time slots limits how many actions the player can take, and the day's end resets it and forces prioritization.

definition: Owns a timetable per agent or group mapping time-of-day blocks to activity categories (sleep, work, eat, leisure), set by the player, authored, or generated. Each tick the current block filters or biases which actions an agent may choose and which areas it may enter; block boundaries trigger mass movement. Prison Architect regimes are hourly schedules per risk category (Lockup, Sleep, Eat, Yard, Shower, Free Time, Work variants) that confine prisoners to areas rather than forcing actions, and cooks start four hours before an Eat block. RimWorld's schedule assigns each colonist's hours to sleep, recreation, work, or anything. Generative Agents (2023) has a language model draft a day plan of five to eight broad chunks, then decompose it into hour-long and 5-15 minute actions and replan on events. Inputs: clock, block assignments, disruptions. Outputs: synchronized demand peaks and occupancy by room and hour.
design_levers: block granularity (hourly, shift-based, or free-form plans)
who sets the schedule: player, authored routine, or agent-generated plan
strictness: hard confinement, soft bias, or ignorable when needs are urgent
per-group or per-agent schedules and shift staggering
response to disruption: skip the block, delay, or replan
dynamics: Shared blocks produce peaks on food, transit, and services, generating queues and congestion at predictable hours.
Staggered shifts emerge as a player strategy that trades coordination effort for throughput.
Coupled with day-night cycles and crime, schedules create time-dependent risk such as unattended night hours.
failure_modes: Synchronized blocks create rush hours that overwhelm shared facilities such as canteens, showers, and transit.
Agents follow the schedule into danger because blocks override situational awareness.
Authored routines repeat visibly, so the world reads as clockwork after a few days.
Schedules that conflict with needs create deadlocks in which agents go hungry or sleepless between blocks.
name: Daily schedules
open_questions: Can language-model day plans stay coherent across weeks of game time while remaining cheap enough for hundreds of agents?
How much schedule variation is needed before a town stops reading as clockwork?
player_experience: The player thinks in time: staggering shifts so the canteen is not mobbed, protecting sleep, and noticing when one block is starved. Schedules make agents look like they have lives and give the world a daily rhythm the player learns and exploits.
summary: Agents follow time-blocked routines for work, sleep, and leisure that create rhythms of demand across the day.

synergy.note: Synchronized commutes produce rush-hour peaks that stress the network.
Schedules decide when needs can be met, creating crowding at meals and bedtime.

definition: A map mode recolors the world by one per-cell, per-building, or per-segment field: land value, pollution concentration, crime, service coverage, traffic volume or speed, power and water connectivity, temperature, gas composition, germs, or political ownership. It owns no simulation state; it samples a field and maps it through a color ramp or categorical palette, sometimes adding glyphs such as flow arrows. Update rule: when active, sample the field each frame or on change and redraw; some games switch an overlay on automatically when the player places a related building. Canonical forms: the data maps of SimCity and SimCity 2000, Cities: Skylines info views, the oxygen, temperature, power, plumbing, decor, and germ overlays of Oxygen Not Included, Factorio's pollution cloud on the map view, and the map modes of Europa Universalis IV.
design_levers: which fields get an overlay, since exposing a field makes it an optimization target
continuous gradient versus thresholded bands
fixed absolute scale versus auto-normalized to the current map range
automatic display while placing a related building
instantaneous value versus time-averaged value
single overlay at a time versus composites, and colorblind-safe palettes
dynamics: An exposed field becomes a painting target: players lay out coverage grids until no red remains.
Visible spatial externalities push players toward land-use separation, such as industry far from housing.
In games with diffusing fields (heat, gas), overlays are how players discover emergent flows they did not intend.
failure_modes: Auto-normalized color ramps make a minor problem look red and a severe one look identical.
Overlays without legends or units show where something is high but not how high.
Overlays of fields with hidden formulas, such as land value, show where but not why.
Red-green ramps are unreadable for many colorblind players.
name: Data overlays
open_questions: Can automated annotation of overlays (this plume originates from these three sources) close the gap between where and why?
Which fields should stay without an overlay to preserve discovery and uncertainty?
player_experience: A hunch becomes a picture. The player sees the shape of a hidden field, such as a pollution plume or a coverage gap, and responds spatially by moving, adding, or separating buildings. Overlays are the main debugging tool for layout.
summary: Map layers visualize hidden variables such as land value, pollution, coverage, or traffic.

synergy.note: Overlays make invisible diffusion fields legible.
Traffic overlays turn congestion from a vague complaint into a located problem.
Coverage overlays show gaps that would otherwise surface only as complaints.
Land value maps are the canonical city-builder overlay.

tension.note: Full-information overlays undercut hidden-information play; games must choose what to reveal.

definition: Owns a catalog of models (vehicles, consoles, components, building types), each with an introduction date, a retirement or obsolescence date, and stats, plus the rule that checks the in-game calendar each period and adds models to or removes them from what the player can buy or target. Availability depends only on the date, not on player spending, so every company gains the same options at the same time. New models often arrive with lower launch reliability or a short exclusive preview, and retired models can no longer be bought while existing units keep aging. Transport Tycoon (1994) introduces road, rail, sea, and air models on a timeline across its calendar, so fleets are renewed as better vehicles arrive and old ones lose reliability; Railroad Tycoon releases locomotives by era; Game Dev Tycoon launches and retires fictional consoles on a fixed timeline that forces platform bets. It differs from tech-tree, where unlocks are bought with accumulated research in an order the player chooses; here time alone unlocks.
design_levers: introduction and retirement dates per model, and whether they vary slightly between games
start year and calendar speed, which choose the eras a game covers
prototype or exclusive preview windows and launch reliability
whether old models are withdrawn or stay buyable
size of each generational jump
dynamics: Fleet renewal waves follow major introductions and cause cash crunches and service gaps.
Every company gains new models at once, so competition shifts to who adopts and finances renewal best.
Launch and retirement dates decide which platform bets pay off, as with console choice in Game Dev Tycoon.
failure_modes: Games that run past the last introduction date stall with nothing new to buy.
Retiring a model without a successor leaves a role with no buyable vehicle or platform.
Fixed dates become memorized, so experienced players plan purchases around known release years.
Generational jumps so large that switching is always immediate remove the renewal decision.
name: Dated technology timeline
open_questions: Could introduction dates respond to simulated demand and rival research, making the timeline emergent rather than fixed?
Does a historical timeline reward knowledge of real history in ways that help or hurt replayability?
player_experience: History arrives on schedule. The player watches the calendar for the next locomotive or console, plans when to switch, and lives with a fleet or catalog that ages out from under them. A new era is a forced renewal decision rather than a reward the player earned.
summary: New vehicle models, platforms, or products enter and leave availability on a calendar tied to in-game dates rather than to research, forcing fleet or platform renewal.

definition: Owns a time-of-day value that advances each tick and wraps at a fixed day length, usually split into phases such as day, dusk, and night. Each phase sets ambient light, sometimes temperature, and flags read by other systems: agent schedules, spawn tables, growth, sanity or fear, and shop hours. Don't Starve uses an 8-minute real-time day of sixteen 30-second segments whose day, dusk, and night split shifts with the season; in total darkness the monster Charlie attacks and sanity drains at 50 per minute. Minecraft has a 20-minute day and spawns hostile mobs in low light, and The Long Dark makes nights colder. Inputs are elapsed time and season; outputs are phase flags and light levels.
design_levers: day length in real time and the day, dusk, and night split, fixed or varying by season
how dark night gets and whether light sources are required to act
which systems read the phase: spawns, agent schedules, temperature, growth, prices
penalty for being caught in darkness, from reduced visibility to direct damage
whether the player can skip the night by sleeping
dynamics: Bases cluster around light sources, and trips shrink to what can be done before dusk.
Combined with daily schedules, synchronized agents create rush hours at dawn and dusk.
Night becomes a high-risk, high-reward window when rare resources or creatures appear only in darkness.
failure_modes: Night that is only darker visuals with no mechanical difference becomes an annoyance players remove by raising brightness.
Nights that are too punishing make every night identical: retreat and wait, wasting play time.
Long real-time days make planning trivial; very short ones make players feel unable to finish trips.
name: Day-night cycle
open_questions: Can learned relighting or neural rendering make time-of-day visual variety nearly free, moving authoring effort to behavioral differences?
player_experience: A rhythm of safety and threat. Day is for travel and work, dusk is a warning to head home, light fires, or finish tasks, and night is spent defending, sleeping, or risking the dark for better rewards. The player plans each day around the remaining light and learns to read the sky as a clock.
summary: A diurnal cycle changes light, visibility, temperature, and which agents are active, so activity follows the hour of the day.

definition: Each decorative object, floor, or surface has a beauty value, and dirt, corpses, and filth are negative. The game aggregates values over a radius or a room and samples the result for agents or attractions. In RimWorld a room's beauty is total beauty divided by a weighted size (the size if above 40 tiles, otherwise 20 plus half the size), graded from hideous (below -3.5) to unbelievably beautiful (100 or more), and combined with wealth, space, and cleanliness into impressiveness that sets mood thoughts; colonists also get mood from the beauty around them. In RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, as documented by OpenRCT2, scenery within 5 tiles of a ride's station adds 0.05 excitement per item up to 47 items. The Sims 4 rates rooms by an environment score from decor. Inputs are placed objects; outputs are mood, ratings, or prices.
design_levers: beauty value and cost of each object, and negative values for filth and industry
aggregation rule: per tile, per radius, per room, with or without size normalization
caps or diminishing returns on how much decoration counts
which systems consume beauty: mood, ratings, prices, or visitor choice
per-agent taste variation by trait or culture
dynamics: Traffic creates filth that lowers beauty, which creates cleaning jobs that compete for labor.
In RimWorld, decoration raises colony wealth, and wealth raises raid points, so beauty carries a security cost.
Prosperity funds decoration, and decoration raises mood or ratings and so prosperity, a slow upgrade treadmill.
failure_modes: One object with the best beauty per cost dominates, so players spam it regardless of how the space looks.
Proximity rules that count only a hot spot, such as scenery near a ride station in RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, reward decorating one spot and ignoring the rest of the ride.
Beauty values that disagree with the art (an ugly-looking object rated beautiful) break trust in the system.
If the score is hidden, decoration reads as optional and the mechanic goes unused.
name: Decoration and beauty
open_questions: Can a vision model score the composition of a space instead of summing per-object beauty values, and would players accept its judgment?
Does generated decor reduce the asset cost enough to make beauty a deep system rather than a spam target?
player_experience: Cosmetic choices get a mechanical payoff, so players dress up rooms and paths and watch moods or ride ratings rise. The tension is between beautiful and efficient: every statue costs resources and floor space that production could use.
summary: Decorative objects and scenery carry beauty values that are aggregated over tiles, rooms, or radii and feed agent mood or ratings.

synergy.note: Room quality depends on furnishings and beauty, rewarding interior design.

claims.text: Stellaris launched with a limit on directly controlled core worlds, beyond which penalties applied, and sectors run by governors who develop planets under a player-set focus and taxation.

definition: The player assigns a subsystem (a city, sector, colony, fleet, department, or set of planets) to an AI controller and sets objectives and constraints: a focus, a budget, permissions, and policies. Each decision interval the controller runs the same decision logic the game's opponent AI uses, restricted to that subsystem, and issues actions on the player's behalf. State owned: assignment, goal settings, and permissions per delegated unit; the rest is read from the subsystem. Inputs: subsystem state and player settings. Outputs: build, research, production, or movement actions. Canonical forms: Stellaris sectors, which a 2016 dev diary justified with a core-world limit and in which sector governors develop planets and build mining stations under a player-set focus, Hearts of Iron IV battle plans executed by AI-controlled generals, automated workers in the Civilization series, Football Manager staff responsibilities, and automated traders and miners in X4: Foundations.
design_levers: granularity of goals: single focus, weighted priorities, or explicit rules
permissions such as may build, may demolish, may spend reserves
transparency: whether the manager explains its choices
manager competence relative to a good player
incentives to delegate: hard limits on direct control versus voluntary convenience
ease of reclaiming control and per-item overrides
dynamics: Delegation allows simulations far larger than one player could micromanage, shifting play to allocation among managers.
Partial delegation creates principal-agent tension: players watch managers and intervene at thresholds.
Delegated units pursuing local goals can conflict with each other, such as two governors competing for one resource.
failure_modes: Managers that underperform a competent player turn delegation into a penalty that players avoid at all costs.
Opaque managers make unexplained choices that players cannot correct without micromanaging.
Managers that are too strong remove the game: the optimal play is to delegate everything.
Forced delegation through control caps is widely resented; Stellaris sectors were reworked in later updates.
name: Delegation to AI managers
open_questions: Can language-model managers take natural-language mandates (keep morale high but never let the treasury go negative), explain their tradeoffs, and remain competent?
Does delegation to a learned policy trained against the game's simulation make managers better than humans, and what is left for the player if so?
player_experience: The player moves up a level of abstraction and manages managers. Delegation trades control for attention and enables play at empire scale. When the AI does something dumb it feels like losing control; when it works it feels like governing.
summary: Subsystems are handed to AI managers or governors that pursue player-set goals within bounds.

tension.note: Automating a subsystem removes the skill expression that made it the point.

claims.text: Transport Tycoon pays for deliveries by delivery time as well as distance and cargo.
OpenTTD orders include transfer with partial payment for feeder services.

definition: Owns a payment table per cargo type (a base rate, a distance weight, and a value curve over time in transit) and computes revenue at delivery from quantity, base rate, and distance, multiplied by a time factor that falls as transit time grows; in common implementations the factor holds flat for a cargo-specific grace period before it declines. Fast-decaying cargo such as mail and passengers rewards short or fast routes, while bulk cargo such as coal keeps its value over long, slow hauls. Cargo moved in stages can be paid in parts at transfer points. Transport Tycoon (1994) pays by cargo type, distance, quantity, and delivery time, and OpenTTD keeps the model and adds transfer orders with partial payment for feeder services. It differs from vehicle-route-scheduling, which owns the order lists that move cargo, and from contracts-orders, which owns discrete jobs with fixed payouts and deadlines; here every delivery is priced continuously by how long it took.
design_levers: base rate per cargo type
shape of each cargo's value curve (grace period, slope, floor)
distance measure, straight-line between endpoints or route length
partial payment rules for transfers and feeder legs
inflation or era scaling of rates
dynamics: Cargo sorts by mode, with mail and passengers on fast services and bulk goods on slow ones.
Faster vehicles pay back through higher rates, coupling payment to fleet renewal.
Congestion and signal delays cost money directly, so network design is priced.
failure_modes: Paying by route length rather than endpoint distance rewards deliberate detours.
Near-identical curves make every cargo the same and remove route specialization.
Transfer credits shown at feeder stations can make feeder vehicles look profitable while the final leg shows a loss, confusing players about which vehicles earn money.
Decay so steep that slow modes earn nothing collapses mode choice to the fastest vehicle.
name: Delivery-time payment
open_questions: Could time sensitivity come from simulated recipients' needs, such as a town short of food paying more for fast grain, rather than fixed per-cargo curves?
player_experience: Speed has a price per cargo. The player matches cargo to mode, putting mail on fast trains or aircraft and coal on slow freight, and reads every delay at a junction as lost money. Upgrading to faster vehicles becomes an investment with a visible return.
summary: Payment for a delivery depends on cargo type, quantity, distance, and transit time, with each cargo losing value at its own rate the longer it travels.

definition: Each deposit holds a remaining quantity that every extraction cycle decrements. At zero the node disappears or the extractor stops; some games instead decay the extraction rate toward a floor. Factorio ore patches store an amount per tile that mining drills consume, while crude oil fields report a yield percentage in which 1% equals 300 pumpjack cycles and depletion stops at a 20% floor. Warcraft and Age of Empires gold mines and The Settlers II mountain mines run dry. Satisfactory is the counterexample: its nodes are infinite and differ only in purity. Inputs: extraction cycles. Outputs: remaining amount, current rate, and an exhaustion event that idles the extractors and any chain they feed.
design_levers: starting quantity per deposit and its distribution across the map
whether depletion ends output or decays the rate toward a floor
efficiency upgrades that change output per unit removed, such as Factorio mining productivity research
visibility of remaining amounts and warnings before exhaustion
whether deposits regenerate, can be rediscovered, or have substitutes
dynamics: Pushes expansion outward, which raises defense, logistics, and threat costs at new outposts.
Creates contested chokepoints in competitive maps as the last deposits run out.
Drives substitution toward recycling, alternate recipes, or trade once local supply ends.
Staggers rebuild cycles, giving long games a rhythm of boom at new sites and decline at old ones.
failure_modes: Depletion that is too fast makes relocation the whole game and punishes building anything permanent.
Depletion that is too slow is never felt within a session.
Hidden remaining amounts cause sudden collapses that read as bugs.
Infinite nodes or high rate floors remove expansion pressure, so the map stops mattering after the first claims.
name: Deposit depletion
open_questions: Can procedural geology models generate deposits whose size players can estimate from surface signals, turning prospecting into inference?
What depletion time relative to session length keeps relocation interesting rather than tedious?
player_experience: A visible timer the player cannot stop. Every mine is temporary, so the player keeps scouting, claiming, and rebuilding at new sites, and judges how much infrastructure a deposit deserves given how long it will last. Losing a key deposit mid-chain creates a scramble to relocate before stocks run out.
summary: Extractable deposits hold finite quantities and run out, forcing expansion, relocation, or substitution.

definition: The player builds a design (a coaster track, a bridge, a machine program), the game runs or analyzes it, and a metric vector is computed from what happened. Metrics gate success, set income, or rank the design. In RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, as documented by OpenRCT2, a test run yields excitement, intensity, and nausea from peak positive, negative, and lateral g, number of drops, highest drop, inversions, and nearby scenery; excitement stops rising after 9 drops and 6 inversions, is cut 25% when intensity exceeds 10 with further cuts at 11, 12, 13.2, and 14.5, and is halved when lateral g exceeds 3.1. Poly Bridge drives vehicles over a bridge and shows member stress under a budget. SpaceChem scores solutions on cycles, reactors, and instructions, and Opus Magnum on cost, cycles, and area. State: the design and its last metric vector; update: re-evaluate on test or edit.
design_levers: which metrics exist and how many are orthogonal
formula shape, caps, and penalties, such as excitement penalties for excessive intensity
hard pass or fail thresholds versus continuous scores
when evaluation runs: an explicit test run, continuous re-evaluation, or end of level
how much of each metric's derivation the game exposes
comparison against other players' results
dynamics: Designs converge on formula sweet spots, such as stopping at the drop and inversion caps that end excitement gains.
Multiple competing metrics produce distinct design schools, such as cheap versus fast solutions in Zachtronics games.
When ratings set prices or demand, design quality couples directly to the economy.
failure_modes: Players optimize the formula instead of the fantasy, producing designs that score well but look absurd.
A single scalar score collapses the design space onto one optimum.
Opaque formulas require community reverse engineering; RollerCoaster Tycoon 2's rating rules are documented in detail only through the OpenRCT2 project.
Scores that contradict intuition (a ride that looks thrilling rates low) make the simulation feel arbitrary.
name: Design performance rating
open_questions: Can a learned critic rate open-ended designs on qualities like elegance or thrill that hand formulas miss, without becoming a new exploit target?
Does showing per-term contributions to a score widen or narrow the range of designs players explore?
player_experience: Build, test, read the numbers, revise. Players learn the hidden physics through the scores, enjoy beating a threshold, and then chase better tradeoffs between metrics that pull against each other.
summary: Player-built designs are run or analyzed and scored on simulated metrics such as ride excitement, bridge stress, or cost and cycles.

synergy.note: Rating the assembled design closes the build-test loop.
Stress and load ratings turn structural rules into a score (Poly Bridge).

definition: The player paints a designation onto tiles or objects (mine, chop, harvest, build, haul, deconstruct, hunt) instead of commanding a specific agent. Each designation creates a job entry with location, type, required skill or tool, and priority. Agents that are free and allowed to do that work query the job pool, score candidate jobs by priority, distance, and reachability, reserve one, path to it, and execute it; the designation clears on completion. State owned: the set of designations and their job entries and reservations. Inputs: player marks; outputs: jobs consumed by agent action selection. Canonical forms: Dwarf Fortress dig, chop, and gather designations, RimWorld mine, cut, haul, and deconstruct designations, Oxygen Not Included errands with 1 to 9 priorities, Dungeon Keeper digging, and Going Medieval.
design_levers: per-designation priority levels
job claiming: nearest agent, best-skilled agent, or first free
reservation and timeout rules for unreachable or abandoned jobs
area painting tools versus per-object marking
whether designations wait on prerequisites (materials, tools) or fail immediately
interaction with per-agent work priorities and restrictions
dynamics: Throughput depends on agent count, travel, and hauling, so mass designation exposes logistics bottlenecks.
Accidental designations produce stories, such as mining into an aquifer or magma.
Order of designation becomes a planning skill, since agents take jobs in the order the claiming rule finds them.
failure_modes: Unreachable designations jam the queue and agents repeatedly attempt and abandon them.
Agents cross the whole map for a single low-value job because claiming ignores travel cost.
Large designations starve critical work such as feeding and hauling without clear priority overrides.
Players cannot see why a designation is not being worked: no one allowed, no path, or no materials.
name: Designation orders
open_questions: Can players state work goals in language (dig a three-room hall near the stockpile) and have a model translate them into designations reliably?
Which claiming rule best balances efficiency with legible agent behavior?
player_experience: The player states what should happen and watches agents figure out who and how. Painting a mine and seeing dwarves converge on it feels like management rather than puppetry, and the gap between intent and execution, such as a dwarf walking across the map for one job, becomes a source of frustration and stories.
summary: The player marks tiles or objects for work such as dig, chop, or build, and autonomous agents claim and execute the jobs.

synergy.note: Designated work creates items that must be hauled, chaining jobs.

definition: A machine is a tree of parts with a removal-order dependency graph, each part carrying a condition or fault state. A job arrives with symptoms; the player uses tests and tools to reveal hidden part states, removes covering parts in valid order, replaces or repairs faulty ones, reassembles, and verifies with a final test. In Car Mechanic Simulator 2018 and its 2021 sequel the player examines engine, suspension, and chassis, removes parts in a realistic order to reach a damaged component, buys a replacement or repairs it at higher levels, and uses a test track to find brake and suspension problems. PC Building Simulator applies the same loop to computers. Unlike diagnosis-treatment, the target is a machine whose state is fully deterministic once revealed. Inputs: fault state, symptoms, tools. Outputs: repaired machine, payment, and experience.
design_levers: how symptoms map to faults, and how many faults hide behind one symptom
tool set and what each test reveals
disassembly depth and how many parts block access
repair versus replace economics
job time limits and payment for partial fixes
dynamics: Players build mental models of real machine structure and speed up dramatically with experience.
Tool unlocks reshape the diagnosis strategy, since better tests skip disassembly.
Coupled with economy and workshop progression, choosing which jobs to accept becomes a planning layer.
failure_modes: When the game highlights faulty parts directly, diagnosis disappears and only the removal chore remains.
Deep disassembly for a single part becomes tedious once the novelty fades.
Faults that do not follow from symptoms make diagnosis guesswork.
name: Diagnose and repair
open_questions: Can fault states generated from a causal model of the machine, rather than authored per job, produce varied but solvable diagnoses?
Could a language-model customer describing symptoms in their own words make diagnosis a real inference task?
player_experience: Methodical, calm problem-solving with a clear finish. Players narrow down causes from symptoms, enjoy the order of unbolting and rebolting parts, and see a fixed machine run again. Learning the real structure of an engine or PC is part of the appeal.
summary: The player inspects a machine, finds faulty parts with tools and tests, disassembles in order to reach them, and repairs or replaces them.

synergy.note: Breakdowns create the repair work; repair makes wear a skill problem rather than a tax.

definition: Owns, per patient, a hidden condition, a set of symptoms (some visible, some revealed only by examinations), a diagnosis certainty or candidate list, and a deterioration timer. Each examination reveals symptoms or raises certainty at a cost in time and capacity; once certainty passes a threshold or one candidate remains, the patient goes to the matching treatment, whose success depends on staff skill or equipment. Untreated or mistreated patients worsen or die. Theme Hospital sends patients from a GP's office to diagnosis rooms, lets policy raise the required diagnosis level, and can kill patients when a guessed cure is wrong; Project Hospital has examinations uncover symptoms drawn from real medicine, tunes symptom overlap so one examination rarely settles a case, and requires finding dangerous hidden symptoms in time. Inputs are arrivals and examination capacity; outputs are cures, deaths, and throughput.
design_levers: number of conditions and the overlap of their symptom sets
information gained per examination and its time, cost, and capacity
certainty threshold for treatment and whether the player can override it
deterioration rate of untreated patients and the cost of misdiagnosis
staff skill and equipment effects on test accuracy and treatment success
dynamics: Diagnosis capacity becomes a bottleneck that creates queues, so room layout and staffing drive outcomes.
Guessing cures to clear queues trades throughput against deaths and reputation.
Contagious conditions couple diagnosis speed to outbreaks inside the facility.
failure_modes: Distinctive symptom sets let one examination solve every case, removing the uncertainty that defines the mechanic.
Opaque certainty math leaves players unable to tell whether a death was bad luck or bad policy.
Conditions are expensive to author, so case variety runs out and players memorize answers.
name: Diagnosis and treatment
open_questions: Can language-model patients that describe symptoms in their own words make history-taking a real diagnostic channel?
Can generated cases keep symptom overlap tuned so diagnosis stays uncertain but solvable?
player_experience: Detective work under time pressure. The player weighs another test against the risk of the patient worsening and decides when certainty is good enough to act. In management games the same choice becomes a policy over many patients: how much diagnosis to buy before treating.
summary: Patients present symptoms, examinations reduce uncertainty about a hidden condition, and the correct treatment cures it while wrong or late treatment harms.

synergy.note: Patients queue at each diagnostic step, so hospital layout is queue design (Theme Hospital).

definition: A card holds a prompt, two to four options, and per-option effects on meters, resources, relationships, or flags, sometimes with hidden or delayed outcomes. A deck sampler draws the next card by weights conditioned on state and history. In Reigns, advisors present cards that the player swipes left or right; each choice moves some of four meters (church, people, army, treasury), and the reign ends if any meter becomes completely full or empty, after which a successor continues with newly unlocked cards. FTL beacon events, This War of Mine encounters, and Paradox event pop-ups use the same option-and-effect format inside larger simulations. Inputs: current meters and flags. Outputs: meter deltas, flag changes, and the next card's eligibility.
design_levers: number of options per card and whether one is a safe default
how much of each option's effect is shown in advance (which meters, direction, magnitude)
effect magnitudes and whether meters fail at one bound or both
deck weighting, repetition limits, and state conditions for eligibility
delayed consequences that resolve cards later
dynamics: Two-sided meters push players to keep every value near the middle, which creates oscillation as they correct overshoots.
When eligibility depends on earlier flags, players steer toward or away from card lines across runs.
Inside a larger sim, choice effects feed other systems, so a cheap answer can surface as a crisis many turns later.
failure_modes: Repeated cards expose a small deck and turn dilemmas into memorized answers.
A dominant option on common cards removes the tradeoff.
Fully hidden effects make outcomes feel random; fully shown effects make them arithmetic.
Without a simulation underneath, choices do not interact and the format becomes a sequence of isolated quizzes.
name: Dilemma cards
open_questions: Can a language model write cards conditioned on live simulation state while keeping effects inside a balanced, typed budget?
How much effect preview maximizes deliberation time without reducing choices to arithmetic?
player_experience: Quick, weighty decisions where every answer costs something. Players weigh which meter can absorb the hit, try to predict hidden effects, and learn the deck over many runs. Two-sided limits, as in Reigns, make even popular choices dangerous.
summary: Discrete choice events present a situation with a few options that each shift meters, values, or flags in tradeoff.

synergy.note: Laws presented as dilemmas make policy a moral choice with permanent consequences (Frostpunk).

definition: The player maps controller or keyboard input to one character's locomotion (walk, run, jump, swim, fly) and interactions (pick up, use, attack, build) in real time. State owned: the avatar's position, velocity, facing, stance, and interaction target. Update rule: each frame, read input, apply a movement controller (kinematic or physics-based) subject to collision and terrain, and resolve interaction requests against objects in range. The world simulation runs around the avatar, often with only the area near it simulated in detail. It contrasts with overseer control, where the player commands at a distance. Canonical forms: Minecraft, Stardew Valley, The Long Dark, Subnautica, Valheim, and the farmer in Harvest Moon; hybrid games such as Satisfactory and Factorio put a factory builder in an avatar.
design_levers: movement speed, traversal options, and fast travel, which set how large the world feels
interaction reach and whether actions take time or animate
physics-based versus kinematic controller
whether the avatar has needs or survival meters
camera: first person, third person, or top-down
how much of the world simulates outside the avatar's vicinity
dynamics: The avatar's travel time becomes the hidden limiting resource, pushing players to build transport and automation.
Embodied presence makes environmental systems such as weather, temperature, and day-night directly threatening.
Avatar location sets what is simulated, so player movement shapes world state in games that simulate only loaded chunks.
failure_modes: Large worlds with slow movement turn logistics into walking chores until fast travel or automation unlocks.
Simulation limited to the avatar's surroundings freezes distant systems, breaking the illusion that the world runs without the player.
Avatar control competes with overseer tools in hybrid games, forcing awkward building from a character's viewpoint.
name: Direct avatar control
open_questions: Can learned motion models (physics-based character controllers trained by RL) give avatars natural interaction with arbitrary simulated objects without per-object animation?
In generative world models where the world is rendered from the avatar's action stream, what simulation persistence can survive outside the view?
player_experience: The player is in the world rather than above it. Scale, distance, and danger are felt in the body: a long walk to a resource, a fall, darkness. Systems are learned by touching them, and attachment shifts from managed agents to one's own character.
summary: The player directly controls one embodied character's movement and actions in the simulated world.

definition: Owns a lineage graph over characters, a succession law, and the mapping from the player's identity to a living character. When the player character dies, the law ranks eligible heirs by kinship, age, gender rules, or election; titles and assets are assigned, possibly split among several heirs; and control passes to the designated player heir. If no valid heir exists, the run ends. Crusader Kings III offers primogeniture, ultimogeniture, house seniority, three partition variants, and elective laws for feudal titles; the player continues as the player heir, normally the primary heir, and partition splits realms among siblings; with no valid heir titles pass to the liege, and the run ends without a playable heir. Reigns (2016) continues with a successor monarch who keeps unlocked cards. Inputs: lineage, laws, deaths. Outputs: the new player character, title distribution, opinion resets, claimants.
design_levers: succession law catalog and how players can change laws
what carries over to the heir: wealth, titles, opinions, skills, unlocks
partition versus single-heir distribution
opinion penalties and claimant uprisings at succession
game-over condition when no heir exists
dynamics: Rulers invest in heirs' education and marriages, coupling succession to lifecycle and romance.
Succession crises spawn claimant wars, connecting lineage to diplomacy and conflict.
Long runs become multi-generation stories that players chronicle as family histories.
failure_modes: Partition fragments a large realm into small pieces, which players experience as punishment and work around with exploits.
Successors who inherit everything make death meaningless.
Heir-killing exploits (arranging deaths to reach a better heir) become optimal play.
Sudden game over from a missing heir feels arbitrary if eligibility rules are opaque.
name: Dynasty succession
open_questions: Can generated character arcs give each heir a distinct reign narrative while succession rules stay mechanical?
How much should the heir inherit to keep death meaningful without punishing long-term investment?
player_experience: Death becomes a chapter break. The player plans for succession by raising, educating, and marrying heirs, fears the untested successor, and feels continuity through the dynasty rather than one person. Partition laws make every death a crisis of fragmentation.
summary: When the player character dies, play continues as an heir chosen by inheritance rules.

synergy.note: Inherited traits make succession a long-term breeding and planning problem (Crusader Kings).

definition: Owns an education level per citizen or the population's distribution over levels, and school capacity and coverage. Each period, school-age or eligible citizens with access and seats advance a level after a study period; capacity and budget limit throughput, and aging and migration change the mix. Jobs and buildings require minimum levels, so the distribution decides which industries can be staffed. Cities: Skylines uses uneducated, educated, well educated, and highly educated, with elementary schools of 300, high schools of 1,000, and universities of 4,500 seats; jobs carry education requirements, higher building levels need more educated workers, and citizens take lower jobs when nothing else is open. Victoria 3 moves literacy toward education access and grants pops qualifications for professions each month. Inputs: seats, budget, age structure. Outputs: the qualified worker distribution that labor matching reads.
design_levers: number of levels and job requirements per level
school capacity, upkeep, and study duration
who studies: age gates, coverage radius, cost to citizens
whether over-educated citizens accept lower jobs
side effects of education on crime, garbage, or consumption
dynamics: Education shifts the industry mix toward offices and high tech, changing pollution and land value.
Generational lag: the education mix follows age structure, so baby booms create later waves of graduates.
Mismatches between education and jobs produce unemployment and shortages simultaneously.
failure_modes: Over-education: when educated citizens fill matching jobs first, basic industry reports worker shortages while graduates compete for offices.
Long study times hide the lag between investment and effect, so players misread cause and effect.
Single-step jumps with large schools make education a one-time checkbox.
name: Education and workforce
open_questions: Can agent-level career choice and schooling decisions by learned agents replace fixed education ladders without losing planning legibility?
Which matching rule between education and jobs avoids both over-education collapse and meaningless education?
player_experience: The player invests now for a different city later: schools cost upkeep for years before industry can upgrade. Players watch over- and under-education and adjust capacity, policies, and job mix to avoid unemployable graduates or empty offices.
summary: Education levels gate job types, and schooling converts the labor pool into higher levels over time.

synergy.note: Education reshapes which jobs can be filled.
Children age into a workforce whose skills depend on schooling.

definition: Owns an election calendar, an electorate (simulated voters, voting blocs, or real players), candidates or parties, and a counting rule. At each election every voter's choice is computed from satisfaction, group membership, and campaign effects, or cast by a real player; the counting rule (plurality, threshold, single transferable vote) picks the winner, which sets tenure, a ruler, or party strength. Losing can end the game or remove the player's powers. Democracy 4 (2020) gives each simulated citizen membership in several overlapping voter groups, so elections depend on keeping enough groups content; before each election the player makes two promises, and broken promises raise cynicism. Frostpunk 2 (2024) has a council of 100 faction delegates vote on each proposed law, needing 51 votes, or two thirds for laws that expand the Steward's power. Tropico lets El Presidente hold or rig elections. EVE Online has real players elect the Council of Stellar Management, using single transferable vote since the eighth council.
design_levers: election frequency and whether the player can call, delay, or cancel elections
voter model: aggregate approval, blocs, or individually simulated voters with overlapping groups
franchise rules that decide who votes and with what weight
counting rule and thresholds
consequence of losing (game over, loss of office, reduced powers)
manipulation options such as rigging, promises, or campaign spending, and their costs
dynamics: Election cycles create policy rhythms: unpopular measures early in a term, giveaways before the vote.
Overlapping voter groups make every policy please someone and anger someone, which pushes players toward coalition math.
Promise systems couple short-term electoral gain to long-term credibility.
failure_modes: Elections that only test approval above 50% add a pass or fail check without strategy.
Cheap rigging or postponement removes the threat, so elections become a formality.
Real-player elections with low turnout let organized blocs capture outcomes, which can be accepted as play or felt as unfair.
name: Elections
open_questions: Can LLM-driven voters and rival candidates respond to the player's actual speeches and platform, so campaigning is persuasion rather than slider tuning?
How should simulated electorates balance realism (stable partisanship) against responsiveness to player choices?
player_experience: A deadline for popularity. The player tracks polls, times unpopular reforms for just after an election, courts swing groups, and feels the stakes rise as election day nears. In player-run elections the experience shifts to campaigning and alliance-building.
summary: Periodic votes by simulated or real voters determine tenure or policy.

definition: The player's continuous inputs (stick, wheel, pedals, mouse, motion controllers) drive the control surfaces or actuators of a physically simulated mechanism, and the challenge is the skill of producing good inputs, not choosing goals. State owned: mapping from input devices to actuator commands, including curves, deadzones, and assists. Update rule: each physics step, read inputs, apply response curves and optional assists (stability control, auto-trim, autopilot), and send commands to the mechanism model, such as flight aerodynamics or vehicle dynamics. Skill emerges because the mechanism has inertia, delays, and nonlinearities the player must learn to anticipate. Canonical forms: hand-flying in Microsoft Flight Simulator, X-Plane, and DCS World; driving in iRacing, Gran Turismo, and BeamNG.drive; and deliberately clumsy hand control in Surgeon Simulator.
design_levers: fidelity of the underlying mechanism model
assist layers that can be turned on or off (traction control, stability assist, auto-rudder, autopilot)
input device support and response curves
feedback channels: force feedback, motion, sound, and visual cues
deliberate awkwardness of control mapping for comedy, as in Surgeon Simulator
consequences of error: reset, damage, or permanent loss
