dynamics: Skill becomes a personal progression system independent of unlocks, sustaining long-term play in racing and flight communities.
Hardware investment (wheels, HOTAS, VR) forms around the mechanic and reinforces community identity.
Combined with damage models, small control errors cascade into dramatic, unscripted failures.
failure_modes: Keyboard or gamepad play of a mechanism tuned for wheels or sticks is nearly impossible, splitting the audience by hardware.
Missing tactile and vestibular cues make real-world techniques fail on screen.
Assists that are all or nothing leave no learning ramp between novice and full simulation.
name: Embodied skill control
open_questions: Can learned coaching models watch input traces and teach technique the way an instructor does?
Can adaptive assists, trained to keep the player near the edge of competence, replace fixed difficulty toggles?
player_experience: Competence lives in the hands. The player practices, crashes, and gradually internalizes how the mechanism responds until difficult maneuvers feel fluid. Mastery is personal and hard-won, and assists let novices participate before they have the skill.
summary: Real-time motor skill operating a simulated mechanism, such as hand-flying, driving, or surgery, is the main challenge.

synergy.note: Detailed handling models reward motor skill and hardware like wheels and pedals.

tension.note: Real-time motor skill and time compression are hard to offer together.
Turns remove the real-time pressure motor skill depends on.

definition: Owns each company's share count, share price, and ownership table. Share price is recomputed from company value (cash, assets, earnings, debt) and moved by trading pressure, so purchases raise it and sales lower it. Players buy and sell shares in their own and rival companies for dividends or gains. Crossing an ownership threshold, usually a majority, transfers control: the target is merged, its assets absorbed, or its owner eliminated. Railroad Tycoon (1990) starts each railroad with $1 million split between equity and a loan and lets players trade shares in themselves and rivals in a miniature stock market. Offworld Trading Company (2016) makes buyouts the win condition: a player who loses majority control of their own company is eliminated, and the game warns a player when a rival can afford to buy them out without telling the rival. Capitalism (1995) makes being bought out by a competitor a loss, and Transport Tycoon sells rival company shares in 25% blocks.
design_levers: share price formula (book value, earnings multiple, dividend yield, recent trading pressure)
price impact per share bought or sold
control thresholds and their consequences (merger, elimination, board control)
restrictions on buying, such as minimum company age or share blocks
dividends and buybacks as defensive tools
visibility of who owns what and warnings before a takeover
dynamics: Owning shares of rivals turns their success into the player's dividends, softening competition into partial alliance.
Late-game cash races emerge as players hoard money for buyouts instead of investing in production.
Buying back one's own stock converts operating profit into takeover defense, starving expansion.
failure_modes: A leading player can buy out weaker rivals early, ending the game before economic play matters.
AI companies that do not defend their float become free takeover targets.
Share prices driven only by book value can be gamed by moving cash into assets before a buyout.
name: Equity and buyouts
open_questions: Can learned or LLM-driven investor agents produce believable sentiment (bubbles, panics) without a hand-tuned price formula?
What takeover thresholds keep buyouts a threat without ending multiplayer games early?
player_experience: Reading a rival's balance sheet as a target. The player buys a rival's stock while it is cheap, defends their own float by buying back shares, and feels dread when a competitor's cash nears the price of a takeover. Endgames become races to accumulate cash.
summary: Companies issue shares whose price tracks performance, and players buy them for profit or accumulate a majority to take control of rivals.

synergy.note: Buyouts give competition a decisive end state (Offworld Trading Company, Capitalism).

definition: Owns a compute budget and the cost charged against it: a per-tick allowance with an optional carryover bucket, a time cost per operation, or a fixed capacity such as instruction slots or memory. Each run or tick the game charges each operation or program its cost; when the budget runs out the program is terminated, throttled, or simply takes longer in game time, and unused allowance may accumulate. Screeps gives each player a CPU limit per tick (20 without CPU Unlock), banks unused CPU in a bucket of up to 10,000, lets a tick draw up to 500 from it, and terminates scripts at the limit. The Farmer Was Replaced charges simulated ticks per operation: literals and assignment are free, arithmetic costs 1, and a successful move() costs 200. Autonauts caps each bot's program at 12 to 32 instructions by its head part. Bitburner charges each script a RAM cost that must fit on the server running it. Player-programming owns the language and interpreter; this mechanic owns only the metering, so one language can run under tight, loose, or no budgets.
design_levers: budget type: real CPU time, simulated tick cost per operation, instruction count, or memory
size of the per-tick allowance and of a carryover bucket that allows bursts
per-operation cost table, especially the ratio between cheap computation and expensive actions such as moves
overrun consequence: termination, throttling, or slower simulated time
how the budget grows: progression, hardware parts, or payment
dynamics: Players adopt caching, memoization, and scheduling patterns that resemble real systems engineering.
Expensive actions relative to computation push players toward code that plans a lot and acts rarely.
Communities share profilers and optimized libraries, spreading efficient patterns across players.
failure_modes: Budgets measured in real CPU time vary with server load, so the same code can pass or fail unpredictably.
Budgets that are too tight make debugging feel like fighting the platform rather than solving the problem.
When budget increases are bought, as with Screeps' CPU Unlock, competitive outcomes mix code quality with spending.
Cost tables that charge almost nothing for computation let players brute-force problems the budget was meant to constrain.
name: Execution budget
open_questions: When AI assistants write working code from a description, does the budget become the main remaining challenge, and does that keep programming games interesting?
Which budget types (time per tick, cost per operation, memory) teach the most transferable efficiency skills?
player_experience: Optimization becomes the game once the code works. Players profile, cache paths, batch work, and count moves, because the same behavior written more cheaply runs more units, farms faster, or fits on the bot. A routine that finally fits under the cap, or a tick that stops overrunning, feels like a real engineering win.
summary: Player-written programs are metered against a simulated compute budget, such as CPU per tick, tick cost per operation, instruction slots, or RAM, which makes efficiency the scarce resource.

definition: Owns a relation value for each pair of factions, the modifiers feeding it, and agreement states such as war, peace, truce, alliance, and vassalage. Events (trade, gifts, border friction, attacks, broken treaties) change the value, and many games drift it toward a baseline. A proposal is accepted when an AI evaluation combining relation, interests, relative power, and reputation passes a threshold. RimWorld faction goodwill runs -100 to 100: hostile at -75 or below, allied at 75 or above until it falls to 0; civil outlanders drift back into -50..50; trade gives +1 per 500 silver and returning a prisoner +12, while pirates stay at -100. Europa Universalis IV caps opinion at +200 and -200 with itemized reasons, adds 5 to alliance acceptance per point of diplomatic reputation, and allows a base of 4 diplomatic relations. Inputs: events, interests, power. Outputs: war declarations, trade access, military aid, coalitions.
design_levers: relation scale, thresholds for state changes, and baseline drift
modifier catalog and decay per event type
AI acceptance formula (relation, power, interests, reputation) and how much of it is shown
agreement types and their obligations, such as alliance calls to arms and truce lengths
limits such as relation slots or diplomat counts
dynamics: Coalitions against an expanding player form from shared grievances, a balancing loop on growth.
Alliance chains pull factions into wars they did not choose, producing cascading conflicts.
Trade raises goodwill, which opens more trade, a reinforcing loop between economy and diplomacy.
failure_modes: Gift exploits: money converts linearly into friendship, so diplomacy becomes a purchase.
AI that ignores its own interests or the balance of power feels suicidal, while AI that refuses for unshown reasons feels arbitrary.
Factions locked at permanent hostility remove diplomacy from most of the threat model.
Coalitions that form against the leader regardless of context read as rubber-banding.
name: Faction diplomacy
open_questions: Can language-model negotiators bargain, bluff, and keep commitments with players in ways players accept as fair and legible?
How should opinion and interest be separated so AI factions betray for reasons players can foresee?
player_experience: The player manages a web of relations as a resource: buying goodwill with gifts, timing betrayals, and reading acceptance breakdowns to see what a deal needs. Wars feel like consequences of accumulated grievances rather than random events.
summary: Factions hold relations with each other, and treaties, alliances, and wars follow from interests and opinion.

synergy.note: Standing with a faction gates treaties and trade.

definition: The world is a 2D grid where each cell stores a material id and sometimes temperature, velocity, or lifetime. Each update a cell applies its class rule: powders fall straight or diagonally, liquids fall then spread sideways and swap with lower-density neighbors, gases rise then spread, and solids stay. Reaction rules convert cells, such as fire igniting flammable neighbors and water turning to steam. In Noita (2019) liquids compare densities to swap, wood burns for a set time and is destroyed, and explosions turn pixels into collapsing sand. The world is split into 64x64 chunks with dirty rectangles, updated bottom-up across threads in four checkerboard passes, with each pixel able to move 32 pixels beyond its chunk. Rigid bodies made of pixels (Box2D) recompute their shape and split as pixels are destroyed. The Powder Toy (2008), with 258 elements as of 2025, is the long-running sandbox in this lineage.
design_levers: material catalog and per-material density, flammability, and melting point
update order and randomization, such as alternating left and right scans
reaction table between materials
simulation region: whole world or only near the player
whether mass is conserved
dynamics: Hazard chains such as oil fires spreading, steam forming, and floors collapsing.
Players engineer traps and terrain with the same rules that threaten them.
The level is permanently reshaped by play, so no two runs stay alike.
failure_modes: A fixed scan order biases movement in one direction unless it alternates or randomizes.
Compute limits restrict simulation to areas near the player, so distant regions freeze.
Chain reactions kill the player suddenly, which can read as unfair.
Rules that duplicate or delete material break conservation and enable exploits.
name: Falling-sand materials
open_questions: Can neural cellular automata or learned rules produce new materials with plausible behavior at runtime?
Can GPU compute extend per-pixel simulation to whole persistent worlds instead of the area near the player?
player_experience: Everything is simulated, so play becomes experiment. Players pour, burn, flood, and dig, and they die to chain reactions they set off themselves. Wonder and danger come from the same rules.
summary: Every pixel or cell holds a material whose class rule makes it fall, flow, or rise by swapping with neighbors, with reactions layered on top.

synergy.note: Per-pixel materials with reaction rules produce chemistry players can exploit (Noita, Powder Toy).

definition: Owns a burning state per cell, tile, or object (unburnt, burning, burnt), often with fuel and heat values. Each tick a burning unit consumes fuel and tries to ignite neighbors with a chance or rate scaled by their flammability, moisture, and wind direction; it goes out when fuel runs out or when water, rain, or firefighters remove it. Inputs are material flammability, weather, and suppression; outputs are destroyed structures and terrain, heat, and sometimes smoke or updrafts. SimCity spreads fire between flammable tiles and fire stations put it out; Breath of the Wild's chemistry engine lets fire change the state of materials such as grass, whose burning creates updrafts, and rain stops it; Far Cry 2 and Dwarf Fortress propagate fire through grass and trees.
design_levers: ignition sources and their rates: lightning, overheating, arson, player tools
flammability, fuel load, and burn duration per material
spread probability per neighbor and the wind bias on it
moisture and weather modifiers, such as rain suppressing ignition
suppression tools: water, firefighters, fire station coverage, firebreak materials
dynamics: Players build firebreaks and separate flammable storage, which changes settlement layout.
Fire couples with weather and terrain: dry seasons and wind produce larger fires, and rain ends them.
Players repurpose fire as a weapon or tool, such as burning grass under enemies or clearing forest.
failure_modes: Spread tuned slightly too high burns the whole map before the player can react; slightly too low makes fire a nonevent.
Fire that ignores construction choices, such as stone burning like wood, removes the decision space.
Large burning areas in cell-based implementations cost noticeable frame time during big fires.
name: Fire spread
open_questions: Can learned combustion and smoke surrogates make fire visually rich while its spread stays readable and controllable?
player_experience: A small spark becomes an emergency. The player races to contain fire before it reaches stockpiles or homes, or uses it as a tool: burning a field to clear it, lighting grass to drive enemies, or riding the updraft. Fire teaches the player to read the map as fuel and firebreaks.
summary: Fire ignites and spreads across flammable cells or objects at rates set by fuel, wind, and moisture, consuming what it burns.

synergy.note: Wind and dryness govern fire spread.

definition: The aircraft state holds position, attitude, linear and angular velocity, control-surface deflections, and engine state. Each physics step computes aerodynamic forces from airspeed, angle of attack, sideslip, and air density, adds thrust and gravity, and integrates six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body motion. Two families exist. Coefficient-table models look up lift, drag, and moment coefficients per flight condition. Blade element models, as in X-Plane, divide wings, control surfaces, and propellers into small elements, compute forces on each from aircraft geometry rather than relying only on performance tables, and sum them, so stalls, spins, and ground effect arise from the geometry. Arcade games use simplified models that keep the aircraft stable. Outputs are aircraft motion and instrument readings.
design_levers: model fidelity: arcade, coefficient tables, or blade elements
assists such as auto-trim, stability augmentation, and stall protection
stall and spin behavior near the edge of the envelope
weather and turbulence coupling
control response curves and input filtering
dynamics: Weather and terrain create emergent challenges such as crosswind landings and mountain wave turbulence.
System failures interact with aerodynamics to produce scenarios no one scripted.
Energy management becomes the core tactical resource in air combat.
failure_modes: Over-stable models feel on rails and remove the skill.
Without assists, high fidelity makes flight unflyable for new players.
Table-driven models misbehave in regimes outside their data, such as spins or ground handling.
Each new aircraft needs costly per-model tuning before it feels right.
name: Flight aerodynamics
open_questions: Can learned surrogates trained on computational fluid dynamics give accurate flight models for aircraft without hand tuning?
Can an AI instructor read the flight model state and coach novices through stalls and landings?
player_experience: Hands-on control with real consequences. Players learn energy management, trim, stall warnings, and landings, and skill grows visibly over hours. Arcade variants keep the feeling of speed without the workload.
summary: Lift, drag, thrust, and control-surface forces computed from airspeed and attitude govern aircraft motion.

synergy.note: A faithful flight model makes real procedures necessary rather than ceremonial.

definition: Fluid state is stored per cell (mass, depth, pressure, element) or as velocity and density fields. Cellular games move mass between neighbor cells in proportion to height or pressure differences and sort elements by density, as in Oxygen Not Included, where each cell holds one gas or liquid element with a mass, and Dwarf Fortress, where water depth runs from 1 to 7 per tile. Continuous solvers follow Jos Stam's Stable Fluids for games (2003): add sources, diffuse implicitly with Gauss-Seidel relaxation, advect semi-Lagrangian by tracing cells back through the velocity field, and project velocity to be divergence-free by solving a Poisson equation, which stays stable at any time step. Outputs feed breathing, flooding, pressure damage, and heat transport.
design_levers: representation: cellular mass transfer, particles, or velocity fields
grid resolution and update rate
one element per cell or mixtures
compressibility and pressure limits
viscosity and flow speed per fluid
whether mass is strictly conserved
dynamics: Leaks contaminate connected spaces and couple room layout to air quality.
Floods spread through open layers and paths and reshape priorities across a colony.
Coupled with heat, fluids carry temperature and drive phase changes.
failure_modes: Non-conserving rules let players delete or duplicate fluid, which becomes an exploit.
Fluid simulation dominates compute and forces small maps or reduced update rates.
Semi-Lagrangian solvers lose detail to numerical dissipation, so flow looks thick and smoothed.
Gases are unreadable without overlays, so players misjudge spreading hazards.
name: Fluid and gas simulation
open_questions: Can learned fluid simulators run 3D liquids at game budgets while conserving mass well enough for gameplay?
What overlays make invisible gas flow legible without constant mode switching?
player_experience: Managing something that spreads on its own. Players seal leaks, vent gases, pump floods, and plan around pressure they can only see through overlays. Small mistakes spread slowly, then all at once.
summary: Liquids and gases stored per cell or as fields flow, mix, and pressurize across space according to pressure and density differences.

synergy.note: Gases and liquids carry heat, so thermal management becomes plumbing (Oxygen Not Included).

definition: Pipes connect producers, consumers, tanks, and pumps into networks that carry one fluid type per segment. The update rule ranges from discrete packets to pooled segments to pressure solvers. Oxygen Not Included moves one packet of up to 10 kg per pipe segment per second, giving 10 kg/s per line, and exchanges heat between the liquid, the pipe, and its tile. Factorio 1.x simulated flow between adjacent pipes, so throughput fell with distance and depended on build order; Factorio 2.0 merges connected pipes into segments where producers push freely, consumers pull at a rate proportional to the fill ratio, and fluid does not propagate. SimCity games treat water and sewage as coverage networks; GlassBox modeled units of water as agents moving through pipes. Inputs: producer output, consumer demand, topology, pumps. Outputs: fluid delivered per consumer and stored per segment or tank.
design_levers: flow model: packets, pooled segments, or pressure simulation
throughput limits per pipe and whether distance matters
fluid mixing rules and penalties
pumps, valves, and priority controls
thermal and phase-change behavior in pipes
dynamics: Fluid networks couple to thermal systems, as when hot pipes in Oxygen Not Included cook a base or freeze lines.
Shared networks create priority conflicts between consumers.
Tanks act as buffers, changing timing behavior across networks.
failure_modes: Distance-dependent throughput with no in-game feedback, as in Factorio 1.x, made long pipelines fail mysteriously; the developers rewrote the system for predictability.
Accidental fluid mixing can contaminate a network permanently if cleanup is costly.
Pressure models that are realistic but invisible make players guess.
name: Fluid pipe networks
open_questions: Could learned fluid surrogates give pipe networks pressure realism at low compute while keeping behavior predictable?
Which fluid behaviors (pressure, mixing, heat) add decisions rather than confusion?
player_experience: Plumbing problems. Players learn that fluids behave differently from items: they mix, back up, and run out at the far end. When the model is predictable, routing is satisfying; when it is not, pipes become a source of mysterious shortages.
summary: Fluids such as water, oil, sewage, or gas flow through pipes with pressure or throughput limits between producers and consumers.

claims.text: Walter Bright's 1977 game Empire is credited as the earliest video game use of fog of war, and Warcraft and StarCraft keep previously seen areas visible as terrain while hiding changes to enemy units.

definition: For each player the world holds a visibility state per cell or entity, usually three-valued: unexplored, explored but not currently visible, and visible. Each tick visibility is recomputed from the sight radius of the player's units, buildings, and sensors, optionally modified by line of sight, elevation, weather, and target stealth. Visible cells show live state; explored cells show the last observed snapshot, so changes there go unseen. Inputs are observer positions and sensor ranges; outputs are a per-player view and a hidden-information gap between true and known state. Walter Bright's Empire (1977) is credited as the earliest use; Warcraft and StarCraft used the explored-but-stale shroud. In simulation games: Factorio's radar charts distant chunks slowly and keeps nearby ones live, unexcavated tiles in Dwarf Fortress stay unknown, and Against the Storm keeps forest glades hidden until opened.
design_levers: two-state (unexplored or visible) versus three-state with stale memory
sight radius per unit or building and terrain, elevation, and weather modifiers
radius check versus true line-of-sight raycasts
whether remembered cells show last-seen enemies or only terrain
reveal tools: scouts, radar, satellites, traded maps
whether the AI obeys the same fog or has full knowledge
dynamics: Hidden information enables ambushes, bluffs, and a scouting economy where information has a price.
Stale memory produces errors such as attacking a base that has since been reinforced.
Coupled with procedural terrain, fog turns every map into an exploration problem rather than a known layout.
failure_modes: An AI given full map knowledge to compensate for weak reasoning feels like cheating once players notice.
Fog that hides only static terrain becomes a one-time clearing chore with no lasting tension.
Cheap, fast scouts make fog trivial and reward spamming them.
In simulations whose threats are systemic rather than adversarial, fog adds travel tedium without decisions.
name: Fog of war
open_questions: Can learned opponents that keep beliefs about unseen state replace AI map-hacking without losing challenge?
If a generative world model creates unobserved regions only when observed, does fog become a generation trigger rather than concealment?
player_experience: The edge of the known map pulls the player outward. Scouting becomes a decision with costs, darkness reads as threat, and finding a resource deposit or an enemy base feels like discovery rather than lookup.
summary: Parts of the world stay hidden or stale until observed by the player's units, structures, or sensors.

synergy.note: Sensor coverage and concealment are central to operational play.

definition: Owns population counts per species (aggregate) or individual animals (agent-based) and a directed feeding graph of who eats whom. Each tick prey grow toward a carrying capacity set by plants or habitat, predators remove prey in proportion to encounters, and predators reproduce from food eaten and starve without it. The Lotka-Volterra form, published by Volterra in 1926, has prey growing at rate a and consumed at rate b times predators, and predators converting prey into growth while dying at a constant rate; the result cycles without damping. Games add carrying capacity, starvation, migration, and respawn so species do not drift to extinction. SimLife and Species: Artificial Life, Real Evolution let creatures eat each other on a shared map; Eco simulates plant and animal populations that players can overhunt; Viva Pinata attracts visitors and predators according to garden contents. Inputs are species, habitat, and harvesting; outputs are population trajectories.
design_levers: feeding graph topology: number of species, diet breadth, and omnivores
prey growth rate and carrying capacity from plants or habitat
predation efficiency and conversion of food into offspring
starvation and natural death rates, and the minimum population before extinction
immigration or respawn rules that rescue extinct species
aggregate populations versus individually simulated animals
dynamics: Trophic cascades: removing a top predator lets herbivores strip vegetation, which lowers carrying capacity for everything.
Player hunting or harvesting acts as an extra predator and can tip a stable cycle into collapse.
Coupled with habitat or climate change, species ranges shift and new feeding links form.
failure_modes: Undamped predator-prey cycles drift until a population hits zero, so ecosystems collapse without any player error.
Hidden population floors or respawns added to prevent extinction make overhunting consequence-free.
Long delays between action and population response hide cause and effect, so players read crashes as random.
name: Food web
open_questions: Can learned behavior models give individually simulated animals plausible foraging and avoidance at ecosystem scale without hand-written AI?
Which visualizations make delayed predator-prey feedback legible without population graphs?
player_experience: Tending a system the player cannot command. Adding a predator to fix overgrazing can crash the herbivores and then starve the predator a few generations later. The player learns to act through balance and delay, watches population graphs, and feels responsible when a species disappears.
summary: Species eat and are eaten along a feeding graph, so populations rise, crash, and oscillate under predator-prey dynamics.

synergy.note: Predation supplies selective pressure; selection reshapes the food web over generations.
Habitat defines which species can co-occur, which sets the possible food webs.

definition: A forecaster computes and displays projected future values of selected variables: days of food left at current consumption, next period's budget balance, upcoming temperature or storms, population trend, or completion time for a project. It owns a forecast method, a horizon, and a refresh interval, but no simulation state. Common methods are runway (stock divided by net rate), linear extrapolation of recent trend, lookup of an authored or pre-rolled schedule of events, and rarely a short simulated lookahead. Outputs are numbers, countdowns, or projected curves. Canonical forms: Frostpunk's temperature forecast showing cold snaps days ahead, budget projections in SimCity and Cities: Skylines, turns-to-complete counters in Civilization, and Football Manager's projected finances.
design_levers: forecast method: runway, extrapolation, authored schedule, or simulated lookahead
horizon length
accuracy and whether uncertainty is shown, such as ranges or confidence that improves with upgrades
which variables get forecasts
whether forecasts include the player's queued actions
proactive display versus on demand
dynamics: Players stock to the forecast horizon, so a forecast that underestimates causes synchronized shortfalls.
Forecast crises create preparation sprints followed by slack, a characteristic rhythm in survival city builders.
Shifting play from reactive to anticipatory raises the value of storage and buffers relative to throughput.
failure_modes: Linear extrapolation misleads when rates are seasonal or batched, producing false alarms or false security.
Perfect forecasts of every threat turn disasters into checklists with no uncertainty.
Noisy forecasts with no stated error teach players to ignore them.
name: Forecasting
open_questions: Can a learned surrogate of the full simulation give cheap probabilistic forecasts (a 70 percent chance of famine within two seasons) for coupled systems that games now only extrapolate?
What forecast accuracy maximizes preparation decisions without removing surprise?
player_experience: Monitoring turns into planning. The player sees the cliff before reaching it and acts early, buffers to the forecast horizon, and feels dread when the projection is grim. Surprise drops; preparation becomes the challenge.
summary: The interface projects future states such as resource runway, budget balance, or upcoming weather.

definition: The player picks a structure type, position, and usually rotation. The game tests the footprint against occupancy, terrain slope, required neighbors (road access, a water tile, an ore patch), and cost. A valid placement writes the structure into the occupancy grid or spatial index and deducts cost; demolition reverses it, often with a partial refund. Tile grids (SimCity, Factorio, RimWorld) make footprints exact; gridless placement (Manor Lords, Foundation) allows arbitrary angles and curved streets. A ghost preview tinted valid or invalid is the standard interface. The occupancy map is the input to pathing, coverage, adjacency, and room detection.
design_levers: grid, offset grid, or gridless placement, with or without snapping
footprint sizes and shapes, and whether rotation changes them
terrain rules: slope tolerance, water, and foundations
requirement rules such as road adjacency or resource tiles
demolition refund and rebuild cost, which set how much commitment a placement carries
dynamics: Early placements constrain later ones, producing path-dependent layouts and eventual rebuilds.
Space becomes a resource that players trade against throughput or beauty.
Players converge on standard modules, which leads to blueprint copying and sharing.
failure_modes: Gridless placement leaves slivers and gaps that waste space and look untidy.
Free demolition and full refunds remove commitment, so placement stops being a decision.
A red ghost with no reason given makes hidden placement rules feel arbitrary.
Permissive rules with abundant space make layout trivial.
name: Building placement
open_questions: Can natural-language or sketch placement ("put a market near the docks") keep the puzzle while removing the click cost?
Which footprint rules make gridless placement as plannable as a grid?
player_experience: A spatial puzzle with immediate feedback. Players plan space, fit footprints together, and live with early decisions as the layout fills. Gridless placement adds expressive freedom but also the chore of aligning things by eye.
summary: The player places discrete structures on a grid or freely, and placement constraints turn layout into a spatial puzzle.

definition: Player input (free text, a combination of objects, or a request) plus selected game context is sent to a generative model, usually a large language model, and the output is either shown as content or parsed into game state such as a new item, a combination result, or a rule change. AI Dungeon continues a story from Do, Say, Story, and See inputs, first on GPT-2 (1.5 billion parameters in AI Dungeon 2, 2019) and later GPT-3, with a player-editable memory field. Infinite Craft asks a model to name the result of combining two elements and records first discoveries. Suck Up! and Whispers from the Star use models to drive character responses. Key parts: a context builder, an output schema or parser, a cache that may make results deterministic, and moderation. Inputs: player request and context window. Outputs: text or structured content.
design_levers: what the model may change: presentation only, or typed game state through a constrained schema
caching and determinism: fresh generation per request versus a shared global cache
context and memory construction, such as summaries, retrieved facts, and player-pinned memory
moderation filters and their false-positive rate
model size, latency budget, and per-request cost
authored seeds, examples, and rules that anchor tone and balance
dynamics: Players treat the model as a system to probe, sharing prompts that produce surprising or broken outputs.
A shared global cache turns generation into a discovery race, with first discoveries as social status.
When outputs are typed into game state, they combine with other systems and can unbalance economies or progression.
failure_modes: Models forget earlier content beyond their context, so stories contradict themselves (a criticism of AI Dungeon).
Unprompted inappropriate output, and broad filters that flag harmless text, both damaged AI Dungeon's community in 2021.
Output that does not alter simulation state feels weightless, because nothing it says has consequences.
Per-request inference cost and latency limit how often generation can run and push it to servers.
name: Generative content on demand
open_questions: What output schemas let a model add items or rules to a running simulation without breaking its balance?
Can on-device models make generation cheap enough to run per tick rather than per player request?
How should generated content be persisted and versioned so that worlds stay consistent across sessions?
player_experience: Open-ended curiosity. Players try things no designer anticipated to see what the model will produce, and part of the fun is probing its boundaries. When the output changes game state, finds feel personal; when it is only text, players notice that nothing is remembered or consequential.
summary: A generative model creates new content such as text, items, recipes, or rules at runtime in response to player input.

synergy.note: Language input invites generated responses; generated content invites further language input.

tension.note: Generated content resists the authored preconditions event chains rely on.

claims.text: In Populous, raising and lowering land is the most basic power, mana comes from followers building houses, and increasing mana unlocks earthquakes, floods, swamps, and volcanoes.
In Black & White, villagers worshipping around the Temple generate power for miracles, which can be cast by gestures with the Hand.

definition: The player is an external force that cannot command agents directly but can cast powers on the world. State owned: a power pool (mana, belief, prayer power) and the set of unlocked powers with costs and cooldowns. The pool fills from a simulation quantity, typically the number or devotion of followers, and casting spends it to apply an effect at a target: raise or lower land, flood, earthquake, swamp, volcano, rain, lightning, heal, or summon. Effects then propagate through the other systems (terrain, hydrology, population). Canonical forms: Populous, where raising and lowering land is the basic power, mana comes from followers building houses, and more mana unlocks earthquakes, floods, swamps, and volcanoes; Black & White, where worshipping villagers generate power for miracles cast by gesture; From Dust; WorldBox.
design_levers: power source: followers, belief, devotion, or time
cost, area, and cooldown per power
unlock order of powers
whether powers are destructive, constructive, or both
casting input: menu, gesture, or physical manipulation
how much the world's systems amplify or resist each power
dynamics: Follower-funded power creates a reinforcing loop: help followers grow to gain power to help them more.
Terrain-altering powers chain into hydrology and settlement systems, such as floods that relocate a whole population.
In competitive god games, power denial (reducing enemy followers) matters as much as casting.
failure_modes: One dominant power used repeatedly trivializes opponents.
Gesture recognition that misreads input makes casting frustrating and unreliable under pressure.
Powers with fixed scripted effects feel like animations rather than interventions in a simulation.
name: God powers
open_questions: Can players describe a miracle in language and have a generative system produce effects grounded in the world's physics rather than from a fixed list?
How do learned agents that react to miracles, such as fear or worship, change the follower loop?
player_experience: The player feels large and indirect. Problems are solved by reshaping the world rather than ordering people, and destruction is satisfying. The loop of growing followers to earn more power to help or punish them gives a sense of patronage.
summary: The player spends a power resource on miracles that alter terrain, weather, or creatures.

synergy.note: Miracles that raise land or move water are terraforming delivered as power.

definition: Each household, residence, or population tier consumes a basket of goods at fixed per-capita or per-residence rates. Consumption draws from a market, warehouse, or delivered stock; the satisfied fraction of each need feeds population size, satisfaction, tax income, or eligibility to upgrade. Anno 1800 splits needs into basic needs, which raise inhabitants per house, and luxury needs, which raise taxes and happiness, and requires full houses before residents advance a tier. Caesar III houses evolve only when supplied with several food types and goods such as pottery, furniture, oil, and wine, and devolve when supply lapses. Victoria 3 pops buy goods from a market to meet their needs. Inputs: population counts and supplied goods. Outputs: stock drawdown, fulfillment ratios, and growth or downgrade signals.
design_levers: consumption rate per capita for each good and how it scales with tier
which needs are mandatory for population or upgrades versus optional bonuses
substitutability between goods (any of several food types) versus strict requirements
penalty curve for unmet needs: lost population, lower taxes, unrest, or downgrade
delivery path from stock to consumer: global pool, market radius, or walker delivery
dynamics: Population growth raises consumption, which requires more production, which requires more workers: the expansion loop of Anno-style builders.
Tier requirements create layered dependency trees that couple distant islands or regions through trade.
Shortages propagate to labor because unhappy or downgraded populations work less or leave.
failure_modes: Fixed rates make ideal ratios solvable once, after which consumption becomes a spreadsheet exercise.
Downgrade cascades, where one lapsed good devolves a district and collapses its labor supply, feel disproportionate.
Too many required goods per tier create micromanagement that crowds out spatial decisions.
name: Goods consumption
open_questions: Can learned demand models give populations preferences that shift with culture and events instead of fixed baskets?
What is the smallest basket that still produces interesting supply-chain planning?
player_experience: The population is a mouth the player must keep feeding at scale. Players compute production ratios, such as producers per hundred residents, and expand supply ahead of demand. Each tier upgrade raises income but adds new goods to the basket, so success creates the next shortage.
summary: A population consumes goods at per-capita rates; unmet consumption lowers satisfaction or blocks advancement.

synergy.note: Each tier consumes new goods, so advancement drives production expansion (Anno).

definition: Owns per-agent knowledge sets (facts, rumors, beliefs about events or other agents), optionally with source and confidence, and the social graph they travel over. When two agents interact, each fact the speaker holds passes with a probability set by salience, relationship, and personality, possibly distorted; receiving a fact can trigger opinion or memory updates. Most games skip this and treat events as known to all: Comme il Faut's social facts database in Prom Week records every event as known to every character. Generative Agents (2023) shows diffusion through language-model conversation: over two game days, awareness of a Valentine's Day party grew from 1 to 13 of 25 agents and of a mayoral candidacy from 1 to 8. Inputs: interactions, event salience, the social graph. Outputs: who knows what, reputation and opinion effects that lag the event, misinformation.
design_levers: transmission probability per interaction and decay of salience over time
graph structure: who talks to whom in households, workplaces, and gathering places
distortion rate and whether sources are tracked
which facts are worth gossip and how they change opinions
player tools to plant, suppress, or trace rumors
dynamics: Information cascades through social hubs such as innkeepers and leaders, so centrality determines influence.
Lagged knowledge lets players act before consequences arrive, enabling crime, deception, and damage control.
Distorted rumors create conflicts over events that did not happen as told.
failure_modes: Slow or patchy propagation makes consequences feel disconnected from actions.
Untraceable chains make reputation changes look random.
Tracking every fact for every agent costs memory and update time in large populations.
Language-model gossip can invent facts that never happened and corrupt game state.
name: Gossip propagation
open_questions: Can language-model gossip be constrained to facts in the simulation log while keeping distortion as a designed, tunable variable?
What propagation speed makes consequences feel both earned and suspenseful?
player_experience: Actions have a spreading radius: a crime matters once someone talks, so the player manages witnesses, timing, and who to tell. Watching news reach a rival late creates suspense and room for deception.
summary: Information about events spreads through social contacts, changing what agents know and believe.

synergy.note: Reputation travels through gossip, so deeds have audiences.
What agents hear about each other changes how they feel.

definition: Owns a preference profile per species or crop (acceptable ranges or targets for terrain type, temperature, humidity, water, foliage, space, and company) and computes a suitability score for each tile, region, or enclosure by comparing local conditions to the profile, often as a weighted sum or as the worst single factor. The score gates where things can be placed or survive and scales growth, yield, welfare, or breeding. Zoo Tycoon and Planet Zoo grade each enclosure on terrain mix, foliage, area, and biome for each animal; Anno 1800 gives each island fertilities that decide which crops it can farm; Viva Pinata spawns a species only when the garden meets its requirements. Inputs are terrain and climate state; outputs are a scalar per location used by other systems.
design_levers: number of factors in the profile and how narrow each acceptable range is
combination rule: weighted average, product, or worst single factor
hard gate on placement versus soft multiplier on growth or welfare
how the score is shown: checklist, percentage, overlay, or only through outcomes
whether conditions change at runtime through seasons, climate, or terraforming
dynamics: Different profiles force specialization by location, which drives trade between regions or islands.
Coupled with climate or seasons, suitable areas move and populations must migrate or be relocated.
Players terraform to manufacture suitability, creating demand for terrain tools and materials.
failure_modes: Checklists with exact percentages become form-filling once the player knows the threshold values.
Averaging factors lets a perfect score on one factor hide a fatal mismatch on another.
Static suitability makes each location solved once, removing reasons to revisit it.
name: Habitat suitability
open_questions: Can species distribution models learned from ecological data generate plausible, varied requirement profiles for procedurally generated species?
player_experience: Matching puzzles on the map. The player reads a species' or crop's profile, then sculpts terrain, plants foliage, or picks locations until the indicator turns green. Unmet requirements show up as unhappy animals or missing harvests, so the player iterates on the place rather than on the creature.
summary: Species or crops thrive only where conditions such as terrain, temperature, water, and cover match their needs, scored per location.

synergy.note: Terrain edits change biome conditions, letting the player engineer habitats (Terra Nil, Equilinox).

definition: The player holds an inventory of components and a set of known recipes, each mapping an input multiset to an output item. A craft checks that inputs are present, any required station (workbench, forge, furnace) is nearby, and the recipe is unlocked, then consumes the inputs and produces the output instantly or after a short delay. Minecraft uses a 2x2 grid in the inventory and a 3x3 grid at a crafting table, with shaped recipes keyed to spatial arrangement; Don't Starve, Valheim, and Subnautica use menu lists gated by stations and blueprints; Ultima Online ties success to a crafting skill. Infinite Craft replaces the recipe table with a language model (Llama 2, later Llama 3.1) that generates the result of any new pair and stores it so every player gets the same answer. Inputs: carried items, station proximity, unlock state. Outputs: new items and consumed components.
design_levers: recipe count and depth of intermediate components
discovery model: all visible, unlocked by research or blueprints, or found by experimentation
station gating and whether stations must be nearby
craft time and whether crafts can be queued or batched
spatial grid versus list interface
inventory limits that bound how much can be carried to a station
dynamics: Tool tiers gate access to materials, which gate the next tool tier, producing a progression ladder from rules alone.
Inventory limits couple crafting to base building and storage chests.
In multiplayer worlds players specialize in crafting lines and trade, as Ultima Online crafters did.
failure_modes: Hidden recipes without in-game discovery aids push players to wikis, as in early Minecraft before its recipe book.
Long chains of trivial intermediates turn crafting into inventory sorting.
Crafting that is strictly better than found loot, or strictly worse, makes one of the two systems irrelevant.
name: Hand crafting
open_questions: Can generative models produce open recipe spaces like Infinite Craft whose outputs also have balanced, mechanically meaningful stats rather than only names?
How should discovery be explained to players when a model rather than a table decides what a combination yields?
player_experience: Gathering with intent. The player looks at a desired item, works back to its components, and goes out to collect them, so the recipe list becomes a shopping list that structures exploration. The first craft of a new tool is a small power spike that opens the next zone or task.
summary: The player or avatar combines carried components into items from a recipe list, gated by workstations and known recipes.

definition: Items on the ground or in the wrong storage generate hauling jobs that name a source item and a destination with space. Idle agents with hauling enabled pick jobs by priority and distance, path to the item, carry up to their capacity, and deliver. Throughput is bounded by the number of haulers, walking distance, carry capacity, and competing work. RimWorld haulers move items to the highest-priority stockpile with space, even out of lower-priority stockpiles; Dwarf Fortress splits hauling into labors for stone, wood, food, refuse, and furniture; The Settlers passes every good from flag to flag along roads, with one carrier per road segment; Banished and Timberborn rely on laborers or haulers whose numbers set delivery speed. Inputs: item locations, destinations, agent availability. Outputs: item movement and a job backlog.
design_levers: carry capacity per agent and the effect of tools such as wheelbarrows or carts
job selection rules: priority, distance, or reservation
how many agents haul and whether hauling is a separate role
stockpile priorities and filters that generate jobs
whether production buildings have local storage or need pickup
dynamics: Distance between production and storage becomes a hidden cost, rewarding compact layouts.
Hauling competes with every other job, so labor shortages appear as slowdowns everywhere at once.
Coupled with needs, haulers take breaks, creating rhythmic dips in throughput.
failure_modes: Hauling backlogs are hard to diagnose because the bottleneck is spread across many agents.
Item ping-pong between stockpiles with similar priorities wastes agent time.
Agents abandoning urgent work to haul low-value items reads as AI stupidity.
name: Hauling jobs
open_questions: Could learned job dispatch reduce visible AI stupidity while keeping hauling a resource the player manages?
How should backlogs be visualized so players can find the true constraint?
player_experience: Watching the colony carry its own weight. Players notice that new production does not help when no one is free to carry it, then shorten distances, build local stockpiles, or assign more haulers. The constraint is visible on screen as piles of goods and idle workbenches.
summary: Agents pick up and carry items between locations via a job queue, making hauling capacity a hidden throughput constraint.

synergy.note: Where stockpiles sit determines how much hauling labor the colony spends.

definition: Each cell, room, or object holds a temperature and often mass, specific heat capacity, and thermal conductivity. Each tick heat flows between neighbors in proportion to the temperature difference and a conductance from both materials, and temperature changes by heat divided by mass times heat capacity. Thresholds trigger melting, boiling, freezing, damage, and effects on agents. In Oxygen Not Included a tick is 0.2 s; cell-to-cell transfer uses q = dT x dt x k x 1000, multiplied by 25 between solids and gases and 625 between liquids; transfer stops below a 1 C difference or 0.1 DTU, and one tick may close at most a quarter of the difference. Insulated tiles divide conductivity heavily. RimWorld holds one temperature per room that equalizes with outdoors through walls and doors and is driven by heaters and coolers.
design_levers: per-material specific heat capacity and conductivity
phase-change temperatures and their consequences
transfer multipliers between solids, liquids, and gases
tick length and per-tick caps for stability
insulation strength and environmental heat sinks
damage and agent thresholds
dynamics: Machines emit heat as a byproduct, so a growing industrial base slowly overheats itself.
Seasons, fire, and magma couple to temperature and drive phase changes and evacuations.
Heat moved by fluids links plumbing layout to thermal management.
failure_modes: Rounding and phase-change edge cases let players create or delete heat, which becomes a standard exploit.
Per-cell diffusion across a large map becomes a late-game performance cost.
Without overlays, rising temperature is invisible until a threshold fails.
If equilibrium takes far longer than a session, heat stops mattering; if it is fast, it becomes noise.
name: Heat transfer
open_questions: Can forecasting tools that project temperature trends turn slow thermal failure into a readable planning problem?
player_experience: Thermal engineering. Players insulate, vent, and cool, and they watch overlays for creeping heat. Late failures arrive slowly: a base heats a fraction of a degree per cycle until crops die or machines stop.
summary: Temperature diffuses between cells, materials, and objects by conductivity and heat capacity, and thresholds trigger phase changes and damage.

synergy.note: Temperature thresholds trigger material state changes and reactions.
Temperature drives rot rates.

definition: A recorder subscribes to simulation events, filters them by significance, and stores structured records (actor, action, target, place, time, cause) indexed by entity. Browsers present the records as biographies, site histories, and timelines; some games feed records back into play. Dwarf Fortress Legends mode lists historical figures, sites, artifacts, written works, regions, and civilizations, with Chronicles by Age, records the player's own fortress and adventurer achievements, and exports XML that can reach about a gigabyte for long histories. RimWorld records tales that its art system uses to describe what a sculpture depicts. Inputs: the event stream. Outputs: a queryable archive, generated descriptions, and knowledge that agents or items can carry.
design_levers: significance filter: which event types and thresholds get recorded
record granularity and causal links between records
retention policy and summarization as the archive grows
presentation: raw log, templated prose, timeline, or map
feedback paths: art, books, rumors, or agent knowledge drawn from the archive
export formats for external tools
dynamics: Players reconstruct and embellish stories from sparse records, and communities share them as written retellings.
Fed back into the world, records let artworks, books, and rumors reference real past events.
Third-party legends viewers and map tools grow around exported data.
failure_modes: Recording everything floods the archive with trivial entries and very large files.
Templated, tabular text is dry, so most players never open the browser.
Records without causal links list events but do not explain why they happened.
name: History chronicle
open_questions: Can language models turn structured event logs into faithful narrative summaries that do not invent causes?
Which significance measures best predict the events players later retell?
player_experience: Looking back over a run turns scattered events into a story. Players browse to find out who caused what, discover that a minor figure had a long history, and retell their runs to others. When chronicles feed art or rumors, players see their own history reflected inside the world.
summary: The game records significant simulation events into a structured history that players can browse and other systems can reference.

synergy.note: Directed incidents become chronicle entries, so pacing produces a retellable history.
Pre-play generated history populates the same archive that records play (Dwarf Fortress legends).

definition: After terrain and biomes exist, a coarse simulation runs the world forward for a chosen number of years: civilizations found sites, grow, migrate, trade, make war, and found religions, and a subset of individuals is tracked as historical figures with families, titles, kills, and relationships. The final state is the starting map for play, and the event log feeds a chronicle. In Dwarf Fortress the player sets history length (worlds of 1,000 or 10,000 years are possible), populations and deaths counters rise during generation, only part of each site's population becomes historical figures (nobles, megabeasts, villains, their families), and a cap with optional culling limits their total. Caves of Qud generates sultan histories and Crusader Kings seeds dynasties from authored history instead. Inputs: map, races, parameters. Outputs: sites, factions, figures, artifacts, and an event archive.
design_levers: history length in years
number and type of civilizations and their behavior rules
which individuals are tracked as historical figures and the cap on their count
abstraction level of populations, battles, and trade during generation
event types simulated (wars, migrations, religions, artifacts, monsters)
how much of the generated history is revealed versus discoverable in play
dynamics: Generated grudges and alliances set the political situation the player starts in, so two seeds play differently.
Historical figures and artifacts become quest targets, visitors, and threats during play.
Players share notable generated histories as stories in their own right.
failure_modes: Long histories take a long time to generate and produce very large saves.
Coarse rules can produce degenerate worlds, such as one civilization conquering everything or all civilizations dying out.
History that never surfaces in play is invisible effort.
name: Simulated history generation
open_questions: Can language models turn coarse simulated histories into readable myths and chronicles without contradicting the record?
What is the cheapest history abstraction that still yields grudges and relationships players recognize in play?
player_experience: The world feels older than the player. Ruins, feuds, and legendary artifacts have causes the player can look up, and players discover that the world they inherited contains specific grudges, heroes, and lost wars. Long generation times build anticipation.
summary: World generation simulates years to centuries of civilizations, figures, and events before play begins, producing the starting world.

synergy.note: Generated terrain constrains where simulated civilizations settle, fight, and leave ruins.

definition: Owns water depth per cell on a terrain heightfield, often with source and sink rates, flow velocity, and soil moisture. Each tick water moves from higher to lower surface height between neighboring cells, evaporates, and is added by springs, rain, or rivers; moisture spreads from water to nearby land and gates crop growth. Timberborn links each tile to its four neighbors by virtual pipes, ticks every few hundred milliseconds, evaporates water, and runs recurring droughts that switch sources off and grow harsher; dams, levees, and floodgates regulate flow, and moisture falls off with distance and sharply uphill. From Dust and Cities: Skylines also simulate terrain water, while Pharaoh schedules a yearly Nile flood that waters floodplain farms. Inputs are terrain, sources, weather, and player structures; outputs are water levels, floods, and moisture.
design_levers: grid resolution and tick rate of the flow solver
source strength schedules, including drought and flood cycles and how fast they ramp
evaporation rate, seepage, and moisture spread distance
structures: dams, levees, floodgates, pumps, canals, and their flow controls
whether water erodes or deposits terrain
dynamics: Upstream structures change downstream conditions, creating spatial dependencies across the map.
Reservoir capacity becomes a stock that buffers seasonal or drought variability.
Flooding couples with building placement, farmland, and disasters such as dam failure.
failure_modes: Fixed flow values on structures cause oscillations and waves; Timberborn's developers avoided hard-coded dam values for this reason.
Abrupt switching of water sources makes water slosh unrealistically; Timberborn ramps source strength down before a drought starts.
Water that leaks through gaps or ignores terrain edits reads as a bug and breaks trust in the system.
Large water grids can dominate simulation cost and cap map size.
name: Hydrology
open_questions: Can learned shallow-water surrogates run large terrain water at interactive rates while staying predictable enough to engineer against?
player_experience: Engineering with a moving material. The player shapes terrain and builds dams to store water for dry spells, protects low ground from floods, and watches a mistake travel downstream. Droughts turn reservoir size into the main survival question, and a dam failure is a visible, traceable disaster.
summary: Water flows across terrain and through rivers by height differences, producing floods, droughts, irrigation, and dam management.

synergy.note: Reshaping terrain redirects water, so terrain editing becomes water engineering (From Dust, Timberborn).

definition: Owns an attractiveness score per settlement or region, computed from jobs, housing vacancy, wages or standard of living, services, happiness, and reputation, and a flow rule that turns the score difference against an outside reference or other regions into arrivals and departures per period. Arrivals usually need free housing, and departures follow sustained low scores. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, residential migration rises and falls with employment, the ratio of jobs to residents. Victoria 3 moves pops within a market toward states with higher migration attraction, set mainly by standard of living, while migration laws filter who may move. RimWorld instead adds colonists through storyteller events such as wanderers joining. Inputs: jobs, housing, satisfaction, policy. Outputs: population inflow and outflow by type.
design_levers: factors in the attractiveness score and their weights
reference point: a fixed outside world, competing regions, or other players
flow elasticity per unit of score difference
housing requirement and arrival batch size
selectivity: which classes, cultures, or skills migrate, and policy filters
dynamics: Growth raises demand for services and jobs, which lowers attractiveness until supply catches up, a balancing loop.
Booms and busts as migration lags job creation.
Inter-regional competition: improving one region drains its neighbors.
failure_modes: Overshoot: migration responds fast to jobs, then unemployment spikes, then emigration, oscillating.
Unconditional arrivals make population trivially easy and remove the planning puzzle.
Opaque scores leave players unable to tell why people leave.
Mass arrivals overwhelm services in one step and trigger cascades.
name: Immigration by attractiveness
open_questions: Can migration models calibrated to real census or survey data make city builders useful for planning education without hurting playability?
How should attractiveness be explained so players can attribute departures to causes?
player_experience: The player grows population indirectly by making the place worth moving to, and loses it the same way. Growth feels earned and fragile: a housing shortage or unemployment spike shows up as people leaving.
summary: Population arrives or leaves based on attractiveness such as jobs, housing, and happiness relative to alternatives.

definition: Owns, per creature, a tree of body parts with hit points, tissue layers, or functions, plus a list of conditions such as cuts, burns, fractures, bleeding, infection, scars, and missing or artificial parts. Damage lands on a sampled part; part health feeds capacities such as consciousness, moving, manipulation, sight, breathing, and blood pumping, which scale work speed, combat, and survival. Each tick bleeding drains blood, infections race against immunity, and tended wounds heal. RimWorld derives capacities from parts: consciousness below 30% keeps a pawn from waking, moving below 15% incapacitates, each arm supplies half of manipulation, blood pumping at 0% is fatal, poor tending raises infection and scarring risk, and each bionic leg adds 12.5% moving. Dwarf Fortress damages tissue layers per part; Project Zomboid tracks wounds per body region. Inputs are damage and treatment; outputs are capacity multipliers, pain, and death.
design_levers: granularity of the body tree: regions, organs, tissue layers
mapping from part damage to capacities and from capacities to actions
bleeding rate, infection chance, and healing rate, and how treatment quality modifies them
permanence: scars, lost parts, chronic pain
replacement options such as prosthetics, bionics, and transplants, and their availability
dynamics: Injured agents work slower, lowering output and raising pressure on healthy ones.
Demand for medicine, doctors, and prosthetics creates a medical economy.
Disabilities shape character identity and the stories players tell about them.
failure_modes: Too many parts and conditions make the health screen unreadable, so players cannot tell what is lethal.
Fine-grained damage with high lethality makes outcomes feel like dice rolls, such as death from one hit to a vital organ.
Permanent disabilities without replacement paths make injured characters dead weight the player discards.
name: Injury body model
open_questions: Can language models narrate injuries and recovery so deep body models stay legible without a dense health tab?
player_experience: Injuries become specific stories: a colonist missing a hand works slower, a hunter with a shattered leg cannot flee. The player triages by which wound threatens life first, stops bleeding before worrying about infection, and plans around lasting disabilities or replaces parts with prosthetics.
summary: Bodies are hierarchies of parts with their own damage, and wounds, bleeding, infection, and prosthetics change capacities such as moving and manipulation.

definition: Owns a set of groups within the polity, each with members, clout (political power), ideology or preferences over laws and policies, and approval. Clout is recomputed from members' wealth, numbers, and enfranchisement; approval from how well current laws match the group's preferences, whether it is in government, and events. Approval and clout gate what the player can do and trigger effects: favorable traits, petitions, obstruction, radicalization, or revolt. Victoria 3 (2022) is the canonical form: each pop gives political strength to the group it supports based mainly on wealth and the voting law, clout is the group's share of the national total and classifies groups as powerful, influential, or marginalized, marginalized groups cannot activate traits, and law enactment chances depend on the endorsement or opposition of groups in government. Tropico 6, Stellaris factions, and Frostpunk 2's factions are other forms.
design_levers: number of groups and how distinct their preferences are
clout formula (wealth, population, votes, offices held)
approval inputs (laws, government membership, events, promises)
effects at each approval and clout band (traits, petitions, obstruction, revolt)
how members move between groups as their economic conditions change
dynamics: Laws that empower a group raise its clout, which helps it block reforms that would weaken it, so institutions entrench.
Economic change moves people between groups, so industrialization shifts political power over decades.
Angry groups with high clout radicalize into movements that can force concessions or civil war.
failure_modes: When one group's clout dominates and nothing shifts it, politics freezes into one optimal coalition.
Approval effects that are too weak make groups ignorable, and too strong make reforms impossible.
Opaque clout and approval math makes political outcomes feel random without detailed tooltips.
name: Interest groups
open_questions: Can LLM-driven group leaders negotiate, make demands, and remember broken deals in ways that stay consistent with the clout and approval model?
Can interest groups form and dissolve from the population's actual interests rather than from a fixed authored list?
player_experience: Governing through coalitions. The player reads which groups are strong and what they want, brings friendly groups into government, placates or marginalizes opponents, and accepts that every reform makes someone angry. Power is never absolute.
summary: Factions within a polity have clout and preferences over policies, and their approval gates what the player can do.

synergy.note: Policies gain or lose group approval, so lawmaking becomes coalition management.
Alienated groups radicalize into unrest.

definition: Owns the worker supply by type (education, class, or profession) and the job slots by type that buildings offer, and matches them. Unmatched workers are unemployed; unfilled jobs leave buildings understaffed, and output scales with staffing. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, Employment = jobs / (residents / 8) drives migration of (residents / 8) x (Employment - 1) per cycle, a labor ratio of residents to jobs clamped to 0-1.3 scales projected commercial and industrial growth, and unemployment is one of the problems citizens complain about. Cities: Skylines and Workers and Resources split workers by education, so a city without educated workers cannot staff offices or advanced plants. Victoria 3 hires pops into buildings by profession and wage, and Anno 1800 requires each residence tier to staff that tier's production buildings.
design_levers: number of worker types and whether higher types can fill lower jobs
staffing-to-output curve (linear, threshold, or minimum crew)
commute or catchment limits on which workers can reach which jobs
migration response to unemployment and vacancies
wages as a lever that shifts who takes which job
dynamics: Jobs attract migrants, migrants demand shops and services, and those create more jobs, producing boom cycles.
A large employer far from housing generates commuter traffic and congestion.
Education pays off with a long lag, so labor mismatches appear whenever the economy shifts.
failure_modes: Aggregate matching hides the cause of shortages, so players see idle buildings without knowing which worker type is missing.
Education systems that push the whole population past the available jobs can stall industry with no clear fix.
Instant matching removes the lag that makes workforce planning interesting.
name: Labor market
open_questions: Can agent-level career choice by learned or LLM agents produce realistic structural unemployment without hand-tuned migration formulas?
How much labor detail (types, commutes, wages) can players manage before the mechanic becomes opaque?
player_experience: Balancing homes against jobs. The player reads unemployment and vacancy numbers, builds housing or schools when factories sit idle, and learns that a new industry is useless without workers to run it.
summary: Workers fill jobs by type and education; mismatches create unemployment or labor shortages that throttle production.

definition: Owns a value per tile or block, recomputed periodically from distance to centers, nearby amenities and nature, and nuisances. In Micropolis, the open-source SimCity engine, each developed 2x2 block gets value = 4 x (34 - distance to the population-weighted center) + a bonus for nearby trees and water - pollution, minus 20 where crime exceeds 190, clamped to 1-250. The value then drives residential growth (value minus pollution, scaled and capped), picks which of four building quality tiers develops, raises tax revenue through the city average, and lowers crime, which is computed as 128 - land value + density - police coverage. SimCity 4 computes desirability separately for each wealth level, and Cities: Skylines levels up buildings partly on land value raised by services and parks and lowered by pollution and noise.
design_levers: components of the value formula (center distance, amenities, terrain, pollution, crime, noise) and their weights
radius and falloff of each amenity or nuisance
smoothing and update frequency of the value field
thresholds that map value to building tiers, density, or wealth class
whether value feeds taxes, rents, or residents' wealth directly
dynamics: Low value raises crime and crime lowers value, so neglected districts slide toward slums unless policing or amenities break the loop.
Rising value upgrades buildings and density, which adds traffic and noise that cap further gains.
Value-based tax revenue rewards beautification, coupling aesthetics to the budget.
failure_modes: Stacking cheap amenities such as parks in one spot maxes value and becomes a dominant pattern.
When the formula is visible only as an overlay color, players cannot tell which factor holds a block back.
A strong distance-to-center term makes every city look the same: dense core, poor fringe.
name: Land value
open_questions: Could a learned hedonic model trained on real property data give land values that feel like real cities, and would players accept its opacity?
Can land value include speculation and expectations, not only current neighbors, without destabilizing growth?
player_experience: Shaping neighborhoods. The player places parks, transit, and services to lift values, keeps factories away from homes, and watches shabby blocks turn into towers. Checking the land value overlay becomes a planning habit.
summary: Each location's value is computed from nearby amenities, nuisances, and access, and it drives density and building upgrades.

synergy.note: Zones develop according to land value, so placement decisions compound over time.
Service coverage raises land value, rewarding complete coverage with density.
Pollution depresses land value, creating the industrial-residential separation puzzle.

definition: Owns each agent's age (or an age-structured population count) and a table of life stages with durations, capabilities, needs, and mortality. Each tick age advances; crossing a stage boundary changes what the agent can do (work, marry, study), what it needs, and how it looks; mortality rises with age until death. Births add agents through reproduction rules. The Sims 2 has seven stages (baby, toddler, child, teen, young adult with University, adult, elder): babies become toddlers after 3 Sim days, children become teens after 8, teens live 15 days, adults become elders after 29, and elder lifespan depends on the aspiration meter. Victoria 3 aggregates the same idea: natural growth is birth rate minus mortality, both falling as standard of living rises. Inputs: time, health, birth rules. Outputs: workforce and dependents, deaths, succession and inheritance triggers.
design_levers: number and duration of life stages relative to the game calendar
capabilities and needs per stage, such as child labor rules or elder frailty
mortality curve and whether death is fixed-age or probabilistic
birth rules and fertility windows
player controls such as aging toggles and lifespan settings
dynamics: Age structure sets dependency ratios that throttle labor and drive housing and school demand.
Founding cohorts create waves of births, retirements, and deaths that repeat across generations.
Deaths trigger inheritance, succession, and grief, coupling lifecycle to social and dynastic systems.
failure_modes: Lifespans short relative to play pace make characters die before players attach, so games add lifespan settings or aging toggles.
Demographic echoes: one founding cohort ages together and causes a labor collapse or mass death decades later.
Children are pure cost with nothing to do, so players avoid births.
name: Lifecycle and aging
open_questions: Can generative models keep a character recognizable across ages in appearance and personality while allowing growth?
What ratio of lifespan to play pace maximizes attachment and generational play?
player_experience: Time becomes personal: the player watches characters grow up and grow old, plans careers and heirs, and grieves. Aging turns a static roster into a pipeline in which the player raises the next generation of workers.
summary: Agents are born, age through life stages with different capabilities, and die.

synergy.note: Generations turn over, carrying inherited traits forward.
Families form and produce the next generation.

definition: Owns outstanding principal, an interest rate, a repayment schedule, and a borrowing limit. Each period interest is charged to the treasury, and principal is repaid on schedule, at will, or at bond maturity. The limit and rate often depend on a credit rating, net worth, or the number of outstanding loans. Missed payments trigger penalties, forced liquidation, bankruptcy, or game over. Railroad Tycoon (1990) starts each railroad with $1 million split evenly between equity and a loan and lets players sell bonds for more capital. SimCity 2000 adds bonds to the city budget, Theme Hospital offers loans through a policy setting, and Transport Tycoon lets companies raise and repay a loan in increments up to a cap.
design_levers: interest rate and whether it rises with debt load, credit rating, or economic conditions
borrowing cap tied to net worth, rating, or a fixed limit
repayment structure (amortized, interest-only, bond maturity, repay at will)
default consequence (penalty, asset seizure, bankruptcy, game over)
priority of debt service relative to wages and services when cash runs short
dynamics: Leverage amplifies booms and busts: borrowed capital grows revenue faster but turns a demand dip into bankruptcy.
Rates that rise with debt load create spirals in which new loans pay old interest.
Interest acts as a money sink that drains surplus in the late game.
failure_modes: Cheap debt with high early returns makes borrowing the maximum at the start a dominant opening in many tycoon games.
Default with no warning or recovery path ends runs abruptly and teaches players never to borrow.
Fixed rates in a growing economy make debt irrelevant once revenue scales.
name: Loans and debt
open_questions: Could AI lenders that assess a player's plans and history negotiate terms in language, making credit a relationship rather than a slider?
What rate curves keep leverage a real choice across a whole game rather than an opening move?
player_experience: Betting on the future. The player borrows to build faster than income allows, watches interest eat margins, and times repayment. A downturn while leveraged turns a confident plan into a scramble to stay solvent.
summary: Capital can be borrowed at interest with repayment schedules, so leverage accelerates both growth and failure.

definition: Owns the rules applied to an entity's assets at death: which items are destroyed, which drop into a container (corpse, tombstone, wreck) at the death location, who may loot it and for how long, and what compensation applies, such as insurance payouts or protected items. On death the inventory is partitioned by those rules, a container entity is spawned with a despawn timer or permanence, and the character respawns elsewhere or not at all. Ultima Online left corpses lootable by other players and added item insurance in 2003; EVE Online destroys ships for good and drops part of the cargo and fittings in a wreck. Valheim leaves the player's items in a tombstone at the death site; Minecraft drops the inventory where the player died. Unlike permadeath, which removes the character, this mechanic removes or relocates possessions while the character usually continues.
