design_levers: share of assets destroyed, dropped, or kept
who can loot dropped assets and for how long before they despawn
insurance or protected-slot systems and their cost
respawn location relative to the death site
additional death costs such as skill or experience loss
dynamics: Asset destruction creates steady demand for replacements, sustaining player crafting and markets.
Corpse runs become memorable expeditions, often with friends.
Players match the value of a loadout to the risk of the area, producing cheap disposable kits for dangerous trips.
failure_modes: Full loot in open player-versus-player worlds lets strong players farm weak ones, a problem Ultima Online answered by splitting off the consensual-PvP Trammel facet in 2000.
Short despawn timers turn a death far from home into an unrecoverable loss that ends play sessions.
Players hoard their best gear and never use it, so the items the loss rule protects stop being played.
name: Loss on death
open_questions: Could AI-run recovery services or scavenger agents make dropped assets part of the world's economy rather than a pure loss?
What mix of destroyed and recoverable assets keeps risk meaningful without driving players to hoard?
player_experience: Risk is measured in gear. The player decides what to carry into danger, keeps backups at home, and after a death makes a tense run back to recover a corpse or tombstone. In player-versus-player worlds the same rule makes every fight a gamble for the other side's equipment.
summary: When a character or ship is destroyed, its carried or fitted assets are lost or dropped at the death site for the owner or others to recover, with insurance or retrieval rules as softeners.

definition: Owns, for each producing machine, a set of modifier slots or settings and the effect vector they sum to: speed, productivity (extra output per cycle), energy use, and sometimes pollution or quality. Cycle time divides by one plus the speed bonus, productivity fills a bonus bar that yields free outputs, and power draw scales with the boost, often superlinearly. Satisfactory clock speed runs from 1% to 250%, each of up to three Power Shards raises the cap by 50 points, and power scales with exponent 1.321928, so 250% draws 335.77% of base power. Factorio fills module slots with speed, productivity, efficiency, or quality modules, beacons project module effects onto nearby machines, and productivity bonuses are capped at +300%. Dyson Sphere Program coats items with proliferator so machines consuming them gain extra products or speed. Captain of Industry spends Unity on building boosts. Unlike production-chain, which owns recipes and buffers, and quality-tiers, which owns item grades, this mechanic owns the cost-benefit curve of pushing a single machine harder.
design_levers: shape of the power or cost curve per unit of boost, linear or convex such as Satisfactory's exponent of about 1.32
separate effect axes (speed, productivity, efficiency, pollution) and the tradeoffs bundled into one slot
slot counts per machine and whether boosts can be shared with neighbors, as with beacons
cost of the boost itself: crafted modules, rare world pickups such as Power Shards, or a currency such as Unity
caps on stacked bonuses, such as Factorio's +300% productivity limit
which machine types accept boosts: assemblers, drills, labs, turrets
dynamics: Players trade space for power: compact boosted builds compete with sprawling unboosted ones.
Productivity bonuses on late stages save every upstream input, so players boost the end of a chain first.
Boosting a bottleneck moves the bottleneck to power generation, coupling factory design to the grid.
failure_modes: Productivity bonuses that stack without a cap create net-positive loops; Factorio caps productivity at +300% to prevent this.
One dominant configuration, such as productivity modules everywhere with beacons for speed, becomes a solved template.
Convex power costs that are not shown make overclocking feel like a sudden grid failure.
Boosts gated on rare pickups push players into exploration chores unrelated to factory design.
name: Machine boosting
open_questions: Can planners that solve module and clock settings for a target rate coexist with players who enjoy solving them by hand?
Which cost curves keep boosted and unboosted builds both viable through the late game?
player_experience: An optimization layer on top of ratio planning. Players decide whether to build more machines or push the ones they have, weighing floor space and materials against a growing power bill. Slotting the last productivity module or overclocking a bottleneck machine is a satisfying fix, and the power spike that follows is the bill.
summary: Per-machine modifiers such as modules, beacons, clock speed, or coatings trade extra power, scarce items, or currency for faster or more productive machines.

definition: Entities carry material tags (wood, metal, grass) and element states (burning, wet, frozen, electrified). A rule table maps element-material and element-element pairs to state changes applied on contact or within an area each tick. In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, Takuhiro Dohta described a chemistry engine beside the physics engine: physics is a rule-based movement calculator and chemistry a rule-based state calculator. Elements (fire, water, ice, electricity, wind) change the states of materials and of each other, and materials do not change each other. Divinity: Original Sin uses surfaces where oil burns and water conducts lightning. Outputs are state changes that trigger damage, movement, and new elements.
design_levers: number of elements and material tags
density of the interaction table: which pairs react
propagation: contact, area, or spread rate over time
duration and decay of states
how closely rules follow real-world intuition
how strongly reactions are telegraphed visually
dynamics: Chained reactions, such as fire on grass creating an updraft for gliding in Breath of the Wild.
Environmental kills and accidents emerge from mixing combat with terrain and weather.
Players find puzzle solutions designers did not plan.
failure_modes: An interaction that works in one place but not another breaks trust in the whole system.
Combinatorial growth of pairs produces untested reactions and bugs.
One reaction combo dominates combat and flattens choice.
Authored puzzles with single intended solutions conflict with systemic shortcuts.
name: Material interactions
open_questions: Can a language model judge interactions for arbitrary pairs of materials at runtime while staying consistent across a session?
What is the smallest rule table that still produces chains players experience as emergent?
player_experience: Asking "what if" and having the world answer consistently. Players combine elements for creative solutions in puzzles and fights, and the satisfaction is in solutions that feel discovered rather than designed.
summary: A rule table defines how elements such as fire, water, and electricity change materials and each other on contact.

claims.text: Satisfactory's Space Elevator has five Project Assembly phases that unlock tiers 3-4, 5-6, 7-8, 9, and the ending; phase 1 needs 50 Smart Plating, and phase 5 needs Nuclear Pasta, Biochemical Sculptors, AI Expansion Servers, and Ballistic Warp Drives.
Dyson Sphere Program solar sails are fired by EM-Rail Ejectors, last 5,400 seconds by default, and are absorbed permanently by completed shells, while Small Carrier Rockets build frames.
shapez 2 operator goal lines grow exponentially in cost per level, for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth.

definition: Owns one or more megaprojects, each a sequence of phases with large delivery requirements (item types and quantities, or energy), the deliveries accumulated so far, and the reward for each phase or the whole project (unlocks, power, a victory, or an ending). Delivered goods are consumed, so the project converts factory throughput into progress and gives an open-ended economy both a target and an outlet. Satisfactory's Space Elevator takes five Project Assembly phases, from 50 Smart Plating in phase 1 to Nuclear Pasta, Biochemical Sculptors, AI Expansion Servers, and Ballistic Warp Drives in phase 5, and its phases unlock tiers. Dyson Sphere Program builds its sphere from solar sails fired by EM-Rail Ejectors and frames carried by rockets, and sails expire after 5,400 seconds unless a completed shell absorbs them. shapez 2 operator goal lines grow exponentially in cost per level. Factorio's rocket silo is a similar sink for rocket parts. It differs from milestone-unlocks, which tests thresholds without consuming goods, and from goods-consumption, which feeds a population's recurring needs rather than a one-off structure.
design_levers: number of phases and the quantity curve across them (linear, geometric, exponential)
which goods are required and how deep in the production chain they sit
reward per phase (unlocks, power, cosmetics, an ending)
whether deliveries persist or expire, as Dyson sphere sails do
whether play continues after completion
shared versus individual progress in multiplayer
dynamics: Players design factories backward from the project's bill of materials, so it organizes the layout.
Exponential requirements push players to rebuild for throughput rather than add variety, as with shapez 2 operator levels.
Completed phases unlock technology that raises throughput for the next phase, a reinforcing ramp.
failure_modes: A finale that ends the game abruptly leaves large factories without purpose.
Requirements that only scale quantity turn the endgame into waiting rather than designing.
A phase gated on one bottleneck good stalls the whole project.
A sink too small to matter fails to absorb late-game surplus, so production has no outlet.
name: Megaproject sink
open_questions: Can megaproject requirements adapt to the player's factory so the finale tests its weak points rather than a fixed list?
Does an endless exponential sink keep factory games engaging longer than a fixed finale, or does it reduce play to scaling?
player_experience: A monument to throughput. The player reads the bill of materials, works backward through the factory to supply it, and watches a structure fill phase by phase. It turns an endless sandbox into a campaign with a finish line, or in endless versions a scoreboard of scale.
summary: A terminal construction absorbs very large quantities of produced goods in staged phases and serves as the long-run goal and output sink of a production game.

definition: Owns a per-agent list of memory entries, each with a type, a source (event, object, or other agent), an effect magnitude, a start time, and an expiry or decay. Events append entries; each tick expired entries drop and the active set is summed into mood or opinion, with stacking rules that cap and discount repeats. RimWorld memory thoughts list mood effect, duration, stack limit, and a stack multiplier (mostly 0.75): My son died is -20 for 30 days, Ate lavish meal +12, and some traits nullify specific thoughts. The Sims 3 and The Sims 4 show the same idea as timed moodlets. Generative Agents (2023) stores memory as a natural-language stream retrieved by the sum of normalized recency (decay 0.995 per game hour), language-model-rated importance (1-10), and embedding relevance, and writes reflections when summed importance exceeds 150. Inputs: events with sources. Outputs: mood and opinion contributions, and retrieved context for decisions and dialogue.
design_levers: magnitude and duration per event type
stack limit and multiplier for repeated events
decay shape (fixed expiry, linear, exponential) and which memories become permanent
trait filters that nullify or amplify memory types
retrieval weights (recency, importance, relevance) when memories drive decisions or dialogue
dynamics: One disaster writes negative memories into many agents at once, synchronizing their breakdown risk.
Players schedule offsetting positive events, turning mood into a budget managed against expiry timers.
Memories that name other agents seed opinions and grudges that outlive the event.
failure_modes: Long lists of small thoughts become noise that players stop reading.
Cheap positive thoughts (fine meals, art) are easy to farm and swamp negative events, draining drama.
Short durations make tragedies trivial; long ones create unavoidable spirals after a single disaster.
Natural-language memory streams grow without bound, raising retrieval cost and surfacing irrelevant memories.
name: Memories and thoughts
open_questions: How should natural-language memory streams be compressed so retrieval stays relevant across years of game time?
Which memories should be promoted from temporary modifiers to lasting personality change, and can that rule be learned?
player_experience: The player can read why an agent feels the way it does, line by line, and plans around expiry: a funeral penalty will pass in days, and a lavish meal can offset it now. Itemized memories turn hidden state into stories players retell.
summary: Events create itemized, time-limited mood modifiers or lasting memories that shape later behavior.

synergy.note: Itemized, expiring thoughts give mood a history the player can read and story-tell around (RimWorld).

definition: A milestone is a predicate over aggregate state (population at least 1,000, output of an item, cumulative revenue, a tier of residents) paired with a set of unlocks. State owned: the ordered list of milestones and which are reached. Update rule: periodically test the next milestones; on success, permanently unlock their content and notify the player. Unlike research, the player spends nothing directly; progress is a side effect of growth. Canonical forms: Cities: Skylines population milestones that unlock services, zoning types, policies, and map tiles; Anno resident tiers whose population thresholds unlock new buildings. Satisfactory names its HUB unlocks milestones, but they are paid for with item deliveries, which places them closer to a tech tree.
design_levers: threshold variable: population, output, money, or satisfaction
spacing of thresholds, linear or geometric
which content is gated and in what order
whether milestones can be lost if the variable falls back
option to disable gating for sandbox play
dynamics: Players inflate the gated variable artificially, such as dense cheap housing to reach a population tier, then rebuild.
Milestone order shapes city or factory layout, since early buildings lock in space before later ones arrive.
As a tutorial pacing tool it teaches systems in sequence; experienced players disable it.
failure_modes: Gating essential services, such as sewage or healthcare, behind milestones forces players to build broken cities before they can fix them.
Thresholds hit too quickly flood the player with unexplained tools.
Thresholds placed far apart produce long stretches of growing without new decisions.
name: Milestone unlocks
open_questions: Can milestones be selected adaptively from what the player has not yet engaged with, rather than fixed by the designer?
Does gating by behavior (built a working transit line) teach better than gating by aggregate size?
player_experience: Growth is rewarded with options. The player expands toward the next threshold, gets a burst of new tools, and learns systems in the order the designer chose rather than all at once.
summary: Reaching thresholds such as population, output, or score unlocks new buildings, areas, or features.

definition: Each unit is an agent with a platform record (speed, endurance, signatures), sensors with detection models against target signatures, weapons with ranges and hit or kill probabilities, and a doctrine or rules-of-engagement profile that governs when it fires and emits. The simulation advances in continuous or stepped time with acceleration; contacts are detected, classified, and engaged under that doctrine, often without per-shot player input. Command: Modern Operations, from Warfare Sims, gives operational control of units on a map of Earth through missions or direct orders, runs scenarios lasting hours to days with time acceleration, and draws platforms and weapons from databases such as DB3000; a Professional Edition adds database editing and Monte Carlo analysis for defense customers. Harpoon is the lineage ancestor. Inputs: orders, missions, doctrine settings. Outputs: detections, engagements, losses, and mission outcomes.
design_levers: fidelity of sensor and signature models
kill probabilities and countermeasure effects
doctrine, rules-of-engagement, and emission-control settings available to the player
database breadth and accuracy
time acceleration and command granularity (mission versus direct orders)
dynamics: Emission control creates cat-and-mouse play, because radiating sensors reveal the radiating unit.
Munitions and fuel limits turn engagements into logistics problems over long scenarios.
Monte Carlo repetition shows outcome distributions, so planning targets probabilities rather than certainties.
failure_modes: High fidelity buries the player in parameters, and new players cannot tell why an engagement failed.
Database errors or outdated data undermine credibility with expert players.
Automated unit behavior that ignores doctrine settings reads as the simulation disobeying orders.
name: Military operations
open_questions: Can reinforcement-learning opponents trained in operational simulators provide credible adversaries without scripted behavior?
Can language interfaces let players issue operational orders at the level of commander's intent?
player_experience: The player is a commander, not a pilot. They plan patrols, set emission and engagement rules, manage fuel and munitions, and watch detections develop, so most decisions concern information and timing. Success comes from planning; failure arrives as a missile on the screen that should have been detected earlier.
summary: Units with modeled sensors, weapons, platforms, and doctrine conduct operations at operational fidelity, mostly under player orders and automated behavior.

synergy.note: Operations stall when supply is cut.

definition: The game exposes two surfaces: data definitions for entities, recipes, and parameters that the engine loads at startup, and a scripting runtime that registers handlers for game events and calls an API to read and change state. Factorio mods use modified Lua 5.2 and pass through settings, prototype (data), and runtime (control) stages in a fixed lifecycle, with the runtime stage event-driven. RimWorld loads XML definitions and C# assemblies; Crusader Kings III exposes event, trigger, and effect scripting; Minecraft's Java Edition relies largely on third-party loaders. A mod manager resolves load order and dependencies. Inputs: mod files. Outputs: changed content, rules, and UI.
design_levers: surface breadth: data only, data plus scripting, or full code injection
sandboxing and determinism requirements, such as lockstep multiplayer
API stability and versioning policy
load-order and dependency management
distribution channel and discovery, such as an official mod portal or Steam Workshop
dynamics: Popular mods become de facto features, and developers later absorb them into the base game.
Moddable games keep long active communities and sales tails.
Mods expose and fix balance problems faster than official patches.
failure_modes: Game updates break mods, and players delay updating or abandon saves.
Large mod lists conflict and degrade performance in ways that are hard to diagnose.
Unsandboxed code mods carry security risk to players' machines.
name: Modding API
open_questions: Can coding models let non-programmers write working mods from natural-language descriptions against a documented API?
What API design keeps generated mods sandboxed, deterministic, and compatible across updates?
player_experience: Players reshape the game to their taste, from small fixes to total conversions, and the game keeps renewing years after release. Modders gain a creative outlet and an audience, and non-modders browse mod lists to assemble their own version of the game.
summary: Official hooks for scripts and data definitions let players change and extend the simulation's content and rules.

definition: A design is a set of parts joined at attachment points. Each part carries stats (mass, thrust, fuel, capacity, power, abilities) and sometimes a collision body. Behavior is computed either by aggregating stats or by simulating the assembled structure. Kerbal Space Program stacks tanks, engines, and decouplers into stages whose delta-v follows from mass ratios and simulates the craft as jointed parts. Besiege simulates blocks, hinges, and powered wheels as rigid bodies. Spore's creature editor grants abilities from attached parts. Armored Core assembles mechs from frame parts under weight and energy limits. Space Engineers builds small and large grids from blocks such as thrusters, reactors, conveyors, and deformable armor. Constraints such as budget, mass, power, or part count bound the design space.
design_levers: part catalog size and granularity
stat aggregation versus full physical simulation of the assembly
attachment rules: fixed nodes, free attachment, symmetry tools
constraints: cost, mass, energy, part count
test environment and how clearly failure causes are shown
dynamics: Players invent contraptions designers did not anticipate, such as flying machines in Besiege, and share them.
When parts are unlocked by progression, the assembly space widens over time and old designs get rebuilt.
Coupled with physics, small design changes produce large behavioral differences, which drives iteration.
failure_modes: Joint strength limits and physics instability in large assemblies make craft wobble or break apart; Kerbal Space Program players call unexplained destruction the Kraken.
Part count drives simulation cost, so ambitious builds slow the game down.
A dominant part combination becomes the only competitive build.
Catalog bloat buries useful parts and overwhelms new players.
name: Modular assembly
open_questions: Can reinforcement-learned controllers make arbitrary player-built bodies walk, swim, or fly convincingly at runtime?
Can generated parts with stats derived from their geometry replace hand-authored part catalogs?
player_experience: Tinkering and test-to-failure. Players build, watch the contraption flip, explode, or fail to lift off, diagnose why, and rebuild. A working design earns engineering pride, and many get shared.
summary: The player builds machines, vehicles, or creatures from parts whose stats and physical arrangement determine how the result behaves.

synergy.note: Physics decides whether an assembled machine works, so building becomes experimentation (Besiege).
Rocket design is meaningful because orbits demand specific delta-v budgets (Kerbal Space Program).

definition: Owns a per-agent mood value equal to a baseline plus the sum of active modifiers (needs, memories, environment, traits), usually smoothed toward that target, and a set of thresholds. While mood sits below a threshold a hazard rate rolls for a break whose severity rises with depth; during a break the agent leaves player control. High mood can roll for positive states. RimWorld: base mood 22 to 42 by difficulty; the bar moves toward its target at up to +12 per hour rising and -8 falling; break thresholds are 35%, 20%, and 5% (traits shift the minor one, capped 1-50%), with mean times between breaks of about 4, 0.8, and 0.5 days; above 49% mood, inspirations arrive with a mean interval of 410 - 400 x mood days and grant effects such as x1.8 work speed for 8 days. Dwarf Fortress keeps a hidden stress value, scaled by personality facets, that can end in tantrums or depression. Inputs: needs, memories, traits. Outputs: lost labor, destructive acts, temporary buffs.
design_levers: baseline per difficulty and weights of each mood input
threshold levels and trait offsets
hazard rate per band and severity table
break catalog (sad wander, binge, tantrum, violence) and whether breaks harm others
chance and size of positive states at high mood
dynamics: Breakdown contagion: breaks generate negative memories in witnesses that lower their mood, a reinforcing loop.
Players build mood infrastructure (recreation, beauty, fine meals) as defense, coupling mood to the economy.
Inspirations reward stable groups with bursts of output, so content colonies pull further ahead.
failure_modes: Cascades: one break creates negative memories in witnesses, and the group spirals beyond recovery after a random event, which feels unfair.
Mood that is easy to max removes the system from mid and late game.
Breaks that destroy hours of work feel punitive rather than dramatic.
Opaque mood sources make breaks feel random.
name: Mood and breakdowns
open_questions: Can breaks be generated as character-specific behavior by language-model agents instead of drawn from a fixed catalog, and still be legible?
What hazard shape keeps breaks dramatic without producing unrecoverable cascades?
player_experience: The player manages risk rather than events: watching mood bars near thresholds, removing stressors, and bracing when a disaster pushes several agents under at once. Breaks are memorable because they are partly random and partly the player's fault.
summary: Mood aggregates needs, memories, and environment, and crossing thresholds triggers mental breaks or inspired performance.

synergy.note: Unmet needs feed mood; breakdowns make neglect dramatic instead of a silent efficiency loss.

definition: Owns the mapping from a player utterance to a game-meaningful interpretation and the character's reply. A parser or model classifies free text or speech into intents, or produces an open reply, and the result updates character state, relationships, or plot. Facade (2005) maps typed text through about 800 hand-authored template rules (compiled to about 6,800 Jess rules) into 24 discourse act types such as agree, criticize, and flirt, plus a catch-all for non-understanding; the rules are permissive, accepting false positives to avoid non-understanding, and a drama manager sequences story beats from the result. AI Dungeon (2019) passes player text to GPT-2 and from 2020 GPT-3 to continue the story. Seaman (1999) took microphone input, and Suck Up! (2023) has players talk their way into homes of language-model characters. Inputs: text or speech, game state. Outputs: intent or discourse act, state updates, generated dialogue.
design_levers: interpretation target: a fixed intent set, discourse acts, or open generation
fallback behavior when input is not understood
grounding constraints that tie replies to game state and authored canon
input modality (typed or voice) and response latency
how strongly language outcomes change simulation state versus adding flavor only
dynamics: Players develop phrasing strategies (flattery, logic traps, role-play) that work as skill expression.
Language outcomes feed relationship and opinion systems, making conversation a primary social lever.
Players share transcripts, so interactions become community content.
failure_modes: Non-understanding loops: the system misreads input and the player rephrases repeatedly.
Open models drift from canon or game state and promise things the simulation cannot deliver; AI Dungeon was criticized for forgetting earlier content.
Players manipulate characters with meta-instructions, trivializing persuasion goals.
Moderation filters misfire; AI Dungeon's 2021 filter flagged harmless content.
name: Natural-language interaction
open_questions: How can free-form dialogue be grounded so that what characters say always matches simulation state and what they can do?
What evaluation shows that language input adds agency rather than guesswork compared with dialogue menus?
player_experience: The player says what they mean instead of picking from a menu, which raises both agency and anxiety: phrasing becomes a skill and characters can surprise. Misunderstandings and off-topic replies break immersion quickly, so players probe the system's limits.
summary: The player communicates with characters by free text or voice, and the system interprets intent and responds.

synergy.note: Free-text conversation can move relationship state in ways menu choices cannot enumerate.

definition: Owns no trait values itself; it is the rule that ties reproduction and death to how well an individual's traits fit the environment, so populations change without a designer choosing outcomes. Each generation, individuals that find food, avoid predators, and tolerate climate leave more offspring; with heritable variation the trait distribution moves toward fitter values, and when populations split by geography or genetic distance new species can form. Species: ALRE (Early Access 2018) charges energy for movement from skeleton forces and torques, lets creatures eat only within head reach, and defines species by interbreeding within a genetic distance. SimLife (1992) lets players edit genetics and environments and watch evolution. Spore (2008), by contrast, has players design creatures directly and is not natural selection. Inputs: heritable traits, environment, mortality and reproduction. Outputs: changing trait distributions, speciation, extinction.
design_levers: fitness sources (energy budgets, predation, climate tolerance, mate choice)
generation time relative to play pace
population size, which sets drift versus selection strength
speciation rule (genetic distance, geography)
player interventions such as culling, feeding, catastrophes, and nurseries
dynamics: Arms races between predator and prey traits.
Environmental shocks cause extinction and radiation into emptied niches.
Coupled with food webs, species composition and trait distributions shift together.
failure_modes: Evolution is too slow to see within a session, so players perceive nothing happening.
Degenerate optima: populations converge on one exploit body plan and diversity collapses.
Fitness hidden behind physics is opaque, so players cannot tell why traits win.
Games that call designed progression evolution set expectations they do not meet; biologists criticized Spore's model.
name: Natural selection
open_questions: Can learned simulators or GPU-accelerated physics make open-ended evolution fast enough to watch in a session?
What visualizations let players see selection pressure acting, not just its outcome?
player_experience: The player shifts from designer to gardener: setting conditions and watching which bodies and behaviors win. Results surprise and teach, as in finding why the long-necked line died out after an ice age.
summary: Differential survival and reproduction by fitness shifts trait distributions across generations.

synergy.note: Selection needs heritable variation; inheritance needs selection to produce adaptation.

definition: Each agent holds a vector of bounded need stocks (typically 0-100). Every tick each stock decays at a per-need rate, optionally modified by traits, activity, and environment. Actions or objects restore specific needs by fixed or quality-scaled amounts. Low values feed downstream systems: mood, action selection priority, health, or death.
design_levers: number of needs and which are lethal versus mood-only
decay rate per need and modifiers by trait, age, or activity
restoration amount and duration per action or object quality
threshold values that trigger warnings, priority overrides, or breakdowns
whether needs are shown as raw meters, icons, or only through behavior
dynamics: Synchronized decay creates rush hours at kitchens, beds, and bathrooms.
Needs compete for agent time, so throughput falls as needs rise, coupling productivity to comfort.
Better objects restore more per use, creating an upgrade treadmill.
failure_modes: Too many needs turn play into chore management with no strategic choice.
Uniform decay rates make every agent identical and remove personality.
Fast decay with slow restoration produces unavoidable death spirals early in a run.
Hidden needs read as random misbehavior when agents act on them.
name: Needs decay
open_questions: Can needs be inferred from behavior by learned agents rather than declared as fixed meters?
What is the minimal need set that still yields distinct personalities?
player_experience: Constant low-grade triage. The player reads meters, anticipates which need will bottom out first, and arranges the environment or schedule so agents can meet needs without supervision. Neglect is visible and personal.
summary: Each agent has needs such as hunger, energy, social, and fun that decay over time and are restored by actions.

synergy.note: Objects advertising need restoration turn decaying needs into autonomous, legible daily behavior (The Sims).

claims.text: Theme Park includes wage and supply negotiations.

definition: Owns a negotiation session: the terms on the table (wage, fee, price, length, bonuses, clauses), the counterpart's reservation value and preferred terms, a patience or round budget, and the outcome. Each round the player proposes terms; the counterpart accepts if the offer clears its reservation value and otherwise counters toward its preference, and patience falls with each round or with offers far from acceptable. When patience runs out talks end, sometimes with a consequence such as a strike, a lost transfer, or damaged goodwill. Reservation values come from simulation state such as the counterpart's ability, reputation, market rates, alternatives, and relationship with the player. Theme Park (1994) has wage negotiations with staff and supply negotiations, where failure brings strikes or lost shipments; sports management games run contract and transfer talks with players, agents, and clubs. It differs from staff-hiring, which owns the roster and wages once agreed, and from faction-diplomacy, which owns standing relations and treaty acceptance rather than a bounded bargaining session over terms.
design_levers: spread between the counterpart's reservation value and its opening demand
number of rounds or patience, and what drains it
how much of the counterpart's position is revealed (hints, agent comments, mood)
which terms can be traded against each other (wage, length, bonuses, clauses)
consequence of failure (walkout, strike, lost deal, damaged relationship)
whether rival bidders negotiate at the same time
dynamics: Reservation values tied to reputation and form make success raise future wage demands, a balancing loop on dominant teams.
Competing bidders turn talks into auctions that push prices up for scarce talent.
Failed wage talks cascade into service failures when staff strike, as in Theme Park.
failure_modes: Fixed, discoverable acceptance rules let players always find the minimum, turning talks into a ritual.
Refusals with no visible reason feel random and push players to accept the first offer.
Long multi-clause talks repeated for every signing become busywork.
AI counterparts that accept deals clearly bad for themselves break the economy.
name: Negotiation
open_questions: Can language-model counterparts bargain in natural language while their concessions stay consistent with a calibrated reservation value?
How much of the counterpart's position should be revealed so talks reward reading people rather than brute-force probing?
player_experience: A small poker game inside the management sim. The player probes how low a star will go, risks a walkout or a strike by pushing too hard, and weighs a deal now against losing the target. Talks put a face on the economy's prices.
summary: The player and an AI party exchange offers and counteroffers over wages, prices, or contract terms against the AI's hidden reservation value until a deal is struck or talks fail.

claims.text: The Sims 3 places households in a seamless open neighborhood, and its Story Progression keeps households the player is not controlling aging, working, and forming relationships.

definition: Owns a per-period update for agents or households outside the player's active simulation: unplayed households, agents beyond a radius, or regions not loaded. Instead of running needs, action selection, and pathing, each period it rolls life events for every off-screen unit from a table (age up, take or lose a job, move in or out, start or end a relationship, marry, have a child, die) with probabilities set by coarse state such as age, relationships, money, and household size, and writes the results straight into the shared state that the full simulation reads when the unit comes back into view. Many versions also manage population, moving households in when a town is sparse and out when it is crowded. The Sims 3's Story Progression keeps unplayed households aging, working, and forming relationships across its open neighborhood. It differs from lifecycle-aging, which owns life stages and mortality for every agent, and from autonomy-levels, which filters the choices of agents that are fully simulated; here simulation is replaced by event rolls.
design_levers: which event types may fire off-screen (aging, jobs, moves, romance, births, deaths)
event rates relative to the pace of played households
per-household or per-world opt-outs that protect characters the player cares about
population targets that move households in or out
fidelity of the off-screen model, from pure event tables to simplified versions of the on-screen systems
how off-screen events are reported (notifications, a newspaper, or nothing)
dynamics: Neighborhoods drift into new social graphs over generations, giving long saves a history no one played.
Players protect some households and leave others to the dice, producing a two-tier world of directed and generated lives.
Players install community mods that replace The Sims 3's Story Progression with per-household controls, which shows they want the surprises on their own terms.
failure_modes: Off-screen events split families or move away characters the player was invested in, which reads as the game vandalizing the save.
The off-screen and on-screen models disagree, so an agent returns in a state the full simulation would never produce, such as a job its skills cannot support.
Unreported events leave players unsure why the town changed and push them to wikis or mods.
Unbounded population management fills a town with generated strangers and dilutes authored characters.
name: Off-screen life progression
open_questions: Can a language model write coherent off-screen life summaries for unplayed agents that the full simulation can resume without contradictions?
How large a fidelity gap between on-screen and off-screen agents do players notice, and where does it stop mattering?
player_experience: The world feels lived in: visiting a neighbor reveals a new spouse, a baby, or a funeral the player never saw. The same rule also takes control away, since favorite characters can marry, move away, or die off-screen, so players either embrace the surprises or switch the feature off for the households they care about.
summary: Households or agents outside the player's active simulation advance through life events on a cheap stochastic model, so the world changes between visits.

definition: Owns, for each observer-target pair, a list of named modifiers, each with a value, a source, and an expiry or decay rate. Opinion is the clamped sum of static modifiers (shared traits, faith, dynasty, attraction) and event modifiers (gifts, insults, broken promises), and the list is shown as a tooltip. Event modifiers decay toward zero or expire; some are permanent. Crusader Kings III: most opinion decays to 0, tyranny decays 0.25 per month, Friend gives +60 and Nemesis -120, Broke Truce -50 for 3 years, faith hostility 0 to -30, Beautiful +30 attraction, and predecessor opinion is the only inheritable kind. RimWorld pawn opinions are built the same way from social thoughts such as insulted (-15 for 20 days) and deep talk (+15). Europa Universalis IV caps nation opinion at +200 and -200 with itemized reasons. Inputs: events, traits, relations. Outputs: one opinion number for AI decisions plus its legible breakdown.
design_levers: modifier catalog and magnitudes
decay or expiry per modifier and whether repeats diminish
clamp range and thresholds that change AI behavior
balance between static and event modifiers
which modifiers are hidden from the player
dynamics: Players time requests around expiry, waiting for a negative modifier to lapse before asking a favor.
Shared static modifiers such as faith and culture create blocs whose opinions move together.
Modifier accounting turns relationships into economic decisions priced in gold or prestige.
failure_modes: Additive stacking lets players farm cheap positives, such as repeated gifts or feasts, to override severe grievances.
Long tooltip lists overwhelm, so players read only the total.
Linear sums ignore context, so a murderer can be liked if enough small bonuses stack.
Hidden modifiers that contradict the visible list break trust in the itemization.
name: Opinion modifiers
open_questions: Can modifiers be generated from free-form events described by a language model while keeping magnitudes balanced and itemized?
Which nonlinear combination rules (per-category caps, context checks) keep opinions plausible without losing legibility?
player_experience: The player reads exactly why someone likes or hates them and treats opinion as an account: stacking small positives, waiting out a scandal, or choosing which grudge to pay off. Itemized lists make social systems feel fair and gameable.
summary: Opinions are sums of named, decaying modifiers from events and traits, itemized for the player.

synergy.note: Events add named modifiers, and modifiers gate later events, chaining stories.

definition: Each body holds a position and velocity under gravity. Under the patched conic approximation, used by Kerbal Space Program, each celestial body has a sphere of influence; inside it only that body's gravity is modeled, so the trajectory is an analytic conic propagated on rails, and segments are joined at sphere boundaries by matching position and velocity. This turns the n-body problem into a chain of two-body problems and cannot represent Lagrange points. Full n-body integration, as in Universe Sandbox or the Principia mod for Kerbal Space Program, integrates every body's gravity numerically. Engine burns change velocity, the rocket equation sets the delta-v budget, and maneuver planners preview the orbit that a planned burn will produce.
design_levers: patched conics or n-body integration
scale of the system; Kerbal Space Program uses a planet with a 600 km radius
time warp limits and whether thrust is allowed during warp
maneuver planning tools and how much they automate
atmospheric drag and its coupling to orbits
dynamics: Transfer windows create timing pressure and missions that run in parallel.
Delta-v couples orbital planning to vehicle design, so mission ambition shapes the rocket.
Gravity assists and aerobraking reward players who learn the system deeply.
failure_modes: Many players never get past the learning cliff without external tutorials.
Patched conics cannot model Lagrange points or halo orbits, which surprises experienced players.
Floating-point precision at solar-system distances causes jitter unless the engine re-centers the origin.
name: Orbital mechanics
open_questions: Can an AI mission planner that explains its burns flatten the learning cliff without removing the planning itself?
player_experience: A counterintuitive system that becomes mastery. Players learn that speeding up raises the far side of the orbit, plan burns on maneuver nodes, and earn rendezvous and landings through precise planning.
summary: Bodies move under gravity, and maneuvers spend delta-v to change orbits, intercepts, and transfers.

definition: Owns a period length and a set of update functions that run only when the period elapses. Between ticks the simulation runs continuously or not at all; at the tick, accumulated quantities settle: tax income and upkeep are booked, population grows, crops are harvested, research advances, or reports are produced. Hamurabi resolves a whole year per round: harvest, rats, immigration, plague, and starvation; SimCity books taxes and service funding at each year's budget; Paradox grand strategy games apply income and many modifiers on a monthly tick inside a daily simulation. Different systems can run on different periods in the same game. Inputs are activity accumulated during the period; outputs are discrete jumps in stocks and a report.
design_levers: period length, and whether different systems use different periods
which quantities settle at the tick and which change continuously
what the player sees at the tick: reports, prompts, or a forced pause
whether actions just before the tick can game the settlement
dynamics: Batched income creates sawtooth cash curves, so players keep buffers to survive between ticks.
Synchronized ticks across many agents produce simultaneous demand spikes.
Reports at each tick become the main legibility tool for slow variables.
failure_modes: Players time actions around a tick to exploit settlement rules, such as building just after upkeep is charged.
Large batched computations at the tick cause visible stutter in late game.
Long periods delay feedback until players cannot connect a decision to its result.
name: Periodic ticks
open_questions: Can learned surrogates settle long periods in one step so players can skip ahead without simulating every day?
player_experience: Bookkeeping beats. The player watches the date approach the next settlement, makes changes just before it, and reads the report afterward to judge the period. Ticks create small moments of anticipation and give a long continuous game recurring checkpoints.
summary: Some state changes, such as budgets, harvests, or growth, resolve in batches at fixed intervals like a month or a year rather than continuously.

definition: Death is an absorbing state: when an entity's health or survival condition fails, the entity and its accumulated state (skills, gear, relationships) are removed with no reload. Enforcement lives in the save system: Rogue deleted the save file when it was loaded, and modern ironman modes keep a single autosave. Two scopes exist. Avatar permadeath ends the run, as in FTL, which deletes the save when the ship is destroyed or all crew die, and Project Zomboid. Agent permadeath removes a member from a continuing game, as with RimWorld colonists, Dwarf Fortress dwarves, and Fire Emblem units. Softeners include FTL's clone bay, which revives crew with a skill penalty, downed states before death, and meta-progression that survives the run. Inputs: lethal events from combat, injury, or survival systems. Outputs: entity removal, run termination, or succession.
design_levers: scope: avatar death ends the run versus agent death inside a continuing game
save policy: single autosave, optional ironman toggle, or tolerated save scumming
what persists past death: unlocks, world state, heirs, or nothing
recovery tools such as revival with penalties, downed states, or medical rescue windows
replacement cost and time for lost agents
dynamics: Losing a key specialist cascades: a colony without its only doctor loses more colonists to untreated wounds.
Attachment plus loss produces the personal stories players share from colony sims and roguelikes.
Combined with procedural generation, it makes each run a fresh attempt rather than a retry of the same state.
failure_modes: A single high-variance event ends a long run, which reads as unfair rather than consequential.
Players back up and restore save files (save scumming), bypassing the design.
Fear of loss pushes players into slow, repetitive grinding instead of bold play; Richard Bartle's analysis of virtual worlds notes most MMORPGs avoid permadeath for this and retention reasons.
Bugs or connection drops that kill characters become catastrophic.
name: Permadeath
open_questions: Does making lost agents persist as memories, ghosts, or chronicle entries change how much risk players accept?
What variance profile of lethal events keeps permadeath consequential without making long runs feel like lotteries?
player_experience: Every risky decision carries weight because losses cannot be reversed. Players grow attached to named survivors, play more cautiously, and remember specific deaths as the turning points of a run. A loss late in a long run is the most memorable and the most frustrating moment the mechanic produces.
summary: Death of agents or the avatar is permanent, and the save system prevents undoing it.

synergy.note: Unique generated characters make permanent loss felt.

definition: Authoritative world state lives on servers that advance it continuously in real time; clients submit actions and receive updates, and changes such as built structures, market orders, territory, and destroyed assets persist for everyone. Design choices are shard topology and what the world does while a player is away. Eve Online runs one universe on the Tranquility server rather than parallel copies, takes it offline daily for maintenance, trains character skills in real time while players are logged out, and slows the server clock in crowded systems (time dilation) so large fights stay simulated; the Bloodbath of B-R5RB ran 21 hours. Ultima Online (1997), A Tale in the Desert, Second Life, and Eco are other persistent worlds. Inputs: concurrent player actions and world rules. Outputs: shared, durable state and history.
design_levers: shard topology: one universe, many parallel shards, or instanced zones
offline progression: what continues for absent players (skills, production, decay)
persistence scope: which changes are permanent versus reset
server tick rate and overload handling such as time dilation or queues
world resets, seasons, or wipes
rules for asset loss and protection of offline players
dynamics: Player-driven economies, wars, and politics emerge because consequences persist and accumulate.
Time-zone coverage becomes a strategic resource for groups that hold territory.
Persistent history makes notable events into community lore and news.
failure_modes: Early arrivals accumulate wealth and territory, and new players find no room to matter.
Load spikes in popular locations degrade simulation for everyone present.
Abandoned structures and items clutter the world without decay rules.
The world dies when concurrency falls below what its systems assume.
name: Persistent shared world
open_questions: Can AI agents that stand in for absent players keep a persistent world active at low concurrency without dominating it?
What offline progression rules keep a persistent world fair to players with little play time?
player_experience: Actions matter to strangers, and the world changes while the player sleeps. Players log in to see what happened, plan around other time zones, and take part in events, such as wars or market crashes, that no single player or designer controlled.
summary: A server-side world keeps running and keeps its state for many players, whether or not any one player is logged in.

synergy.note: A persistent world lets player markets accumulate history, monopolies, and scams (EVE Online).
Laws only matter where the world persists long enough to need governance (Eco, A Tale in the Desert).

tension.note: A shared persistent world cannot be paused or sped up by one player.

definition: Owns a small per-agent set of discrete traits or continuous personality dimensions, assigned at generation or during development. Traits hold no dynamics of their own; other systems read them as modifiers: they scale need decay, shift utility scores and break thresholds, nullify or add memories, change opinions of others, and unlock or forbid actions. The Sims (2000) uses points in opposing pairs such as nice/grouchy and active/lazy that scale object advertisements (Feed Fish gives 1-11 Fun by Playful); The Sims 3 lets adults hold up to five traits; RimWorld traits such as Steadfast and Nervous shift the mental break threshold, and Psychopath nullifies several death thoughts. Crusader Kings III characters tend to hold three personality traits gained through childhood events at ages 9, 11, and 13, opposites are excluded, and stress breaks can change them. Inputs: generation or life events. Outputs: differentiated behavior from shared rules.
design_levers: trait count per agent and exclusivity rules
magnitude of each trait's modifiers and which systems it touches
discrete traits versus continuous dimensions
acquisition: fixed at birth, childhood events, life events, or stress
visibility of traits to the player
dynamics: Traits that affect opinion create recurring frictions and friendships between particular pairs.
Players build around trait combinations, so traits become strategy as well as flavor.
Inherited or culturally transmitted traits drift across generations, coupling personality to lineage.
failure_modes: Strictly positive traits make recruitment a search for the same few, flattening variety.
Flavor traits with no mechanical effect feel fake; traits with huge effects dwarf player choices.
Too many traits per agent average out into bland behavior.
name: Personality traits
open_questions: Can a natural-language persona replace a trait list while keeping behavior predictable enough for players to plan around?
What is the smallest trait set that still produces distinct, recognizable characters?
player_experience: Traits are the shorthand by which players recognize and cast characters. The player reads a trait list, predicts behavior, and assigns roles; contradictory combinations become memorable, and players chase or avoid specific traits when recruiting.
summary: Fixed or slow-changing traits change each agent's needs, preferences, and available actions.

definition: Owns a small set of planet-scale stocks such as atmospheric gas fractions, greenhouse level, mean temperature, ice cover, sea level, and biomass, sometimes resolved on a coarse map grid. Each tick emissions, volcanism, and life change the gases, temperature follows radiative balance and albedo, and temperature moves ice, sea level, and where life can grow. SimEarth, advised by James Lovelock, shows gas levels as percentages, melts ice caps and raises seas under warming, cools the planet with volcanic dust, and offers a Daisyworld mode based on Watson and Lovelock's model, in which daisies of different albedo regulate temperature. Civilization added global warming from unchecked pollution; Surviving Mars: Green Planet terraforms by raising planetary parameters toward habitable targets; Eco lets player emissions raise sea level. Inputs are emissions and player projects; outputs are habitability and disasters.
design_levers: which planetary stocks exist and how many feedbacks link them (albedo, greenhouse, biosphere)
time constants between emissions and temperature or sea-level response
presence of tipping points or runaway regimes versus smooth response
player levers: emissions policy, terraforming buildings, direct parameter sliders
spatial resolution: single global numbers or a gridded map
dynamics: Biosphere-climate feedback can stabilize temperature, as in Daisyworld, or amplify change when it breaks down.
Climate shifts move habitat suitability, crop yields, and coastlines, forcing migration or rebuilding.
Shared emissions in multiplayer worlds such as Eco create commons problems between players.
failure_modes: Many coupled variables with long delays make cause and effect opaque, so players change sliders without learning what moved the planet.
Linear, delay-free responses reduce climate to a single meter to keep below a line.
Runaway feedback with no recovery path ends runs because of early mistakes the player could not see.
name: Planetary climate
open_questions: Can learned climate emulators give fast, plausible regional responses to player emissions without hand-tuned equations?
How short can feedback delays be made before climate stops reading as climate?
player_experience: Slow consequence at the largest scale. The player makes small persistent changes, such as emissions or terraforming projects, and watches planet-wide numbers creep toward thresholds where oceans boil, ice advances, or the planet becomes habitable. Success feels like stewardship; failure arrives long after its cause.
summary: Planet-scale variables such as atmospheric composition, temperature, sea level, and biosphere evolve under coupled feedbacks and can be deliberately altered.

definition: Owns per-market order books. Each order has an item, a price, a quantity, a location or range, and an expiry. A new buy order fills against the cheapest compatible sell order and vice versa; any remainder rests in the book. Transaction fees and sales taxes remove currency while NPC bounties and sales add it, so the operator manages faucets and sinks rather than prices. Players make nearly all goods, so prices emerge from their mining, manufacturing, hauling, and speculation. EVE Online (2003) is the canonical form: regional markets where players gather most raw materials and build nearly all ships, price history charts, and large-scale manipulation such as ramping and bear raids; its developer hired an economist in 2007 to monitor the economy. Ultima Online's player vendors and Albion Online's player-crafted gear economy are other forms.
design_levers: market topology: one global book, regional books, or local station markets with hauling between them
fees, sales tax, and order modification costs as sinks and anti-spam measures
how much NPC supply or demand exists to anchor prices
order range, duration, and how much order-book depth is visible
currency faucets (bounties, NPC sales) relative to sinks
dynamics: Trade hubs form where liquidity concentrates, as at EVE's Jita, which concentrates trade further.
Wars destroy goods and raise demand, coupling combat to manufacturing prices.
Speculators anticipate patches and events, so prices move before a change ships.
failure_modes: Faucets that outpace sinks inflate prices and devalue new players' earnings.
Low population leaves thin books where one player sets prices or nothing sells.
Bots and automated relisting dominate when order updates are free and fast.
Manipulation and scams drive away players who did not opt into that kind of play.
name: Player-driven markets
open_questions: Can LLM or RL trader agents supply liquidity for small servers or single-player worlds without becoming exploitable market makers?
Which sink and faucet controls keep a long-running player market stable without visible developer intervention?
player_experience: Being one trader among thousands. The player hunts arbitrage between regions, undercuts by a fraction of a unit, posts low buy orders and waits, and reads price charts like a real trader. Wealth comes from information and patience as much as production.
summary: Players post buy and sell orders in shared order books, and prices emerge from player behavior.

definition: Owns a set of player-authored laws, each a condition and an effect expressed in a structured rule language (for example: when a player fells a tree in district X, charge a tax or block the action), a proposal and voting procedure, and an enforcement hook that checks every relevant action against the active laws. A law passes when its vote meets the threshold set by the world's constitution or government type, after which the simulation enforces it automatically. Eco (early access 2018) lets players form governments and propose and vote on laws that restrict what other players can do or apply taxes and grants to specific actions, to manage an ecosystem that overharvest and pollution can damage. A Tale in the Desert (2003) let players petition and vote on laws that the developers then implemented.
design_levers: expressiveness of the rule language (which triggers, conditions, and effects are available)
voting thresholds, quorum, and who can propose
constitutional limits on what laws may do
enforcement mode: hard blocks, automatic fines, or reports for players to act on
how government offices are filled and how long laws persist
dynamics: Ecological or economic crises create pressure for regulation, and regulation shifts which professions are profitable.
Laws generate evasion strategies and loophole-seeking, which prompts amendments.
Factions form around legislative interests, producing persistent political rivalries.
failure_modes: A small active group can pass laws that grief or exclude other players.
A rule language too limited to express what players want pushes politics into informal agreements the game cannot enforce.
Low participation makes votes meaningless, and governance becomes the hobby of a few players.
name: Player legislation
open_questions: Can LLMs compile natural-language laws into enforceable rules faithfully enough that players trust the translation?
What constitutional constraints prevent minority capture without making legislation toothless?
player_experience: Politics with real teeth. Players argue about what should be allowed, draft rules, lobby for votes, and then live under the result. A logging ban or a carbon tax becomes a social contract that some players obey, some evade, and some campaign to repeal.
summary: Players author, propose, and vote on rules that the game then enforces inside a shared world, such as taxes, bans, and permits.

synergy.note: Organized player groups are the constituencies that write and enforce laws.

definition: An organization entity holds a membership list, a role table that maps roles to permissions (hire, spend, access storage, declare war), shared assets such as a treasury, hangars, or land, and optional revenue rules such as a tax on members' income. Organizations can nest into federations and act as parties to diplomacy and war. In Eve Online, a CEO runs each corporation and assigns roles such as director and accountant, corporations can tax members' earnings, declare war on other corporations for a weekly fee, and join alliances that claim sovereignty over null-sec star systems. Ultima Online guilds, Eco governments, and A Tale in the Desert's guilds are other forms. Inputs: membership and role changes, member income. Outputs: shared pools, permissions, and collective standing.
design_levers: role and permission granularity
shared asset types and access controls
organization taxes and costs of founding or upkeep
size caps and federation rules
war and diplomacy rules between organizations
protection against theft by members with access
dynamics: Specialization inside organizations, with miners, haulers, fighters, and diplomats, creates internal economies.
Coalitions form and split, producing large-scale political history.
Organizations act as onboarding for new players and as a reason veterans stay.
failure_modes: Coarse permissions let a single member empty shared storage; Eve Online has a history of such corporate thefts.
Large blocs coordinate so well that they lock smaller groups out of contested territory.
Leaders who quit leave organizations, and their assets, stranded.
name: Player organizations
open_questions: Can AI officers or members fill organizational roles in small groups without crowding out human players?
Which permission and asset rules best reduce insider theft while preserving trust-based play?
player_experience: Players belong to something larger than their own account. They take on roles such as leader, logistician, or recruiter, coordinate on projects too big for one person, and argue about governance. Betrayal and politics become play.
summary: Players form corporations, guilds, or governments with membership, roles, permissions, and shared assets.

claims.text: In Screeps each player's main module runs once per tick against a fixed game state, and queued commands are applied together at the end of the tick.
Screeps limits CPU per tick (20 without CPU Unlock), with unused CPU accumulating into a bucket of up to 10,000 that allows bursts up to 500 per tick.

definition: The player authors programs in a textual or visual language that the game interprets each tick to drive entities. State owned: program source, interpreter state (instruction pointer, registers, memory), and an execution budget. Update rule: each tick, run each program for up to a budget of instructions or CPU time, read sensors through an API, and issue commands that the simulation resolves. Languages range from real ones (JavaScript in Screeps and Bitburner, Python-like code in The Farmer Was Replaced) to assembly-like puzzle languages (TIS-100, Shenzhen I/O, Exapunks) and visual instruction tracks (SpaceChem waldos, Opus Magnum arms). Screeps is canonical for a persistent world: each player's main module runs once per tick against a fixed state, commands are applied together at tick end, and a CPU limit with a carryover bucket constrains computation.
design_levers: language: real general-purpose, constrained assembly, or visual
execution budget per tick (instructions or CPU milliseconds)
sensor and actuator API surface
debugging tools: stepping, logs, breakpoints, visualization
persistence: programs keep running while the player is offline
scoring of programs by size, speed, or cost
dynamics: Automation through code lets players operate at scales no one could control by hand.
In shared worlds, players' programs compete directly, producing an arms race of strategies and exploits.
Code sharing builds communities around libraries and frameworks.
failure_modes: A steep entry cost excludes players who cannot already program.
A real language with a rich API lets players import libraries and copied code, so the community's code replaces the puzzle.
Execution budgets set too tight make debugging feel like fighting the platform.
Weak debugging tools turn failures into opaque guessing.
name: Player programming
open_questions: When code assistants can write competent bots from a description, what remains of the programming puzzle, and does play shift to specification and review?
Can games teach programming effectively by letting AI assistants scaffold and then withdraw?
player_experience: The player designs behavior rather than performing it. Writing, running, and debugging a program that then works unattended is satisfying in a way direct control is not, and failures are logic errors the player can find and fix.
summary: The player writes code in a language the game executes to control units, machines, or the world.

synergy.note: Both express automation as logic; games that offer both span visual and textual programming.

definition: Owns a directed graph whose nodes are policies (with slider levels), simulation values (crime, GDP, pollution), situations, and voter groups, and whose edges are weighted effect equations. Each turn every node's value is recomputed as a function of its weighted inputs, bounded to a fixed range, and effects can be lagged or averaged over several turns; situations switch on and off when their input values cross thresholds. Voter-group happiness at the end of the chain sets approval and election results. Positech's Democracy series (2005-2022) is the canonical form: its designer describes it as a homebrew neural network in which voters, voter groups, policies, ministers, and events are neurons capped to 0..1 or -1..+1, with most logic in editable CSV files. Democracy 4 added fixed-income neurons that can exceed 1 because percentage effects on a 0-1 income scale gave wealthy voters more than poor ones.
design_levers: graph density: how many effects each policy and value has
effect equation forms (linear, power, threshold) and weights
delays and averaging per edge
value bounds and normalization
situation trigger and clear thresholds with hysteresis
how much of the graph is shown to the player
dynamics: Feedback loops between values (unemployment, crime, GDP) produce virtuous or vicious cycles across several turns.
Situations appear and vanish as values cross thresholds, creating emergent crises from slow drifts.
Overlapping voter-group memberships turn every policy into a tradeoff among coalitions.
failure_modes: Percentage effects on bounded values distort distribution, the problem that led Democracy 4 to add fixed-income values.
Dense graphs with small weights make most policies feel inert while a few dominate.
Long delays without visible pending effects make players misattribute causes.
name: Policy influence network
open_questions: Could learned causal models fit to real policy data replace hand-authored effect equations, and would players accept the loss of authored intent?
Can an LLM generate new policies and situations with consistent graph effects from a text description?
player_experience: Pulling one thread and watching the web move. The player hovers a policy to see lines to everything it touches, raises a tax and sees the deficit shrink while a voter group sours, and plans reforms in sequence because effects arrive with delays.
summary: Policies, indicators, and voter groups connect through a weighted causal graph with delays.

definition: Owns a catalog of policies, each with an active flag or a choice among mutually exclusive options in a group, prerequisites, an enactment cost (money, political capital, influence, or time), upkeep, and a cooldown. Enacting a policy applies modifiers or changes rules: it unlocks an action, alters a rate, or changes how agents behave, with a stated benefit and a stated cost. Frostpunk (2018) has a Book of Laws in which similar laws are sequenced so later ones are harsher, and accepting early compromises makes later ones likelier. Victoria 3 groups laws into mutually exclusive sets and, since update 1.3, requires each law to pass three enactment phases whose success chances depend on interest-group support, with up to three setbacks before failure. SimCity 2000 introduced city ordinances, and Civilization civics and Cities: Skylines district policies are other forms.
design_levers: number of policies and how many can be active at once (slots, groups, budget)
enactment cost, delay, and cooldown
size and visibility of side effects
reversibility: free to revoke, costly, or permanent
prerequisites and sequencing (escalating law chains)
dynamics: Escalating law chains pull players toward harsher policies one reasonable step at a time.
Policies that change agent behavior ripple into economic and social systems in ways their tooltips do not state.
Mutually exclusive groups create identity: a society defined by its chosen laws.
failure_modes: Policies with no real downside become always-on, leaving a menu of mandatory picks.
Too many small modifiers make each choice unnoticeable.
Free revocation lets players toggle policies around events, undermining the tradeoff.
name: Policy toggles
open_questions: Could players draft bespoke policies in language and have an LLM translate them into balanced, consistent rule changes?
Which explanations of second-order policy effects keep surprises interesting rather than unfair?
player_experience: Choosing which tradeoff to live with. The player browses a menu of laws, weighs their benefits against costs and side effects, and commits. In Frostpunk each signature feels like a moral line crossed; in grand strategy, passing a law is a political campaign.
summary: Enactable laws or policies change simulation rules with explicit tradeoffs.

claims.text: Democracy 4 constrains the player with political capital.
Europa Universalis IV uses administrative, diplomatic, and military monarch power to buy technology, and Hearts of Iron IV uses political power for laws and ministers.

In Captain of Industry each fully satisfied settlement need yields about 1-2 Unity per month, spent on edicts, outposts, quick trades, contracts, quick-build, vehicle recovery, emergency repairs, and building boosts.

definition: Owns one or more non-monetary stocks or capacities, each with a per-period income, an optional cap, and a price list of state actions. Income comes from the skill or loyalty of rulers and ministers, faction support, prestige, or satisfied population needs; spending buys discrete actions such as enacting or repealing a policy, issuing an edict, researching, raising stability, claiming territory, or rushing construction. Unlike a treasury, the stock usually cannot be borrowed or traded and its income comes from political or welfare state rather than economic activity, so it rations institutional change per period. Democracy 4 charges political capital, earned through loyal ministers, to introduce or cancel policies. Europa Universalis IV pays administrative, diplomatic, and military monarch points set by the ruler's skills, which buy technology among other things. Hearts of Iron IV spends political power on laws and ministers. Captain of Industry yields about 1 to 2 Unity per fully satisfied need per month, spent on edicts, outposts, quick builds, and emergency repairs. Policy-toggles owns the policies; this mechanic owns the currency that rations them.
design_levers: income sources (ruler skill, minister loyalty, faction approval, satisfied needs) and their weights
cap on the stock and whether overflow is lost
one pool versus several (administrative, diplomatic, and military points)
action prices relative to income, and whether prices scale with realm size or development
banked stock versus a capacity that ongoing commitments draw against
whether the currency converts to or from money
dynamics: Spending on stability or welfare raises future income, a reinforcing loop for well-run states.
Players time large reforms for when income peaks, such as after a strong heir succeeds or the cabinet is loyal.
Saving for expensive actions creates long-term plans that compete with spending to answer crises.
failure_modes: Hitting the cap with nothing worth buying wastes income and makes the currency invisible.
Several parallel currencies with separate shops become spreadsheet optimization detached from the fiction.
Income tied to leader skill makes one bad succession a long drought with few meaningful choices.
Cheap actions let players toggle policies every period, undoing the rationing.
name: Political capital
open_questions: Could political capital be replaced by negotiated backing from simulated ministers or factions without losing the clarity of a single number?
Does currency earned from welfare, as in Captain of Industry, make players value population needs differently from currency earned from leaders?
player_experience: Every turn or month has a political budget. The player decides which reform is worth this period's points, saves up for a large one, and feels the quality of the ruler or cabinet as a faster or slower clock of change. Weak leaders and unhappy populations show up as a shortage of options rather than only as a penalty.
summary: An abstract governing currency accrues each period from leaders, factions, or population welfare and is spent on policy changes, edicts, and other state actions.

definition: Owns a pollution value per cell or chunk. Each update, emitters add pollution, a fraction diffuses to neighboring cells, and terrain, vegetation, or water absorb some; other systems read the local value as a penalty to health, land value, crop growth, or happiness. Factorio stores pollution per 32x32-tile chunk, updates every 64 ticks, diffuses 2% to each cardinal neighbor once a chunk holds 15 or more, absorbs it by tile type and trees (trees are damaged above 60), and lets enemy spawners absorb it to fund attack waves. SimCity computes a pollution map from industry and traffic that depresses land value; Cities: Skylines separates ground, noise, and water pollution, and sewage released upstream contaminates water intakes downstream. Inputs are emitter locations and rates; outputs are a spatial field read by other systems.
design_levers: emission rate per source and modifiers such as efficiency upgrades or filters
diffusion fraction, minimum amount before diffusing, and grid resolution
absorption by terrain, water, and vegetation, and whether absorbers are damaged
what pollution affects: health, land value, crops, happiness, enemy aggression
cleanup tools and their cost
dynamics: Zoning separates polluting and sensitive uses, which lengthens commutes and adds traffic.
In Factorio pollution couples production scale to attack size, so efficiency becomes a defense strategy.
Absorbers degrade under load, so a polluted region can tip into faster spread as forests die.
failure_modes: Pollution that only lowers land value is solved once by zoning distance and then ignored.
Fine-grained diffusion with no threshold or chunking costs compute and produces smeared, unreadable fields.
Effects carried by hidden channels, such as water contamination far downstream, read as unexplained sickness.
name: Pollution spread
open_questions: Can learned dispersion surrogates make air and water pollution fields physically plausible while staying cheap and legible?
player_experience: Growth leaves a visible stain. The player separates factories from homes, plants green buffers, and watches the overlay creep outward; in Factorio a bigger factory directly invites bigger attacks. Cleanup competes with expansion for the same resources.
summary: Pollution emitted by sources accumulates and diffuses across land, water, or air cells and harms health, land value, or growth, or provokes threats.

definition: Owns population counts by stratum and the per-stratum tables of needs, consumption rates, labor roles, taxes, and promotion requirements. Each period residences or pops whose stratum's needs are met may advance to the next stratum, and unmet needs can stall, demote, or anger them; production buildings require workers of specific strata. Anno 1800 residences advance from Farmers through Workers, Artisans, and Engineers to Investors (with Jornaleros and Obreros in the New World) when the house is full, basic needs are met, and construction materials exist; luxury needs raise taxes and happiness, and island level follows the highest tier, such as 1,750 Investors for a metropolis. Victoria 3 groups professions into classes and strata whose standard-of-living expectations drive radicalism. Inputs: goods, services, construction materials. Outputs: workforce by tier, tax revenue, demand for higher goods.
design_levers: number of strata and promotion requirements
per-stratum needs, consumption rates, and tax yields
workforce requirements per building by stratum
demotion or unrest rules when needs fail
whether promotion is player-triggered or automatic
dynamics: Each new tier lengthens production chains, so economic complexity grows with population.
Inequality between tiers creates political pressure when strata link to interest groups or unrest.
Promotion and demotion cycles oscillate around supply shortfalls.
failure_modes: Upgrading drains lower-tier workers, collapsing basic production; Anno players learn to keep a surplus of each worker type.
Top-tier demand chains become so long that one missing good stalls the economy.
Strata as pure progression gates feel like a checklist rather than a society.
name: Population strata
open_questions: Can strata emerge from agent wealth and occupation dynamics rather than authored tiers, and remain legible?
How should mobility between strata be modeled so inequality has political consequences without becoming a death spiral?
