design_levers: representation of uncertainty: masked, range, noisy estimate, or rating
scouting cost and speed per entity or region
scout skill as the noise level of reports
whether knowledge decays over time
whether true values are ever fully revealed, for example after signing
separate uncertainty for current ability and future potential
dynamics: Information asymmetry creates market behavior: overpaying for hyped players and bargains in under-scouted regions.
Uncertain potential couples with skill growth to make youth signings speculative bets.
Rival AI clubs with better knowledge outbid the player, making scouting investment competitive.
failure_modes: Third-party editors and database tools reveal true attributes, collapsing the mechanic for players who use them.
Cheap, complete scouting turns uncertainty into a delay rather than a decision.
Uncertainty that persists after acquisition and long observation feels arbitrary.
name: Scouting knowledge
open_questions: Can language-model scouts write reports whose hedges and biases track their numeric noise, so reading reports is itself a skill?
Does Bayesian updating from observed performance, shown to the player, make uncertainty feel fairer than fixed masking?
player_experience: Recruitment becomes investment under uncertainty. The player decides where to send scouts, weighs a cheap unknown against a known star, and feels vindicated or burned when performance reveals the true value.
summary: Entity attributes are known only with uncertainty that scouting effort reduces.

definition: Owns the season's state: start date, an end condition (fixed duration, a scheduled wipe, or a world-level goal or catastrophe), and the carryover rules that say what survives into the next season (nothing, account-level unlocks, records, or changed rules). When the end condition fires, world state is archived or deleted, a new world is generated or loaded, and carryover is applied. A Tale in the Desert runs in Tellings that average about 18 months and end in a wipe, with rule changes for the next Telling shaped by what players achieved. Eco gives each world a meteor due in thirty days, so a server's run is bounded by stopping it or suffering the impact, and servers are commonly restarted as new worlds. Unlike persistent-world, which assumes continuity, this mechanic owns the bounded lifetime of a shared world and the transition between lifetimes.
design_levers: season length or end condition
carryover: nothing, cosmetics, account unlocks, records, or rule changes
rule variation between seasons, including player-proposed changes
whether players can migrate between seasonal and permanent worlds
announcement lead time before a wipe
dynamics: Activity surges at season start and fades toward the end, giving the population a cycle.
Players refine openings across seasons, and community guides target the first days of a wipe.
Rule changes between seasons let designers and players treat each season as an experiment.
failure_modes: Wipes erase work players were attached to, and some quit rather than start over.
Short seasons reward a known opening rush, so seasons play out the same way.
Carryover that is too generous rebuilds the early-arrival advantage the reset was meant to remove.
name: Seasonal world reset
open_questions: Could AI summaries and chronicles of past seasons preserve their history so wipes feel less like loss?
Which carryover rules keep returning players motivated without restoring early-arrival dominance?
player_experience: Fresh starts on a schedule. Everyone begins equal at the start of a season, so new players can matter, and the end date gives the season an arc of land rush, consolidation, and final push. Players plan around the wipe, deciding what is worth building when it will not last.
summary: A shared world runs for a bounded season and is then wiped and restarted, often with rule changes carried into the next season.

definition: Owns a calendar position that advances by day and maps to a season index, usually four. Each season sets parameters other systems read: which crops can grow, temperature, day length, weather odds, animal behavior, demand for heat or food, and scheduled events. Stardew Valley has four 28-day seasons, and seasonal crops must generally be harvested before the next season arrives; Don't Starve's base cycle alternates 20 summer days and 16 winter days and changes the day, dusk, and night split with them; Banished and Farthest Frontier force food stockpiling for winters without harvests. Inputs are elapsed days; outputs are season flags and parameter sets. Some games make season length a setting.
design_levers: number and length of seasons, and whether lengths vary or can be set
which systems each season modifies: growth, temperature, weather, events, prices
severity of the harshest season and how much stockpiling it demands
transition rules, such as crops dying at the change or gradual change
season-unique content: crops, festivals, creatures
dynamics: Seasonal production with year-round consumption creates demand for storage, preservation, and trade.
Combined with a crisis countdown, the approach of winter structures the year as preparation.
Labor shifts between seasonal tasks, creating idle periods and peaks.
failure_modes: Seasons that only swap textures add art cost without changing decisions.
A harsh season survivable only with one known stockpile size becomes a checklist.
Season-gated content locks players out for long stretches when they miss a window.
name: Seasons
open_questions: Can generative asset models make seasonal variants of every asset cheap enough that seasons become a default rather than a budget decision?
player_experience: Planning in cycles. The player plants for this season while saving for the next, treats the end of a season as a deadline, and gets a fresh start each spring. Winter tests the year's preparation, and the cycle gives long games a felt rhythm.
summary: A seasonal calendar cycles conditions such as temperature, daylight, and growing windows that govern growth, demand, and risk.

definition: Each service building writes an effect value onto a coverage map, within a radius, a network distance, or by dispatching vehicles. Covered cells or buildings read that value to reduce a risk or raise a satisfaction term. In Micropolis each fire or police station adds an effect equal to 1000 times funded over requested budget, halved if unpowered and halved again without road access, to an 8x8-tile block map; the map is smoothed three times, and the smoothed police map is subtracted from each cell's crime score and the smoothed fire map sets fire protection. SimCity 2000 shows coverage as a radius; Cities: Skylines uses network distance and dispatches service vehicles. Capacity limits how many buildings or residents one facility can serve. Inputs: service building locations, funding, power, access. Outputs: per-cell coverage values and the downstream risk or happiness change.
design_levers: coverage shape: Euclidean radius, network distance, or vehicle dispatch
capacity per building and falloff with distance
funding and power effects on strength
how coverage maps to outcomes such as crime, fire risk, health, or education
overlap rules: additive, maximum, or diminishing
dynamics: Coverage shapes city form, rewarding compact grids around service hubs.
Budget cuts weaken coverage everywhere at once, causing simultaneous crises.
Coupled with land value, coverage raises desirability, which raises density, which raises demand for more services.
failure_modes: Radius coverage that ignores the road network lets buildings across a river count as covered.
Overlapping coverage with no capacity limit makes one building per district enough.
Hidden funding multipliers make coverage seem to drop at random.
name: Service coverage
open_questions: Can facility-location solvers act as advisors that suggest placements without removing the planning decision?
Does vehicle dispatch produce more interesting failures than radius coverage at equal legibility?
player_experience: Filling the map with circles. Players place services to cover populated areas, check overlays for gaps, and balance coverage against budget. Uncovered districts show up as fires, crime, or unhappy residents, so the overlay becomes a to-do list.
summary: Service buildings such as police, fire, clinics, and schools satisfy demand within a radius or network distance, up to a capacity.

definition: Each service point (a ride, a clinic room, a checkout) has a service rate and a queue of waiting agents. Arriving agents join if the queue is not too long by their own tolerance; while waiting, their needs keep decaying and their satisfaction falls with waiting time; served agents leave and free the slot. RollerCoaster Tycoon builds explicit queue paths for rides, and guests think aloud about long waits. Theme Hospital and Two Point Hospital queue patients outside rooms; while they wait their health keeps falling, so long queues produce departures and deaths that lower the hospital's reputation. Inputs: arrival rate, service rate, capacity, tolerance. Outputs: queue length, waiting times, and satisfaction changes.
design_levers: service rate per point and number of parallel points
queue capacity and agents' tolerance before they balk or leave
satisfaction decay while waiting
queue discipline: first-in-first-out, priority, or player reordering
information shown about wait times
dynamics: Utilization near 100% causes waiting times to explode, the core queueing-theory result, so players learn to keep slack.
Coupled with needs decay, long waits create secondary demand at food and toilet facilities.
Demand shifts toward shorter queues, balancing load across service points.
failure_modes: Fixed tolerance across all agents makes queues predictable and dull.
Queues that grow without bound because agents never leave freeze the simulation.
Invisible queues inside buildings hide the bottleneck.
name: Service queues
open_questions: Could generative agents with learned patience models make queues produce more varied and memorable behavior?
player_experience: Visible lines are an instant read on capacity. Players add service points, lengthen or shorten queue paths, and redistribute demand, learning from the line itself where the bottleneck is.
summary: Agents wait in lines for limited-capacity services; waiting time feeds back into satisfaction and throughput.

claims.text: Factorio introduced arithmetic, decider, and constant combinators on a circuit network where red and green wire signals entering one entity are summed.
Factorio developers stated a design principle of not adding dedicated logic, bit, or timer combinator types during the 0.13 circuit network work.
Factorio 2.0 added a selector combinator and decider combinators with multiple AND/OR conditions, multiple outputs, and per-wire input selection.

definition: The player places wires between entities and logic elements to build control systems inside the world. State owned: the wire graph, signal values on each network, and logic element configuration. Update rule: each tick, sensors and connected entities write signals (item counts, fluid levels, power, conditions) onto their networks; logic elements read input networks and write outputs, often with a one-tick delay; actuators enable or disable themselves or change settings by condition. Canonical form: the Factorio circuit network, where red and green wires carry item-count signals, signals from both wires entering one entity are summed, and arithmetic, decider, and constant combinators operate on them; Factorio 2.0 added a selector combinator and multi-condition deciders. Others: Minecraft redstone, Oxygen Not Included automation wires with sensors and logic gates, Stationeers logic and IC chips, and Mindustry logic processors.
design_levers: signal type: binary, integer, or multi-channel item vectors
logic primitives provided and whether higher-level elements are deliberately withheld
timing: propagation delay per element and tick order
which entities can read and write signals
debugging aids: signal readouts, wire visualization, element descriptions
physical cost of wires and logic elements
dynamics: Turing-complete primitives lead players to build CPUs, displays, and games inside the game.
Demand-driven control (produce only when stock falls) dampens the oscillations and gluts of always-on production.
Shared circuit designs spread as blueprints, coupling this mechanic to community design culture.
failure_modes: Invisible signal values and per-tick delays make circuits hard to debug without readouts.
Circuit control is optional in many games, so most players never engage and designers cannot build challenges around it.
Missing primitives force contraptions for simple tasks, while too many make the logic trivial.
name: Signal circuits
open_questions: Can a model synthesize circuit layouts from a behavior spec (keep 2,000 plates buffered) and explain existing circuits to newcomers?
What minimal primitive set gives the widest range of player designs without making simple tasks contraptions?
player_experience: The player turns a passive factory into one that senses and responds: lamps that show stock, trains that go where they are needed, power that switches on demand. Building memory, timers, or displays from parts feels like engineering, and the most ambitious players build computers inside the game.
summary: In-world wires, sensors, and logic elements carry signals that read machine state and control machines.

definition: Owns per-object interaction definitions: each interaction carries advertisements (which needs it satisfies and by how much), availability checks, distance attenuation, and the behavior script the agent runs. Agents carry no knowledge of how to use things; when choosing, an agent gathers advertisements from reachable objects, scales them by its needs, personality, and distance, selects one, and runs that object's script. In The Sims, per Forbus and Wright's notes, advertisements cover nine motives, can scale with personality points, attenuate with distance through high, moderate, low, or none presets, and check trees hide unavailable interactions; a toilet advertises 0-70 Bladder. Because behavior lives in objects, new objects add new behaviors without changing agent code, which suits expansion packs and mods. Inputs: objects in range, agent needs. Outputs: candidate actions, need restoration, animations.
design_levers: advertised magnitude per need and whether it scales with personality or object quality
distance attenuation curve per interaction
advertised versus delivered value, which allows deceptive or broken objects
availability and permission checks such as ownership, age, and room
how many agents one object can serve at once
dynamics: Each new object adds behaviors, so the behavior space grows with content packs, which is how The Sims expansions extended play.
Players use objects as lures to route agents, coupling placement to behavior.
Scarce objects create queues and conflicts when several agents select the same one.
failure_modes: An over-tuned advertisement makes one object a magnet that agents queue for regardless of need.
Assuming honest advertisements breaks when objects fail, producing loops of agents repeatedly using broken objects.
Attenuation errors make agents walk past nearby options to distant ones.
Behavior spread across hundreds of objects is harder to debug than one agent controller.
name: Smart objects
open_questions: Can generative models author new objects with consistent advertisements, scripts, and animations, turning content packs into runtime generation?
Should language-model agents read object affordances as numeric advertisements, as text descriptions, or both?
player_experience: Buying or placing an object changes what agents want to do, so the player designs behavior through the environment. Players learn that a better object pulls agents across the room and use placement to steer them.
summary: Objects advertise the need satisfaction they offer, and agents query nearby objects to decide what to do.

definition: Owns a library of social exchange definitions, each with an intent, preconditions on the social state, initiator and responder desire rules, and effects for acceptance and rejection on relationships, statuses, and history. Each cycle an agent scores the exchanges it could start with each other agent, picks one, the responder evaluates acceptance, and the outcome is written to state and history. Comme il Faut in Prom Week defines exchanges with one intent, hard preconditions, initiator and responder influence rule sets, and at least accept and reject instantiations; volition sums the weights of over 5,000 influence rules across 34 statuses and 44 traits. RimWorld rolls chitchat, deep talk, slights, and insults with weights from opinion and compatibility; The Sims 3 defined hundreds of interactions from thousands of production rules (Evans, GDC 2010). Inputs: social state, traits, history. Outputs: relationship and status changes, logged events.
design_levers: size of the exchange library and intents covered
precondition strictness and which norms or statuses gate moves
volition rule weights for initiators and responders
effect magnitudes for accept and reject outcomes
player control: choose moves, suggest, or only watch
dynamics: Logged exchanges become history that later rules reference, so past insults enable future revenge moves.
Status effects spread socially, so one embarrassing exchange changes how a group treats a character.
Exchange outcomes drive relationship values, which change the next exchange's odds, producing escalating arcs.
failure_modes: Small libraries repeat the same exchanges until characters feel scripted.
Rule weights interact unpredictably across thousands of rules, so authors cannot predict outcomes.
Exchanges change numbers without visible performance, so moves feel interchangeable.
Spam: repeating the best-scoring move maxes relationships.
name: Social exchanges
open_questions: Can language models generate performances and new exchange types on the fly while a symbolic layer keeps preconditions and effects consistent?
Can influence-rule weights be learned from player judgments of plausibility rather than authored?
player_experience: The player chooses moves in a social puzzle, or watches agents make them, and learns the norms that make a move land. Rejections and backfires are part of the fun, and players develop social strategies such as softening a target before the big ask.
summary: Discrete social moves such as flirt, insult, or apologize have preconditions on social state and norms, and they update relationships.

definition: An object is a network of nodes (point masses) linked by beams (massless springs with damping). Each step every beam applies force from its length deviation and damping, nodes integrate, and collisions push nodes. A beam whose force passes a deform threshold permanently changes its rest length, and one that passes its strength breaks, so parts detach. In BeamNG.drive vehicles are authored in JBeam: nodes have weight, beams have beamSpring (stiffness), beamDamp, beamDeform, and beamStrength. Beams do not resist bending or twisting, so cross braces are needed for rigidity, and stiff beams on light nodes vibrate or explode (the documentation's example stabilizes a structure by raising nodes from 6 kg to 7 kg). Finite-element and position-based methods are alternatives.
design_levers: node density and placement
beam stiffness and damping per part
deform and break thresholds
physics step rate
which parts are soft and which are rigid or cosmetic
coupling of deformation to function, such as steering or engine damage
dynamics: Damage changes handling, which changes driving, which causes more damage.
Crash testing becomes its own play style and community genre.
Deformed tires and suspension couple to grip and vehicle dynamics.
failure_modes: Stiff beams on light nodes vibrate or explode, so every structure needs stability tuning.
CPU cost per vehicle limits how many soft bodies can run at once.
Hand-building node-beam structures for every vehicle is a large authoring cost.
Too-soft settings make solid objects look like jelly.
name: Soft-body deformation
open_questions: Can node-beam structures be generated automatically from a visual mesh and material labels?
Can learned deformation surrogates run many soft bodies at once on consumer hardware?
player_experience: Visceral, readable damage. Crashes crumple metal where they hit, and the damage changes how the vehicle drives. Players experiment with crashes as much as they drive.
summary: Objects built from mass nodes and spring beams bend, crumple, and break under stress, and deformation persists.

synergy.note: Deforming chassis change handling after impacts (BeamNG.drive).

definition: Each perishable item or stack carries a freshness value or age that advances each tick at a rate set by item type and storage conditions; at a threshold it becomes rotten, converts into a spoiled item, or is destroyed. RimWorld stops rot for food kept at or below 0 C, so walk-in freezers are standard; Don't Starve moves food from fresh to stale to spoiled and finally to rot, with ice boxes slowing the clock; Factorio: Space Age gives biological items spoil times from about two hours down to a few minutes, cannot be delayed, turns spoiled items into Spoilage, and passes ingredient freshness on to recipe outputs. Inputs: item type, time, storage environment. Outputs: current freshness, value or effect scaling, and spoil events.
design_levers: spoil time per item type
storage modifiers such as temperature, containers, and preservation methods
whether freshness is binary (fresh or rotten) or continuous and scales value
what spoiled goods become: nothing, a waste item, or a useful input such as fertilizer
freshness inheritance across recipes
dynamics: Shifts optimal play from stockpiling to just-in-time throughput; Factorio's developers state that buffering is not helpful under spoilage.
Cold storage couples food to power and temperature systems, so a power failure becomes a famine risk.
Seasonal harvests plus spoilage create a winter preservation problem.
Freshness-priority handling (pick freshest or oldest first) creates new logistics rules.
failure_modes: Spoilage that is cheap to stop, such as one freezer that halts all decay, becomes a one-time build tax.
Short spoil times on items with long logistics routes make some chains impossible without explanation.
Hidden freshness values make sudden losses feel unfair.
name: Spoilage
open_questions: What spoil-time distribution across goods produces interesting routing without making long chains infeasible?
player_experience: A clock on every stockpile. Players stop hoarding and start thinking in flow: produce close to consumption, build cold storage, preserve food, or accept waste. Opening a storeroom to find a harvest rotted is a sharp, memorable loss.
summary: Perishable goods lose value or rot over time depending on storage conditions such as temperature and containers.

synergy.note: Storage conditions decide spoilage rates, making cold storage valuable.

definition: Owns an unrest or radicalism stock per region, group, or nation. Each period grievances (unmet needs, opposed laws, taxes, war exhaustion, occupation) add to it and suppression (police, garrisons, concessions, propaganda) subtracts. Crossing thresholds triggers escalating events: protests, strikes, riots, rebel spawns, secession, revolution, or game over. Civilization (1991) puts a city into disorder, halting production, when unhappy citizens outnumber happy ones. Europa Universalis IV accumulates rebel progress in provinces with positive unrest until rebels rise. Victoria 3 starts a revolution clock when a political movement's radicalism is high enough that it turns to revolt, and each time the clock fills the revolution advances through events. Frostpunk (2018) ends in revolt when discontent stays too high or hope too low for an extended period.
design_levers: grievance sources and their weights
suppression tools, their costs, and side effects such as increasing long-term grievance
threshold ladder and escalation speed
spatial scope: per province, per group, or national
warning visibility, such as clocks, meters, and forecasts
dynamics: Disorder halts production, which worsens shortages and raises grievances, a death spiral.
Suppression buys time but raises long-term grievances, deferring rather than resolving crises.
Unrest in one region can spread or inspire neighboring regions.
failure_modes: Cheap suppression makes unrest trivial, as with stacking garrisons or police.
Instant revolt at a threshold feels arbitrary without visible warning.
Revolts that only spawn more units to fight turn politics into whack-a-mole combat.
name: Stability and unrest
open_questions: Can agent-based protest dynamics (social contagion, leaders) replace scalar unrest meters while staying readable?
Can LLM-generated demands make movements negotiable rather than just threats to suppress?
player_experience: A pressure cooker. The player watches unrest rise, decides whether to concede, suppress, or wait it out, and feels the cost of each option. Thresholds create anxious countdowns and dramatic turning points.
summary: Grievances accumulate into unrest that triggers protests, strikes, or revolt.

definition: Owns a candidate pool and a roster. Each candidate has skills or attributes, traits, and a wage demand; hiring moves them to the roster at a recurring wage. Rostered staff are assigned to rooms, roles, or positions, and their skill sets the speed or quality of work there; fatigue, morale, and pay satisfaction change over time and can trigger rest, raise demands, or quitting. Training spends money and time to raise skills. Theme Hospital (1997) has the player hire doctors, nurses, handymen, and receptionists with performance statistics, train doctors, require specialist skills for rooms such as the operating theatre, send staff to rest, and dismiss staff who argue about pay. Football Manager builds a whole game around player and staff attributes, contracts, and wages, and Two Point Hospital follows Theme Hospital's model.
design_levers: number of staff types and skill dimensions
candidate pool size, refresh rate, and quality distribution
wage curve relative to skill and how raises are demanded
fatigue, morale, and quitting rules
training cost, duration, and skill ceilings
how much candidate information is hidden until hired or scouted
dynamics: Strong staff raise income, which funds better hires, so facilities snowball toward elite rosters.
Fatigue and rest create capacity dips that ripple into queues.
Losing a star employee causes a sudden performance drop and a recovery arc.
failure_modes: When one stat dominates, hiring becomes sorting a list and staff stop feeling like individuals.
Raise demands that grow too fast make experienced staff a liability and push players to churn employees.
Generic stats without traits make staff interchangeable and remove attachment.
name: Staff hiring and rosters
open_questions: Can LLM-generated candidates with backstories, interviews, and evolving workplace relationships make rosters as memorable as authored characters?
What is the smallest set of staff attributes that keeps hiring a real decision?
player_experience: Assembling a team. The player compares candidates' stats against their wages, places the best people where they matter most, and nurses tired or unhappy staff. Names and faces make the facility feel staffed by people rather than counters.
summary: The player hires individual staff with skills, traits, and wages to operate a facility or team.

definition: Owns, per engaged unit or stack, strength pools (hit points, manpower, organization, morale) and a vector of combat stats, and, per engagement, a round counter and modifiers from terrain, commanders, and supply. Each round, each side's damage is computed from its attack against the opponent's defense, scaled by modifiers and a random draw, and subtracted from the opponent's pools; a side whose morale or organization breaks retreats or is destroyed. Sid Meier's Civilization compares a unit's attack with the defender's defense under terrain and fortification modifiers and a random draw. Europa Universalis IV rolls dice in alternating fire and shock phases modified by general skill and terrain, and morale damage usually ends the battle. Hearts of Iron IV compares divisions' attack against defense or breakthrough, draining organization. FTL rolls each shot against the target's evasion and absorbs shots with shield layers. Unlike military-operations, there are no modeled sensors, signatures, or flight paths; unlike attribute-match-engine, the output is attrition of unit pools rather than a stream of sports events.
design_levers: stat set: attack and defense only, or separate stats for different damage types and targets
randomness: dice range per round versus deterministic expected values
morale or organization as a separate pool that ends battles before units are destroyed
terrain, river crossing, fortification, and commander modifiers
round length and the number of rounds before a battle resolves
how much of the formula and odds the game previews
dynamics: Players optimize army compositions and commanders around the formula, producing a meta that patches revise.
Morale breaking before units die produces retreats and pursuits, giving campaigns a rhythm of decisive and indecisive battles.
Terrain modifiers make certain regions natural defensive lines, shaping fronts and borders.
failure_modes: One unit composition or stat dominates once players find the formula's best ratio, a recurring issue in strategy communities.
High variance lets a weak unit defeat a much stronger one, which reads as unfair when the odds were not shown.
Opaque modifier stacks make losses impossible to diagnose without community spreadsheets.
name: Statistical combat resolution
open_questions: Can generated battle narration explain why a stat-resolved battle went as it did, so players can separate luck from preparation?
Could learned surrogate models of tactical combat give abstract resolution more of the texture of simulated battles at low cost?
player_experience: Battles are prepared rather than performed. The player stacks advantages (terrain, a better general, the right unit mix, a fresh army) and then watches the bars move, knowing the dice can still go against them. Reading a combat preview and deciding whether the odds justify an attack is the core skill.
summary: Battles between units resolve from attack, defense, morale, terrain, and random rolls in rounds rather than from physics or modeled sensors and weapons.

definition: The game samples aggregate variables (population, money, production and consumption per item, prices, power, happiness, crime) at fixed intervals into time series and renders them as line graphs, stacked areas, tables, or pies. State owned: ring buffers of samples per variable, usually at several resolutions with older data downsampled. Update rule: each sample period, append the aggregate; when a buffer fills, merge samples into a coarser tier. The player picks variables, windows, and breakdowns. Canonical forms: the SimCity graphs window, Factorio production statistics per item across windows from seconds to hundreds of hours, Transport Tycoon company graphs for income and cargo delivered, Oxygen Not Included's daily colony report, and market price history in EVE Online and Victoria 3.
design_levers: which variables are logged and at what granularity (per item, per region, per agent class)
time windows and downsampling scheme
comparison views: against rivals, against previous periods, production versus consumption
drill-down from an aggregate line to its contributors
trend-based alerts and export of data
dynamics: Visible production and consumption rates make ratio optimization possible, as in finding Factorio bottlenecks from item statistics.
Trend reading supports experimental play: change one policy, watch the curve, revert.
Public price histories in shared markets feed speculation and coordinated trading.
failure_modes: Graphs show a decline but give no path to its cause.
Coarse sampling hides short spikes or aliases oscillations into smooth lines.
Dashboards buried in menus are never opened by most players.
Long high-resolution histories bloat save files.
name: Stats dashboards
open_questions: Can natural-language queries over logged history (why did power drop last winter) replace browsing graphs for most players?
Which few variables, logged by default, let players diagnose most failures in a given genre?
player_experience: The player steps back from the moment to read trends, confirm a change worked, and spot slow declines that no single frame reveals. A rising curve is its own reward.
summary: Graphs and tables show the recorded history of simulation variables over selectable time windows.

definition: Owns a set of active stimuli, each with a source position, type (sound, light, smell, sight of the player), intensity, radius, and decay time, plus each agent's perception thresholds and current alert target. When an action fires it emits a stimulus sized by the action (gunshot, smashed window, running, a lit fire); each update, agents within range whose perception exceeds the threshold switch to an investigate state and path toward the source, and some propagate the alert to nearby agents so groups follow. Stimuli fade, and agents that find nothing return to idle or wander. Project Zomboid zombies respond to sight and hearing, and loud actions draw them from a distance; This War of Mine shows noise from scavenging actions that can alert people nearby. Unlike fog-of-war, which hides information from the player, this mechanic models what hostile agents perceive about the player; unlike adaptive-threat-scaling, it changes where threats go, not how strong they are.
design_levers: emission radius and intensity per action, weapon, and tool
perception thresholds per agent type and modifiers such as weather, time of day, and walls
stimulus decay time and how long agents investigate before giving up
alert propagation between agents, which turns individuals into crowds or hordes
player feedback: visible noise rings, audio cues, or no indication
dynamics: Players lure groups away with distractions such as alarms or thrown objects, turning the rule into a tool.
Fighting creates noise that draws more enemies, a reinforcing loop that punishes loud tactics.
Quiet tools and routes become valuable, shaping crafting and travel choices.
failure_modes: Invisible emission rules make attacks feel random when players cannot tell what they did to cause them.
Propagation that is too strong snowballs every mistake into an unwinnable horde.
Agents that ignore walls and distance when following sound feel omniscient and break stealth.
name: Stimulus attraction
open_questions: Can learned agents that reason about what they heard and saw produce searches that feel smarter without becoming omniscient?
Does visualizing emissions improve player decisions or remove the tension of not knowing what heard you?
player_experience: Every action has an audience. The player weighs the speed of smashing a window against the zombies it will call, walks instead of running, and uses noise deliberately as a lure. Mistakes are legible and frightening: a gunshot that brings a crowd teaches the rule at once.
summary: Player actions emit sound or light stimuli with a radius and decay, and agents that perceive them move toward the source, so managing emissions is part of survival.

definition: Storage containers, warehouses, stockpile zones, and machine input or output slots each hold a capacity measured in units, stacks, slots, or volume. Producers push into storage until it is full, then stall; consumers pull from it until it is empty, then starve. Between those limits, buffer level absorbs mismatches in timing. Factorio chests have fixed slot counts and machines hold small input and output buffers; RimWorld stockpile zones accept filtered items in priority order (low, normal, preferred, important, critical) and haulers move items toward higher-priority zones with space; Anno caps each good at an island-wide storage limit that warehouses raise; GlassBox in SimCity (2013) stores everything in capacity-limited resource bins, such as a house holding 20 of 30 food and 4 of 10 people. Inputs: incoming and outgoing flows. Outputs: stock level and full or empty states that gate adjacent processes.
design_levers: capacity per container and whether it is per good, per slot, or shared
filters and priorities that decide what goes where
behavior when full: stall, overflow to the ground, or discard
local buffers on machines versus central warehouses
storage cost in space, money, or construction
dynamics: Buffers absorb shocks such as raids, winters, and broken links, trading space for resilience.
Full buffers propagate backpressure upstream, so one blocked output can stop an entire chain.
Coupled with spoilage, storage becomes a liability instead of a safe stockpile.
Players build overflow sinks or priority splits so critical chains never block.
failure_modes: Very large storage hides every imbalance, so production ratios never matter.
Tiny buffers make chains brittle and turn play into constant stop-and-go.
Full storage stalls without alerts make the cause invisible.
name: Storage and buffers
open_questions: Can automatic buffer sizing advisors teach players about backpressure without solving the layout for them?
player_experience: Buffers give breathing room and hide problems. Players size storage to survive supply gaps, then discover that a full warehouse has silently stopped a production line. Organizing what goes where becomes its own small design task.
summary: Goods occupy finite storage; buffers decouple producers from consumers, and full storage blocks production.

definition: A director process tracks a pacing signal and runs a cycle that selects incidents from a catalog. Left 4 Dead's AI Director keeps an emotional intensity value per survivor that rises with damage, incapacitation, and nearby infected deaths and decays when not engaged; it cycles through Build Up (full threat until peak intensity), Sustain Peak (3-5 s), Peak Fade, and Relax (30-45 s of minimal spawns), spawns mobs every 90-180 s on Normal, and deals boss events (Tank, Witch, nothing) along the route. RimWorld storytellers weigh colony wealth, colonists, recent deaths or wounds, and time since the last major event; incident chance is a base chance times a population-intent factor, and presets differ (Cassandra escalates in cycles, Phoebe leaves long gaps, Randy is irregular). The director decides when and what; magnitude usually comes from adaptive threat scaling. Outputs: incident firing, spawn populations, item placement, music cues.
design_levers: pacing signal: per-player intensity, time since last threat, or colony state
phase thresholds and durations for build-up, peak, and relaxation
incident catalog, base weights, and state conditions such as population intent
selectable presets that change cycle shape and randomness
randomness floor and mercy rules after heavy losses
dynamics: Pressure and relief cycles create natural story beats that players retell as chapters.
Combined with persistent injuries and permadeath, a poorly timed second incident starts cascades that become memorable runs.
Players manipulate the director's inputs, such as population or wealth, to shape which incidents it can choose.
failure_modes: Fixed cycles become predictable, and players learn to exploit relax windows.
Irregular presets can stack several hard events, which feels unfair when combined with permadeath.
Heavy rubber-banding makes skill feel irrelevant because the director compensates for good play.
name: Storyteller director
open_questions: Can a language-model director author new incidents conditioned on colony state and characters, not just select from a catalog?
Can learned models of player stress from play telemetry replace hand-built intensity formulas?
How should a director balance dramatic pacing against fairness when deaths are permanent?
player_experience: Play has a rhythm of pressure and relief that feels authored even though it is generated. Players use calm windows to build and heal, brace when calm runs long, and talk about storytellers as personalities with moods and grudges.
summary: A director AI chooses which events to fire and when, pacing them by a model of tension and the current state.

claims.text: Dwarf Fortress keeps a hidden stress value from -1,000,000 to +1,000,000 with effects from +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000; emotions add or subtract stress and facets such as bravery, stress vulnerability, and anxiety scale it.
In Crusader Kings III, acting against personality traits adds stress that can be lethal, and stress breaks at level 2 or higher can change traits.

definition: Owns a per-agent stress value with slow decay and a ladder of levels. Each experience adds or removes an amount scaled by personality, and the value relaxes toward zero only slowly, so stress is an integral of history rather than a snapshot of current conditions. Crossing a level triggers a break event, a coping trait, a lasting change in behavior, or death at the extreme. Dwarf Fortress keeps a hidden stress value from -1,000,000 to +1,000,000 with effects from +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000: emotions add or subtract stress, facets such as bravery, stress vulnerability, and anxiety scale it, long-term memories keep adding to it, and high stress leads to tantrums, depression, obliviousness, or insanity. Crusader Kings III adds stress when a character acts against its personality traits, fires mental-break events as stress levels are crossed, lets breaks at level 2 or higher change traits, and can kill at extreme stress, all without a mood meter. It differs from mood-breakdown, whose mood is a near-instant sum of current modifiers, and from memories-thoughts, which owns the event entries that can feed it.
design_levers: stress per event type and the personality scaling applied to it
decay rate toward zero and whether relief needs active coping (feasts, hobbies, vices)
level thresholds and what each level triggers
break catalog: tantrums, coping traits, personality change, death
visibility of the value, hidden as in Dwarf Fortress or shown as in Crusader Kings III
dynamics: A shared tragedy stresses many agents at once, so breaks cluster weeks or months after the event.
Breaks generate new stressors for witnesses, a reinforcing cascade, as in Dwarf Fortress tantrum spirals.
Coping traits acquired through breaks permanently change characters, turning stress history into identity.
failure_modes: Hidden stress makes breakdowns look random, since the cause may be months old.
Slow decay plus frequent stressors leaves a population chronically stressed after one disaster, with no recovery path.
Cheap relief actions such as a feast or a vice reduce stress management to a periodic chore.
Lethal stress at the top of the ladder can end a character or dynasty through bookkeeping rather than drama.
name: Stress accumulation
open_questions: Does showing the stress value make breaks feel fair at the cost of drama, or can partial signals give warning without a meter?
Can language-model agents express accumulated stress in dialogue and behavior before a threshold break, so players see it building?
player_experience: The player manages a slow-burning account of bad experiences rather than a moment-to-moment mood: a character can look fine while carrying stress from months ago. In Crusader Kings III this makes roleplay a resource decision, since acting against a character's traits costs stress that must later be shed; in Dwarf Fortress a fortress's past tragedies become a hidden debt that comes due.
summary: A slow per-agent stress stock integrates negative experiences scaled by personality and, as it crosses levels, triggers breaks or lasting changes.

definition: Structural elements form a connectivity graph rooted at grounded elements. Three update rules are common. Connectivity only: an element with no path to ground falls, as in Dwarf Fortress cave-ins and in Teardown, where disconnected voxel pieces become physics bodies. Decaying support: support propagates outward and drops by a material-specific amount per connection, and pieces past the limit collapse; Valheim shows this with a color scale from blue (grounded) to red (at the limit) while the hammer is equipped, and stone and core wood carry farther than wood. Load and stress: a physics solve computes member forces and breaks members past their strength, as in Poly Bridge. Collapse removes elements, spawns debris or rigid bodies, and re-checks dependents, which can cascade.
design_levers: propagation model: connectivity only, per-step decay, or physical stress
per-material strength, maximum span, and support loss per connection
what counts as ground or an anchor
collapse resolution: instant removal, debris, or simulated rigid bodies
visualization of support before failure
dynamics: Attackers and players target supports, turning integrity into a combat and demolition system.
Material limits shape architectural styles, such as regular pillars and stone bases in Valheim halls.
Fire, explosions, and digging couple into chained collapses.
failure_modes: Connectivity-only models let large structures stand on a few voxels; reviewers noted Teardown does not model compressive stress.
Per-step decay limits feel arbitrary when they do not match the visual mass of the structure.
Cascading collapse destroys hours of player work with no warning or undo.
Large collapses cause frame-time spikes.
name: Structural integrity
open_questions: Can learned surrogates of finite-element stress make physically plausible load paths affordable in large player-built structures?
What collapse warnings preserve tension without making failure trivial to avoid?
player_experience: Building with gravity in mind. Players add pillars, braces, and stronger materials, read the support overlay, and feel tension when extending a span. Collapses are spectacular, and demolition becomes a tactic.
summary: Structures carry support values or loads propagated from the ground, and elements that lose support or exceed their limits collapse.

synergy.note: Destruction matters when removing a piece can collapse what it supported (Teardown).

definition: Owns, per vehicle, a list of components (reactor, engines, shields, weapons, sensors, oxygen, hydraulics, individual blocks or parts), each with integrity, a capacity that depends on integrity, and a repair state. Incoming damage is routed to a component by hit location, a targeting choice, or a random draw; the component's capacity falls in steps or to zero, and the vehicle's derived abilities update at once. Repair restores integrity over time, through crew or damage-control teams, or at a dock. FTL ships are rooms holding systems whose power bars are disabled by hits until crew repair them, and players aim weapons at specific enemy systems. Elite Dangerous tracks integrity per module; Space Engineers functional blocks stop working when damaged below a threshold; Kerbal Space Program parts are destroyed by impact or overheating. Unlike wear-breakdown, damage comes from events rather than use and age; unlike injury-body-model, components are machines with capacities, not organisms with wounds and healing.
design_levers: component granularity: a few named systems, dozens of modules, or every block or part
damage routing: hit location, player-targeted subsystems, or random allocation
capacity curve: binary loss, stepped loss, or proportional degradation
repair model: crew time, consumable parts, damage-control assignments, or docking only
cascades such as fires, breaches, or power loss that spread damage to other components
dynamics: Targeting the opponent's key system first becomes a standard opening, such as disabling weapons or shields.
Damage to one component cascades into others: a lost reactor removes power, a lost oxygen system suffocates crew.
Repair crews and damage control become a resource that competes with combat roles.
failure_modes: Random allocation of critical hits ends fights on a single roll, which reads as unfair.
Fine granularity without clear status displays leaves players unsure which component failed.
Repair that is too fast or free removes the decision; repair that requires a dock makes one hit end a mission.
name: Subsystem damage
open_questions: Can AI opponents choose subsystem targets based on a model of the player's ship and plan rather than fixed priorities?
What granularity of components keeps damage readable during real-time combat?
player_experience: Damage is specific and tactical. Losing shields, engines, or oxygen each forces a different response, so the player triages repairs, reroutes power, and targets the enemy's weapons or shields first. A fight can turn on one lucky hit to a key system, and limping home with half a ship working is a story in itself.
summary: A vehicle or ship is a set of named components with their own integrity, and damage to one removes its capacity, such as power, thrust, shields, or sensors, until it is repaired.

definition: Owns a price per good per market, anchored to a base price. Each tick the rule compares demand (consumption, buy orders) with supply (production, stock, sell orders) and raises the price when demand exceeds supply and lowers it otherwise, usually within a band around the base. Common forms are a stock-based price, p = base x f(stock / target stock), and an incremental update, p += k x (demand - supply) / supply. Prices feed back into production profitability and consumption. Victoria 3 (2022) sets each good's national market price from the balance of buy orders from consumption and sell orders from production relative to a base price, scales each state's orders by its market access, and blends local and market prices for poorly connected states. Offworld Trading Company moves prices continuously with every player's purchases and sales.
design_levers: price sensitivity (gain) and the band around base price
base price per good, which sets the default value hierarchy
whether the player's own trades move prices (price impact)
smoothing, inertia, and update frequency
how far price signals propagate between markets
dynamics: High prices attract new producers whose output then pushes prices down, producing cobweb cycles.
Producers crowd into the most profitable good, so profit migrates between goods over time.
Shortages of an input propagate down production chains as price spikes.
failure_modes: High gain causes price oscillation and boom-bust cycles that players read as random.
When the player's trades do not move prices, a single arbitrage loop can be exploited indefinitely.
Tight bands make prices too sticky to signal shortages; loose bands let goods become worthless.
name: Supply-demand pricing
open_questions: Can demand models calibrated on real market data give games more believable price dynamics without making them unreadable?
How much player price impact keeps markets responsive without enabling degenerate exploits?
player_experience: Buy low, sell high, and watch your own trades move the market. The player spots shortages, rushes production to profit from high prices, and sees margins collapse as they and rivals flood the market. Prices become a readout of what the economy lacks.
summary: Prices adjust to supply and demand, so scarcity raises prices and gluts lower them.

synergy.note: Price differentials are what make routes profitable; trade flattens them.

definition: Units or outposts draw supply from sources (hubs, depots, capitals, ports) through a connected path of controlled territory, rail, roads, or sea lanes. Each tick, supply delivered falls off with distance and is capped by the weakest link; units below a supply threshold lose strength, organization, or health. Hearts of Iron IV routes supply from the capital by railway to supply hubs, with hub capacity from 15 to 35 by railway level and capped by the weakest link; supply falls off per province from the hub, and attrition starts at 35% supply or less. Unity of Command makes supply range central to its operational puzzle, and Company of Heroes yields resources only from territory connected to the player's base. Inputs: source capacity, network connectivity, distance. Outputs: per-unit supply level and attrition.
design_levers: falloff curve with distance from source
network carriers: territory, rail, roads, or sea
attrition thresholds and penalties
buffers such as stored supply or foraging
visibility of supply levels and routes
dynamics: Encirclement emerges as the main operational goal.
Infrastructure investment becomes a military priority.
Fronts stall when supply limits are hit, producing realistic operational pauses.
failure_modes: Opaque supply calculations make attrition feel arbitrary.
Supply too forgiving makes logistics irrelevant.
Supply too harsh makes offensives impossible and pins the front.
name: Supply lines
open_questions: Could an AI opponent that reasons about supply networks produce more convincing operational play than current scripted AIs?
player_experience: Strategy at the level of the map. Players plan advances along supply routes, pause to bring up hubs, and seek to cut enemy lines. Encircling an enemy and watching it starve is a strong, systemic win.
summary: Remote units or outposts need a continuous connection to a supply source; cutting the connection causes attrition.

definition: Each surface carries a coverage mask (a texture or vertex grid) storing remaining dirt, paint, or material per cell, sometimes in several layers with different hardness. The tool casts a footprint with radius, falloff, and strength, and each frame it reduces or adds coverage under the footprint, scaled by distance, angle, and tool type versus layer type. Objects report the percentage done and count as complete past a threshold. PowerWash Simulator has four nozzles with different power and spray width, dirt types (dirt, grime, lichen, moss, rust), surface-specific soaps, progress bars per object and level, and a highlight for remaining dirt. House Flipper uses the same pattern for cleaning and painting walls; Hardspace: Shipbreaker's laser cutter is a cutting variant in which cutting electrical wires or coolant pipes can cause an explosion. Inputs: tool parameters and aim. Outputs: coverage state and completion events tied to payment.
design_levers: tool footprint size, strength, and falloff
layer types and which tools or consumables work on them
completion threshold per object
remaining-coverage highlighting and other assists
texture resolution of the coverage mask
tool upgrades and their price
dynamics: Players develop efficient sweep patterns, a real coverage-path optimization.
Tool upgrades change which strategy is efficient, renewing early levels on replay.
Completion feedback rewards perfectionism, which is the core motivation loop.
failure_modes: High completion thresholds turn the last few percent into a hunt for invisible specks; PowerWash Simulator added a highlight for this.
Weak tools or huge areas make sessions drag.
Consumables with unclear benefits feel pointless; reviewers criticized PowerWash Simulator's soap system.
name: Surface work tools
open_questions: Can generative texture models produce varied dirt and wear layouts on arbitrary scanned objects to cut level-authoring cost?
Which feedback cues sustain the relaxation loop across long sessions?
player_experience: Calm, absorbing, visibly productive work. Players sweep a tool across grime and watch clean surface appear, chase the last stubborn patches, and feel satisfied when an object pings complete. The appeal is relaxation and order, not challenge.
summary: The player applies a tool to surfaces to clean, paint, or strip them, and a per-surface coverage state shows visible progress toward completion.

definition: Owns a few bounded stocks on the avatar or party, such as hunger, thirst, body temperature, fatigue, and sometimes sanity or calories. Each tick each stock falls at a base rate modified by activity, weather, and clothing; eating, drinking, resting, or standing near heat restores it. At zero or past a threshold the stock drains health, applies penalties, or kills. Don't Starve uses a default maximum hunger of 150 that drains 75 per game day, and at zero health drains 1.25 per second; The Long Dark tracks calories, body temperature, fatigue, and hunger against cold nights and weather; The Oregon Trail asks each round how much food to eat and kills the party through starvation, cold, or untreated illness. Roguelikes such as Rogue and NetHack use a food clock. Inputs are time, environment, and consumption; outputs are health drain and penalties.
design_levers: which meters exist and which are lethal versus only penalizing
base drain rates and modifiers from activity, temperature, and gear
restoration value of each consumable and its availability in the world
consequence at zero: health drain rate, penalties, or instant death
difficulty presets that scale drain and resource scarcity
dynamics: Low meters reduce the ability to gather, which accelerates decline into a death spiral.
Meters couple the avatar to weather, day-night temperature, and cooking or crafting systems.
Players build bases and routes around reliable sources of food, water, and heat.
failure_modes: Fast drain with scarce restoration forces repetitive eating and drinking that crowds out exploration.
Abundant food trivializes meters by midgame, so they become noise.
Several meters with overlapping warnings overload attention without adding decisions.
name: Survival meters
open_questions: Can drain rates adapted by a learned player model keep survival pressure steady from early to late game without feeling rubber-banded?
player_experience: Constant pressure to keep moving. The player plans every trip around food, water, and warmth, weighs risky exploration against returning to safety, and feels relief at a full stomach by a fire. The meters make the world feel hostile and give mundane items life-or-death value.
summary: The avatar's bodily stocks such as hunger, thirst, warmth, and fatigue deplete over time and, if unmanaged, drain health and kill.

definition: Owns one or more tax rates (global, by zone type, by class, or by good) and converts a tax base into revenue each accounting period, while applying a growth or satisfaction penalty that rises with the rate. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, revenue = population x average land value / 120 x tax rate x a difficulty factor; the rate (0-20%) indexes a table that offsets all three RCI demand valves by +200 at 0%, 0 at 7%, and -600 at 20% on the easiest level, enters the citizens' problem list as rate x 10, and is subtracted from the city score. SimCity 2000 lets players set separate residential, commercial, and industrial rates. Democracy 4 ties tax policies to voter-group happiness and makes very high taxes cause evasion. Victoria 3 derives the tax base from a taxation law and lets the player set an overall tax level.
design_levers: tax base (population, land value, income, trade, goods) and how many separate rates exist
shape of the penalty curve (linear, threshold, accelerating) and where the neutral rate sits
lag between a rate change and its effect on growth or approval
avoidance responses such as evasion, emigration, or capital flight
who bears the tax and which groups react
dynamics: Revenue funds services that grow the tax base while high rates suppress growth, so a revenue-maximizing rate emerges.
Different rates by zone or class let players steer development, such as cutting industrial taxes to attract jobs.
Tax hikes during a crisis can trigger emigration that shrinks the base and deepens the deficit.
failure_modes: A fixed neutral point (Micropolis' 7%) becomes a memorized constant, so the lever is set once and forgotten.
When revenue uses the rate at the moment of collection, as in Micropolis, players can keep taxes low most of the year and raise them just before collection.
A single global rate removes distributional choices and the politics around them.
name: Taxation
open_questions: Could AI-simulated households and firms respond to tax changes with realistic avoidance and migration, making tax design a policy puzzle rather than one slider?
How should tax effects be lagged so the tradeoff is felt without enabling raise-before-collection exploits?
player_experience: Turning a dial between money now and growth later. The player raises taxes to fund services or pay debts, then watches demand or approval sag and searches for the rate the economy will bear.
summary: Player-set tax rates convert economic activity into revenue at the cost of growth, happiness, or competitiveness.

claims.text: A technology tree is a directed acyclic graph; Francis Tresham's 1980 board game Civilization is generally credited with introducing it, and Sid Meier's Civilization (1991) is the iconic video game example.

Stellaris replaces a fixed tree with three semi-random research options per area, weighted by empire ethics, scientist traits, and known techs, plus rare techs and procedurally generated improvement techs.

definition: Technologies are nodes in a directed acyclic graph; each has prerequisites, a research cost, and unlocks. State owned: which techs are researched, current research progress, and queued research. Update rule: each tick or turn, research output (from labs, scientists, or consumed science items) accumulates toward the selected tech; when it reaches the cost, the tech is researched and its unlocks apply. Variants: complete trees where everything is reachable (Civilization), branching trees with exclusive choices, and weighted random draws (Stellaris). Francis Tresham's 1980 board game Civilization is generally credited with introducing the tree, and Sid Meier's Civilization (1991) carried it into video games. Factorio consumes science packs as research input; Stellaris offers three semi-random options per research area, weighted by ethics, scientist traits, and known techs.
design_levers: graph shape: linear, branching, web, or random draws
cost curve per tier
research input: abstract points, science items, or scientists
exclusivity: mutually exclusive branches versus all reachable
repeatable infinite techs for the late game
visibility of future nodes
dynamics: Research pace couples to the economy, so economic snowballing compounds into technological leads.
Exclusive branches create faction or playstyle identity and replay value.
In factory games, science items make research a production target, linking progression to logistics throughput.
failure_modes: A dominant path that every player follows removes strategic choice.
Late-tree techs that do nothing useful leave research facilities idle; some players dismantle labs to save upkeep.
Top techs so strong that the game ends quickly once they are researched, as with the final technologies in Rise of Nations.
Fully random draws frustrate players who plan, since a needed tech may not appear.
name: Tech tree
open_questions: Can a tech tree be generated from the simulation's own physics or chemistry so that research discovers real affordances rather than authored unlocks?
Can RL agents search tree costs and structures for balance faster than human playtesting?
player_experience: A visible map of future capability. The player plans paths, makes long bets on branches, anticipates key unlocks, and feels progress as a chain of small upgrades toward transformative ones.
summary: A research or unlock graph gates buildings, recipes, or abilities behind prerequisites and accumulated research.

definition: Terrain is a height field, often with surface material and water layers. A brush raises, lowers, levels, smooths, or paints cells under the cursor; slope limits propagate the edit to neighbors, and a cost is charged per cell or per volume moved. Downstream systems read the new heights: buildability, water flow, pathing, and views. In Populous (1989) raising and lowering land is the basic divine power, used mainly to give followers flat land for houses, which grows followers and mana. SimCity 2000 and RollerCoaster Tycoon charge money for land edits. Planet Coaster uses voxel terrain that also allows tunnels and overhangs. From Dust moves sand, water, and lava as simulated materials rather than as height edits.
design_levers: brush shapes and sizes
slope limits and how edits spread to neighbors
cost per cell or per volume, and whether material must be conserved
whether terraforming is available in play or only in an editor
how water, pathing, and buildings respond to edited terrain
dynamics: In Populous, flattening land leads to more houses, more followers, and more mana for more powers, a reinforcing loop.
Coupled with hydrology, terrain edits create dams, floods, and reservoirs.
Terraforming against an opponent, such as sinking their land, turns it into a weapon.
failure_modes: Cheap unlimited terraforming flattens the map and removes terrain as a design constraint.
Edits silently break water flow or paths and cause floods or stranded buildings.
Fiddly brush controls make precise shaping tedious.
name: Terraforming
open_questions: Can semantic terrain brushes ("carve a canyon here") backed by generative terrain models keep edits predictable?
How should material conservation be enforced so terraforming stays a resource decision rather than free sculpting?
player_experience: Shaping the world directly. Players prepare sites, carve scenery, and sometimes wield terrain as a weapon. The pleasure is tactile and godlike; the constraint is cost and the knock-on effects on water and access.
summary: The player raises, lowers, flattens, or repaints terrain, usually at a cost, to make land usable or to reshape water and paths.

definition: Ground is a height field with a soft-material layer. Contacts displace material by pressure, wheel slip, and softness; the displaced height persists and changes contact and traction on later passes. In Spintires: MudRunner, according to its lead developer Pavel Zagrebelny, terrain is a regular vertex grid displaced by a height map and covered by a mud layer that artists paint, with a second higher-resolution grid for the mud; when a wheel is in mud or spins too fast, the game computes forces approximating mud physics, and mud displacement runs entirely on the GPU. SnowRunner (2020) extends the approach to snow. Many games deform terrain cosmetically, leaving tracks that do not affect physics.
design_levers: material softness and depth by terrain type
rut depth, persistence, and recovery over time
coupling strength between ruts and traction
simulation resolution and whether it runs on the GPU
how deformation is synchronized in multiplayer
dynamics: Spinning wheels dig deeper and lose traction, a stuck spiral that rewards slow throttle and winching.
Earlier vehicles' ruts change the route for convoy members that follow.
Weather that softens ground couples terrain deformation to route planning.
failure_modes: Cosmetic deformation that does not affect handling creates a mismatch between what players see and feel.
Permanent deep ruts can make a route impassable for the rest of a session.
Deformation state is large and hard to keep synchronized across networked players.
name: Terrain deformation
open_questions: Can learned granular-material models make mud, sand, and snow respond more physically at game frame rates?
player_experience: Struggle and patience. Players read the ground, pick lines, rock the vehicle, and winch out. Every crossing feels earned, and the track left behind tells the story of the trip.
summary: Wheels, feet, and impacts displace soft ground such as mud and snow, and the persistent ruts change traction for later passes.

synergy.note: Ruts and mud change traction, making route reading a skill (SnowRunner).

definition: Owns, per map region (province, county, state, star system, city), an owner, a controller, and an integration state such as core, claim, incorporated, or newly conquered, plus claims that other factions hold on it. Military presence or a completed siege sets the controller; ownership changes only through a peace settlement, inheritance, purchase, or capture rule; and a newly owned region ramps from low to full integration over time or for a price, yielding less and generating more unrest until then. Europa Universalis IV separates owner from controller, makes new provinces costly to core with administrative power, and counts uncored land toward overextension, which raises unrest. Crusader Kings III ties counties to titles and de jure claims and adds a county control value that drops after conquest. Victoria 3 incorporates states over time; Hearts of Iron IV separates core from occupied states; Stellaris takes systems by building outposts and spends influence on claims against rivals. Unlike faction-diplomacy, which owns relations between factions, this mechanic owns who holds each piece of the map.
design_levers: separation of owner and controller, and what occupation alone grants
integration path: time, a currency such as administrative power or influence, or culture and religion matching
penalties for unintegrated land: reduced output, unrest, overextension, or rebel spawns
claim types and how claims are created, fabricated, inherited, or expire
region granularity: provinces, counties, states, systems, or cities
dynamics: Conquest snowballs because new land adds resources and manpower, while integration costs and unrest apply the brake.
Claims and de jure boundaries steer wars toward historically plausible borders.
Occupation without ownership creates leverage for peace negotiations, coupling the map to war score.
failure_modes: Integration costs too low make snowballing conquest the only strategy; too high and expansion stops being worth it.
Border gore and fragmented holdings from inheritance or peace deals become tedious to manage without consolidation tools.
Players treat the map as a coloring exercise and ignore the systems that integration was meant to engage.
name: Territorial control
open_questions: Could AI factions that reason about claims and integration costs expand in ways players read as purposeful rather than greedy?
What integration model keeps conquest consequential without becoming a waiting timer?
player_experience: Expansion has a shape and a hangover. The player plans conquests around claims, watches borders shift as sieges complete, then spends years digesting new land before it pays off. The map itself becomes the scoreboard, and an overstretched realm with restless new provinces is a visible warning to slow down.
summary: Map regions have an owner and a current controller; occupation flips control in war, and peace, purchase, or integration transfers ownership at a cost in time, unrest, or political currency.

definition: Owns a set of track pieces joined end to end, each with a type (straight, curve, slope, switch, bridge, tunnel, or special element such as a loop), an entry and exit position and heading, and a cost. Construction extends an open endpoint with a piece whose entry matches it; the game checks grade and curvature limits, terrain clearance, and collisions with other structures, then charges a cost that depends on terrain (slopes, water, demolition) and piece type. Railroad Tycoon and Transport Tycoon lay track on a tile grid, with slopes, bridges, and tunnels in Transport Tycoon; RollerCoaster Tycoon builds coasters piece by piece on a tile grid by direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews; Planet Coaster adds spline editing; Factorio places straight and curved rail pieces. Outputs: a track graph that vehicles traverse, used by scheduling, signaling, and ride rating. Unlike free-placement, the unit of building is a connected chain rather than a footprint; unlike road-network, it owns segment geometry and its constraints rather than building connectivity; unlike modular-assembly, the result is a path.
design_levers: grade and curve radius limits and their effect on vehicle speed
terrain cost model for slopes, water, tunnels, and demolition
piece set: fixed tiles, free splines, or both
auto-routing tools that pick a path between endpoints
special pieces such as switches, loops, lifts, and brakes
dynamics: Terrain shapes networks and rides: lines follow valleys, and coasters use hills for drops.
Junction and switch layouts couple track design to signaling and throughput.
Track geometry feeds ride ratings and train speeds, so building quality shows up in revenue.
failure_modes: Tile-locked pieces make every layout look the same; free splines without snapping make clean joins hard.
Construction controls that need many precise clicks per segment make building tedious.
Costs too low make terrain irrelevant, so lines ignore the landscape.
name: Track laying
open_questions: Can route-finding assistants that propose track under grade and cost constraints keep the craft while removing click work?
Could generative models propose coaster layouts that hit target ratings for players to refine?
player_experience: Drawing a line through the world under constraints. Players hunt for the gentle grade around a hill, decide whether a bridge is worth its price, and fit a coaster's drops and turns into a cramped park. A clean line that vehicles run smoothly on is a craft object players admire and share.
summary: The player builds rail or coaster track segment by segment under grade, curvature, terrain, and cost constraints, and vehicles then run on the resulting path.

definition: Owns a set of routes, each linking a source market to a destination market for a good, with a volume level or capacity, a transport cost or transit time, and tariffs. Each period profit per unit = destination price - source price - transport cost - tariffs; volume grows when profitable and shrinks when not, which narrows the price gap. In Victoria 3 (2022) routes start at level 1 and change level weekly mainly by profitability, purchase and sale prices are the midpoints of each market's pre- and post-trade prices, tariffs are charged per unit on the base price, sea routes depend on convoys, and each route has a fixed bureaucracy cost that replaced an earlier cap on route count. Civilization's caravans set up routes whose income depends on distance and the cities involved, and Railroad Tycoon pays for delivering goods to stations that demand them.
design_levers: how volume responds to profit (player-set, automatic growth, or capped by vehicles)
transport cost model (distance, time, convoys, ships)
tariffs, trade agreements, embargoes, and their calculation basis
fixed costs per route versus per-unit costs, which decide whether many small or few large routes win
how much information about remote prices the player gets
dynamics: Arbitrage narrows price gaps, so the most profitable routes erode over time.
Trade makes markets interdependent, so a war or blockade in one region causes shortages elsewhere.
Per-unit tariffs on base price hurt high-volume, low-margin routes most, shaping which goods are traded.
failure_modes: Static price gaps that trade does not close create permanent money loops.
With no fixed cost per route, many tiny routes become optimal and flood the interface.
Automated routes that never fail or need attention become set-and-forget income.
name: Trade routes
open_questions: Can AI merchant agents discover and contest routes on their own, giving players competition for arbitrage instead of a static spreadsheet?
What route cost structure keeps trade decisions meaningful without micromanagement?
player_experience: Connecting surplus to scarcity. The player finds where a good is cheap and where it is dear, opens routes, and watches the gap close as the trade succeeds. Tariffs, embargoes, and blockades make trade a lever in diplomacy and a target in war.
summary: Goods are exchanged between settlements, regions, or foreign markets along routes with price differences, tariffs, and transit time.

definition: Trips generated by zones or agents travel over a road network; each segment has a capacity, and travel time rises as volume approaches or exceeds it. Micropolis, the released SimCity engine, has no vehicles: a zone tries a random walk of up to 30 steps along roads until it is adjacent to a destination zone of the required type, and success adds 50 to the traffic density at saved points on the path. Density decays each scan by 34 above 200 and by 24 above 24, and is otherwise reset to zero. Cities: Skylines simulates individual vehicles on lanes. Cities: Skylines II agents choose routes by a combined cost of time, comfort, money, and behavior, spread across lanes, and can be stopped by accidents checked per segment. Inputs: trips, network capacity, route choice. Outputs: per-segment volume, travel times, and delays to services.
design_levers: capacity per lane or road type
route choice model: random walk, shortest path, or cost-based with re-routing
trip generation rate and timing
consequences: lower desirability, delayed services, or lost deliveries
stuck-vehicle handling such as despawning
dynamics: Induced demand: new capacity attracts more trips.
Congestion delays emergency services, so fires spread and crime rises.
Players build hierarchies and transit to shift demand.
failure_modes: Vehicles that crowd into one lane while parallel lanes sit empty, a common complaint about the first Cities: Skylines, produce jams that better road design cannot fix.
Despawning stuck vehicles, as the first Cities: Skylines does by default, hides real congestion problems.
Opaque route choices make traffic feel random.
name: Traffic congestion
open_questions: Could learned driving policies trained on real traffic data make in-game congestion match real-world patterns at city scale?
What level of traffic fidelity improves design decisions rather than just spectacle?
player_experience: Watching gridlock form. Players see jams, trace them to bad intersections or missing routes, and redesign. Congestion is the most visible symptom of a city's structure, and fixing one jam often moves it elsewhere.
summary: Trips route over a capacitated network; volume beyond capacity raises travel time and delays services and deliveries.

definition: Owns a genome per agent (gene list, trait set, or continuous parameters) and the reproduction operator that builds a child's genome from its parents: per-gene selection or crossover, optional dominance, and mutation with set rate and size. The genome then sets appearance, capabilities, or behavior parameters read by other systems. Creatures (1996) uses a haploid genome of about 320 genes coding receptors, reactions, and brain lobes, with crossover at gene boundaries, omissions, duplications, mutations, and genes that switch on at set ages. The Sims 2 passes appearance and personality with dominant and recessive genes; Crusader Kings III passes genetic traits; Planet Zoo genomes set lifespan, size, health, and fertility with an inbreeding penalty; Species: ALRE adds random values to numeric genes. Inputs: parent genomes, mutation parameters. Outputs: offspring traits and variation for selection or breeding.
design_levers: genome representation (discrete traits, numeric genes, structural genes)
