inheritance rule (averaging, per-gene selection, dominance, linkage)
mutation rate and size
inbreeding penalties and diversity rewards
visibility of genotype versus phenotype
dynamics: Selective breeding by the player concentrates traits across generations.
With natural selection, inheritance lets populations adapt to environments.
Inbreeding in small populations produces defect clusters that force outbreeding or trade for new stock.
failure_modes: Averaging inheritance regresses everything to the mean and removes surprise.
Eugenic optimization: players breed for top traits and the system becomes a stat grind, with uncomfortable framing in human-character games.
High mutation rates produce non-viable offspring that read as broken.
Hidden genetics with no inspection make breeding feel random.
name: Trait inheritance
open_questions: Can generative models map genomes to coherent novel appearances and behaviors rather than to a fixed set of parts?
Which inheritance models keep breeding surprising without becoming a pure stat grind?
player_experience: Breeding becomes a long game of chance: the player pairs parents for desired traits, gambles on outcomes, and watches family resemblance and surprises appear. Lineages carry identity.
summary: Offspring inherit traits or genes from their parents with recombination, variation, or mutation.

definition: Owns, per trip or agent, the set of available modes (walk, bicycle, car, taxi, transit), the cost weights used to compare them, and car ownership and parking state. For each trip it computes a generalized cost per mode, such as weighted travel time plus money (fares, fuel, parking fees) plus discomfort (transfers, waiting, crowding, walking distance), and picks the cheapest mode or samples one with logit-style probabilities. Cities: Skylines II combines time, comfort, money, and behavior into its route cost, adds parking fees to driving, and has citizens compare driving, transit, and walking. Outputs are mode shares that load trips onto roads, transit lines, and paths. Unlike public-transit, which owns lines and vehicles, traffic-congestion, which owns per-segment volume, and agent-pathfinding, which searches routes within one network, this mechanic owns the choice between networks.
design_levers: weights on time, money, comfort, and transfers, and whether they vary by age, wealth, or household
car ownership rates and parking supply and pricing
deterministic cheapest-mode choice versus probabilistic choice that spreads demand
transfer and waiting penalties for transit
whether choice is recomputed per trip or fixed per agent
dynamics: Congestion raises driving cost and pushes riders to transit, a balancing loop between roads and lines.
Parking pricing becomes a policy lever that moves demand without building anything.
Dense mixed-use districts shorten trips enough that walking takes a large share, coupling zoning to traffic.
failure_modes: Sticky or opaque choice models keep transit from relieving traffic, so players stop investing in it.
Deterministic choice flips whole populations between modes after a small change, producing oscillating congestion.
Cost terms the player cannot see make empty transit lines look like a bug.
name: Travel mode choice
open_questions: Can discrete-choice models estimated from real travel surveys be simplified enough for players to design against?
Would letting players inspect a citizen's per-mode cost breakdown make transit planning feel fair rather than random?
player_experience: The player shapes behavior indirectly. Instead of ordering citizens onto buses, they raise parking fees, add frequency, or shorten walks to stops, then watch mode share shift in the info views. Success shows up as emptier roads; failure as a new metro line nobody rides.
summary: Agents choose among walking, cycling, driving, and transit for each trip by comparing time, money, and comfort costs, which sets how demand splits across networks.

definition: Each template holds a trigger predicate over state, a selection weight or mean time to happen, an immediate effect block, options with effects, and calls that schedule follow-up events with delays. Hooks such as yearly pulses, births, or deaths evaluate eligible templates and fire them. In Crusader Kings III, events do not fire on their own: on_actions, decisions, or interactions call them; an on_action can fire a list of events, weighted random_events, or the first valid one; and trigger_event schedules a follow-up such as days = { 7 14 } later, so a chain carries saved scopes and flags across months. Europa Universalis IV and Stellaris use the same Paradox script family; Frostpunk and Banished use simpler condition-fired events. Unlike a storyteller director, which paces generic incidents, chains carry authored story state forward. Inputs: state predicates and flags. Outputs: effects, flags, and scheduled events.
design_levers: trigger specificity: broad pulses versus narrow state predicates
weights, mean time to happen, and random delay ranges between links
branching factor and how many chain steps carry state forward
whether follow-ups re-check conditions so chains can fail when the world changes
cooldowns and once-per-game flags that limit repetition
dynamics: Chains link otherwise separate systems, such as health, inheritance, and war, into multi-year storylines.
Overlapping chains on the same characters produce compound situations that no single template described.
Modders extend event pools until mods conflict on shared hooks.
failure_modes: Players see the same chains every playthrough once the event pool is exhausted.
Chains ignore world changes made between links, producing contradictions such as an event about a ruler who has died.
Broad iteration in frequent pulses (the CK3 modding wiki warns against every_living_character in pulse on_actions) causes late-game slowdown.
Authored text quality caps depth, because each branch must be written by hand.
name: Triggered event chains
open_questions: Can a language model write follow-up links conditioned on the actual state reached, keeping chains coherent with world changes?
What fraction of authored chain content could be replaced by generated text while keeping effects hand-tuned?
player_experience: The simulation seems to notice what the player did. A rival's illness leads to a succession dispute, which leads to a war invitation. Players feel stories unfolding from their situation, learn to set up conditions for chains they want, and dread chains they recognize.
summary: Authored event templates fire when state conditions hold, and their outcomes schedule follow-up events that chain into multi-step stories.

definition: Owns the turn counter, the current phase, and the order of actors. Within a turn players act in sequence or submit orders simultaneously; then the world resolves production, growth, movement, combat, and events, and the next turn begins. A turn stands for a fixed span of game time, from a year in Hamurabi to two weeks in The Oregon Trail. Phased variants split a turn into stages, as in Agricola's work and harvest phases or Imperium Romanum II's taxation every third turn; simultaneous variants, called WEGO, such as Diplomacy and Combat Mission, collect all orders and then execute them together. Civilization is the canonical sequential form in strategy simulation. Inputs are player orders; outputs are the resolved world state each turn.
design_levers: game time per turn and whether it changes over the game
sequential, simultaneous, or mixed actor order
phase decomposition and which systems update in which phase
per-turn action limits or action points
time limits on turns in multiplayer
dynamics: Players optimize per-turn efficiency, making the turn itself the unit of strategy.
Batched world resolution makes chains of consequences visible as discrete steps.
Simultaneous orders create bluffing and prediction between players.
failure_modes: Late-game turns with many units or cities take long to play and process, producing micromanagement fatigue.
Sequential order gives first-mover or last-mover advantages that need compensation.
Waiting for other players' turns makes multiplayer sessions long and idle.
name: Turn structure
open_questions: Can learned opponents that negotiate in natural language make phase-based diplomacy viable against AI rather than only humans?
player_experience: Unlimited time to think. The player studies the state, plans, and commits, then watches the consequences resolve at once. Turns make cause and effect easy to trace and support a 'one more turn' rhythm, while simultaneous turns add the tension of predicting what others will do.
summary: The simulation advances in discrete turns, each divided into ordered phases in which players decide and the world then resolves.

definition: The player selects one or more units and gives explicit orders (move here, attack this, use that, stay, guard) that take precedence over the units' autonomous decision making. State owned: per-unit order queue and override flag. Update rule: when an order is present, the unit's action selection is bypassed or constrained to executing it; on completion or cancellation, autonomy resumes. Orders can be queued and may be refused if impossible. In simulation games it often sits beside autonomy: RimWorld's drafting switches a colonist from autonomous work to direct control for combat; The Sims lets the player queue actions for a Sim who otherwise acts on free will; Dwarf Fortress squads take orders while civilians do not. Strategy games make it the default control mode.
design_levers: scope: any unit, only military units, or only drafted units
how long overrides last and how autonomy resumes
order queue length and shift-queue support
whether units can refuse or delay orders based on morale or needs
group orders and formations
what autonomous behavior continues under orders, such as eating or fleeing
dynamics: A dual mode emerges: autonomy in peace and direct command in crisis, giving play a rhythm of calm and intensity.
The cost of micromanagement pushes players to improve autonomy-affecting systems such as priorities and schedules.
Override on one agent shifts load to others, revealing hidden dependencies in job systems.
failure_modes: Orders are needed constantly because autonomy is weak, turning play into micromanagement.
Drafted or ordered agents ignore needs and starve or collapse, producing deaths players blame on the interface.
Unclear return-to-autonomy rules leave units idle after an order completes.
name: Unit commands
open_questions: Can units interpret high-level natural-language orders (hold the bridge until the medic arrives) and decompose them, and how should they report failure?
When agents have language-model reasoning, how should they negotiate or refuse orders without frustrating the player?
player_experience: When autonomy fails or stakes are high, the player takes the wheel. Drafting colonists into a defensive line or forcing a Sim to bed is precise and reassuring, but heavy use turns agents into puppets and the player into a micromanager.
summary: The player issues direct orders to specific units or agents, overriding their autonomous behavior.

definition: Owns per-agent scoring weights and response curves rather than world state. Each decision cycle it enumerates candidate actions, scores each from inputs such as need levels, distance, personality, risk, and context passed through response curves and combined by product or weighted sum, then selects the top action or samples among high scorers. Dill and Mark (GDC 2010) present response curves, population distributions, and weighted random selection as a fix for the abrupt switches of if-then logic. The Sims picks the behavior that most increases happiness from object advertisements; The Sims 3 (Richard Evans) samples with a modified Boltzmann distribution whose temperature rises when a Sim is doing poorly; the Infinite Axis Utility System (Mark and Lewis, GDC 2015) multiplies normalized considerations. Inputs: candidate actions and their considerations. Outputs: the chosen action and, if exposed, a ranked list of reasons.
design_levers: response curve shape per consideration
combination rule (product, sum, max) and normalization
selection rule: argmax, random among the top N, or softmax with a temperature
inertia or commitment bonus that prevents switching between close options
per-agent personality weights
dynamics: Priorities emerge from scores rather than authored order, so new situations get plausible, unscripted responses.
Coupled with needs decay, agents cycle through activities in rhythms that read as routines.
Small weight changes ripple across a population, so balance patches visibly change agent culture.
failure_modes: Dithering: two actions with close scores alternate, so agents start and abandon tasks.
One consideration dominates the product or sum, and agents ignore everything else.
Choices are hard to explain because each score is the product of many curves, so players see randomness.
Weight tuning grows with the number of actions times considerations and resists local fixes.
name: Utility action selection
open_questions: Can language-model agents propose candidate actions that a utility layer then scores, combining open-ended options with predictable tuning?
Can scoring functions learned from player-labeled preferences replace hand-built response curves?
player_experience: Agents look like they are weighing options: they handle the urgent thing first but sometimes surprise. The player steers them indirectly by changing inputs such as needs, objects, and priorities, and reads odd choices as personality.
summary: Agents choose actions by scoring options against needs and context, then picking the highest or sampling among high scores.

definition: Owns a time scale, paused or one of several multipliers, and the rule that converts real time into simulation ticks. At higher speeds the loop runs more ticks per real second up to hardware limits; while paused no ticks run but the player can still give orders. Some games pause or slow automatically on events. RimWorld runs 60 ticks per second at normal speed and multiplies that by 3, 6, or 15, the last only in development mode, and runs as close to the target as the machine allows; SimCity and Paradox grand strategy games offer pause and several speeds; flight simulators call it time compression. Inputs are the player's speed choice and event triggers; outputs are the tick rate of every other system.
design_levers: number of speeds and their multipliers
whether orders can be given while paused
auto-pause and auto-slowdown triggers, such as raids or letters
speed restrictions in multiplayer or during events
whether higher speeds change simulation fidelity, such as larger time steps
dynamics: Players alternate between paused planning and fast-forward waiting, creating a two-tempo play pattern.
Fast-forward exposes the compute cost of every other system, making simulation performance a gameplay issue.
Auto-pause rules decide which events players notice.
failure_modes: High speeds the hardware cannot sustain silently run slower than shown, so late-game fast-forward feels broken.
Larger time steps at high speed can destabilize physics or give different outcomes than normal speed.
Multiplayer games must reconcile players' speed preferences, often by host control or voting.
name: Pause and speed control
open_questions: Can learned surrogate simulators let players skip long quiet stretches without running full-fidelity ticks?
player_experience: Control over attention. The player slows down or pauses for crises and detailed orders, then fast-forwards through quiet stretches such as waiting for crops or construction. Pause makes real-time games playable at a thoughtful pace, and fast-forward removes dead time.
summary: The player pauses the simulation and switches between speed multipliers, trading attention against elapsed game time.

definition: The vehicle state holds the chassis rigid body, wheel angular speeds, suspension compression, engine speed, gear, and often tire temperature and wear. Each physics step routes engine torque through the drivetrain, computes each tire's longitudinal and lateral force from slip ratio, slip angle, and vertical load, applies suspension forces that transfer weight under braking, acceleration, and cornering, and integrates. A common tire model is Hans Pacejka's semi-empirical Magic Formula, which fits force against slip as y = D sin(C arctan(Bx - E(Bx - arctan Bx))). Simulators such as iRacing and Gran Turismo use detailed tire and suspension models; arcade racers simplify grip into tunable curves. Assists such as ABS and traction control act on the same quantities.
design_levers: tire model fidelity: simple grip curve to full Magic Formula
driving assists and their strength
physics step rate relative to frame rate
setup parameters exposed to the player
surface grip by material and weather
force feedback and camera cues that communicate grip
dynamics: Setup choices create a tuning meta per track and car.
Tire wear and temperature create race strategy over a stint.
Changing weather and surfaces force mid-race adaptation.
failure_modes: Grip that falls off too sharply produces snap oversteer that feels unfair.
Tire models become unstable at very low speeds, causing jitter at standstill.
Too little detail feels like ice skating; too much excludes players without wheels.
Physics tied to frame rate makes handling change with performance.
name: Vehicle dynamics
open_questions: Can tire models learned from real telemetry replace hand-fitted coefficients for each car?
player_experience: Feel and control. Players sense grip through the screen or wheel, learn to balance the car at the limit, and tinker with setups. Mastery is slow and physical, and small improvements feel large.
summary: Tire, suspension, drivetrain, and weight-transfer models compute vehicle handling from forces at each wheel.

definition: Each vehicle holds an order list: an ordered sequence of stops, each with load and unload rules and optional wait conditions. The vehicle travels to each stop in turn, applies its rules, and continues. OpenTTD offers full load of any or all cargo, unload, transfer with partial payment for feeder services, no loading, go-via waypoints, timetables, conditional jumps, and shared orders across vehicles. Transport Tycoon pays by delivery time, distance, and quantity, so mail must be fast while coal tolerates long routes. Factorio train schedules use wait conditions such as full cargo, inactivity, or circuit signals. Inputs: orders, vehicles, cargo at stops. Outputs: cargo movement, revenue, and station service frequency.
design_levers: available order types and wait conditions
payment model by distance, time, and cargo type
shared orders and fleet management tools
vehicle capacity, speed, and reliability
station ratings that respond to service frequency
dynamics: Feeder and trunk networks emerge from transfer orders.
Station competition between companies or players shifts cargo flows.
Fleet growth eventually saturates track or roads, coupling routing to signaling and congestion.
failure_modes: Full-load orders at low-supply stations park vehicles forever.
Complex order systems without templates make fleet changes tedious.
Revenue models that ignore time make every route identical.
name: Vehicle routes and schedules
open_questions: Could natural-language order entry ("keep this mine's output moving to the steel mill") replace order lists without losing player control?
player_experience: Programming a fleet. Players design routes, tune load rules, and watch vehicles run. Well-tuned routes make money unattended; badly tuned ones leave vehicles waiting at empty stations.
summary: Vehicles are assigned ordered stops with load and unload rules to move goods or passengers between nodes.

definition: The map is a stack of layers indexed by depth or named by function. Each layer holds its own grid, and cross-layer rules link them: stairs and ramps for movement, support from below, fluids and objects falling through openings, and utilities in a hidden layer serving the surface tiles above. Dwarf Fortress models a full 3D map of z-levels where dwarves dig down, build stairs and channels, and water and magma flow downward through openings. SimCity 2000 adds an underground view for water pipes and subways under the surface grid. Cities: Skylines places metro tunnels and pipes underground, and Factorio: Space Age adds elevated rails over ground tracks. State: per-layer grids plus inter-layer links; update: per-layer rules plus transfer rules at the links.
design_levers: number of layers and whether they are uniform or functionally distinct
what crosses layers: movement, fluids, support, light, utilities
visibility tools: cutaways, layer toggles, isometric views
cost and hazard gradient with depth
dynamics: Digging into water or magma floods layers below or above, a classic Dwarf Fortress disaster.
Vertical separation lets transit and utilities cross without conflicts, relieving surface congestion.
Defenses gain a vertical dimension through chokepoints, drops, and layered walls.
failure_modes: Legibility collapses when players must mentally stack many layers; Dwarf Fortress players used third-party visualizers to see their fortresses in 3D.
A utility layer that mirrors the surface grid becomes a chore with no decisions of its own.
Pathfinding and fluid updates across many layers become a major performance cost.
name: Vertical layers
open_questions: Can automatic camera and cutaway selection make deep 3D colonies as legible as a single-layer map?
player_experience: Depth and hidden infrastructure. Players dig toward risk and reward, route utilities out of sight, and switch camera layers to manage what they cannot see at once.
summary: The world has stacked layers such as z-levels, floors, or underground networks, and rules connect what happens between them.

definition: A generator periodically picks a requester, a template (fetch an item, deliver a gift, clear pests, make a visit), and parameters drawn from current state, such as an item in season or a nearby location. It posts the request with a reward, often relationship points or money, and a deadline. Completing it applies the reward; expiry may cost relationship. Stardew Valley's Help Wanted board posts item delivery and gathering requests from villagers; Skyrim's radiant quests fill templates with locations and targets; Animal Crossing villagers ask small favors; Mount and Blade lords issue procedural tasks. Inputs: requester state, inventory and season, relationship. Outputs: posted tasks and reward deltas.
design_levers: template set and how parameters bind to live state
posting frequency and number of concurrent requests
reward type and size relative to effort
deadlines and penalties for expiry
requester selection by need, relationship, or location
dynamics: Requests pull players across map areas and seasonal resources they would otherwise skip.
Rewards in relationship points couple requests to romance and social progression.
When requests read live scarcity, they double as a signal of what the economy lacks.
failure_modes: Template repetition makes requests read as generic chores; radiant quests in Skyrim drew this criticism.
Requests that ignore state ask for impossible items or locations already cleared.
Low rewards teach players to ignore the system entirely.
name: Villager requests
open_questions: Can requests generated from a character's actual needs and memories, with language-model dialogue, avoid template fatigue?
What request rate keeps them meaningful without crowding out self-directed play?
player_experience: A light stream of small goals that gives daily play direction and makes characters feel like they have needs. Requests nudge players toward activities they might skip and reward them with friendship. Players learn which requests are worth it and ignore the rest.
summary: Characters generate small requests or quests from templates whose parameters are filled from simulation state, with rewards and deadlines.

definition: The world is stored as voxels with a material per cell, sometimes in several separate volumes. Tools, explosions, and fire remove or convert voxels; the engine then recomputes connectivity, and pieces cut loose either become rigid bodies or stay in place. In Teardown every level is built from destructible voxels; each voxel's material comes from an 8-bit palette setting color, roughness, emissiveness, reflectivity, and physical type; the world is split into several voxel volumes; and the engine does not model compressive stress. Minecraft breaks blocks after a mining time set by tool and material, and only some blocks, such as sand and gravel, fall when unsupported. Outputs are the edited world, debris bodies, and new paths.
design_levers: voxel size relative to the player
material hardness and which tools break which materials
connectivity and support rules for loose pieces
debris lifetime and cleanup
fire and explosion coupling
unbreakable materials that preserve level structure
dynamics: Players cut their own routes, turning levels into planning puzzles, as in Teardown's heist missions.
Fire and collapses chain through flammable and weakened structures.
Persistent edits accumulate, so the world reflects a session's history.
failure_modes: Level design is hard because walls and doors cannot block players; Teardown relied on elevation, distance, water, and unbreakable objects.
Synchronizing voxel physics over a network is hard; Teardown's team originally judged multiplayer infeasible, and co-op arrived only in a 2026 update.
Structures stand on implausibly little support when only connectivity is checked.
Destruction at scale caps performance and map size.
name: Voxel destruction
open_questions: Can generative models author voxel levels whose structure holds up to arbitrary destruction?
Can learned fracture models give voxel destruction plausible stress without full physical simulation?
player_experience: Total freedom of route. Any wall can become a door, so players plan paths through buildings and enjoy demolition for its own sake. The world remembers what they broke.
summary: The world is built from small destructible units that can be removed, broken loose, and burned anywhere.

definition: Each service building periodically spawns a walker that follows roads; as it passes, it writes a coverage value to nearby houses, which decays over time until the next visit. In Caesar III, as reproduced by the Julius reimplementation, a roaming walker first heads for a road point about 8 tiles out in a cardinal direction that rotates with each spawn, then wanders, turning pseudo-randomly at intersections and ending its walk at dead ends. Culture, health, and religion walkers set a per-service house value to 96, which decays by 1 on each periodic update; prefects reset fire risk to zero and engineers reset collapse risk to zero. Inputs: building location, road network, random turns. Outputs: per-house coverage values that gate housing evolution and prevent fires or collapses.
design_levers: walker roaming range and spawn interval
turn rule at intersections: random, biased, or destination-based
coverage radius around the walker and decay rate on houses
roadblocks or other routing controls
number of walker types and services per type
dynamics: Standard block layouts (looped housing blocks with services inside) become community conventions.
Coverage gaps produce local fires and collapses that spread.
Road changes can suddenly strand houses by changing walker routes.
failure_modes: Randomness that leaves some houses uncovered causes devolve-evolve flicker.
Walker logic that needs community analysis to understand frustrates players.
Too many walker types multiply layout constraints until blocks become formulaic.
name: Walker service delivery
open_questions: Would walkers with learned or goal-driven routes make coverage more legible or less?
player_experience: Designing for wanderers. Players build looping road blocks so walkers cover the right houses, use roadblocks where available, and watch for houses that a walker never reaches. Knowing that coverage depends on chance makes layout feel like guiding a crowd.
summary: Services are delivered by agents walking routes from their building, so coverage depends on where walkers actually go.

definition: Owns, for each active war, a score per side (or a shared balance) and the list of war goals, plus a menu of peace terms with a cost in score. Each update, battles won, regions occupied, and time spent holding the war goal add score, and casualties and occupation add exhaustion. A peace offer is accepted when its total cost is within the winner's score or when the loser's exhaustion or support crosses a capitulation threshold; otherwise the AI weighs score against demands. Europa Universalis IV prices each demand (provinces, gold, vassalage) in war score. Crusader Kings III lets an attacker enforce the war goal at full war score and allows white peace. Victoria 3 tracks war support that falls with exhaustion until a side capitulates. Hearts of Iron IV holds a peace conference in which winners spend points on demands in turns. In Stellaris a side at maximum war exhaustion can be forced into a status quo peace. Unlike faction-diplomacy, which decides whether factions go to war, this mechanic owns how a war ends and what the winner may take.
design_levers: score sources and their weights: battles, occupation, blockades, holding the war goal
cost table for each peace term, and whether costs scale with the target's size
exhaustion accumulation and its domestic effects such as unrest or lower production
capitulation or forced-peace thresholds, and whether third parties join the settlement
truce length after peace
dynamics: Players carry out limited wars that take exactly what the score allows, then wait out the truce and return.
Exhaustion couples military campaigns to stability and the economy, so long wars bleed the home front.
Multi-party peace conferences produce partitions that set up later conflicts.
failure_modes: Score dominated by occupation rewards sieging empty land over defeating armies.
AI that refuses reasonable terms because of hidden acceptance factors makes wars drag on.
Capitulation thresholds that trigger too early end wars before the strategic situation is resolved.
name: War score and peace terms
open_questions: Can language-model negotiators bargain over peace terms in ways players find legible and hard to exploit?
Would score models that weigh strategic outcomes rather than counts of occupied regions produce more plausible peace deals?
player_experience: Wars become negotiations with a running tally. The player fights for score as much as for ground, deciding when a battle or a siege is worth the cost and when to cash in. Bargaining over which provinces fit within the score turns the end of a war into a planning problem, and exhaustion forces the question of whether to sue for peace before the home front breaks.
summary: Each war tracks a score or exhaustion level from battles, occupation, and war goals, and that value caps what a peace settlement can demand or forces capitulation.

definition: Each asset holds a condition or reliability stock. Each update it decays by a base rate scaled by usage, age, and environment, and a breakdown is drawn with probability that rises as condition falls. A broken asset stops or malfunctions until a repair job, often done by a maintenance agent, restores it. In RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 (as reimplemented in OpenRCT2), reliability starts at 100% and drops every 256 ticks by the ride's unreliability factor plus an age penalty that grows from one-eighth of that factor in year one to double after eight years; breakdown types are weighted, brake failure is likelier in rain, players set inspection intervals for mechanics, and a repair restores reliability in proportion to the deficit. Transport Tycoon vehicles lose reliability between depot services; Theme Hospital machines explode if handymen do not repair them. Per-use item durability, as in Minecraft tools, is a variant without maintenance.
design_levers: decay rate per asset class and its usage and weather modifiers
age penalty curve that forces eventual replacement
breakdown probability as a function of condition, and the menu of breakdown types and severities
maintenance interval, labor required, and repair restoration amount
repair versus replacement cost
a global breakdown setting (off, reduced, normal)
dynamics: Aging fleets and rides create replacement waves that strain budgets years after the original build-out.
Mechanic coverage becomes a routing and staffing problem coupled to park or network layout.
Breakdowns create service queues and satisfaction drops that spread to nearby systems.
failure_modes: Maintenance with no tradeoffs becomes a chore; OpenTTD exposes a setting to reduce or disable breakdowns, and many players use it.
Too few maintenance workers lets breakdowns pile up faster than repairs, a spiral that is hard to diagnose.
Hidden condition values make breakdowns feel random even when the player could have prevented them.
name: Wear and breakdown
open_questions: Can predictive maintenance tools that forecast failure from condition history become part of play instead of a hidden optimization?
When does per-use durability add decisions rather than inventory chores?
player_experience: A steady background of upkeep decisions. The player schedules inspections, staffs mechanics, and decides when an aging asset should be replaced instead of repaired. Breakdowns are visible interruptions with queues of angry customers or stalled trains.
summary: Assets lose condition with use and age, breakdown risk rises as condition falls, and maintenance or repair restores it.

definition: Owns a current weather state, and sometimes a forecast, drawn each day or interval from season-dependent probabilities or evolved as a Markov chain or noise field across the map. The state sets modifiers other systems read: rain waters crops or puts out fire, storms bring lightning that damages things, cold lowers body temperature, wind changes travel or spread, and fog cuts visibility. Stardew Valley picks daily weather, shows tomorrow's forecast on the TV, never rains in winter without a Rain Totem, and lets lightning destroy crops unless lightning rods intercept it; The Long Dark's blizzards and cold nights drive its survival loop; Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020 can stream real-world weather. Inputs are season, location, and random draws; outputs are condition flags and values such as temperature and wind.
design_levers: set of weather states and their transition probabilities by season and region
duration and spatial extent of weather events
which systems each state modifies and by how much
forecast availability and accuracy
protection tools: shelter, lightning rods, clothing, irrigation
dynamics: Weather couples many systems at once: crops, fire, travel, mood, and body temperature.
Forecasts turn weather from noise into a planning input, rewarding flexible schedules.
Rare extreme weather becomes a memorable event that players prepare for.
failure_modes: Purely cosmetic weather costs effects budget without changing decisions.
Severe weather with no forecast or counterplay feels like an unfair random penalty.
Weather rolled independently each day can flip implausibly between extremes.
name: Weather
open_questions: Can learned global weather models supply spatially coherent, plausible weather for procedural worlds at low runtime cost?
player_experience: Adapting plans to conditions outside the player's control. The player checks the forecast, moves tasks indoors on stormy days, waits out a blizzard, or takes advantage of rain. Weather makes days feel different and gives the world a mood.
summary: Weather states such as rain, storms, snow, wind, and temperature change over time and modify activities and other systems.

definition: Owns a matrix of agents by job types holding enabled flags or priority numbers, plus a fixed ordering of job types. When an agent is idle it scans job types in priority order, breaking ties by column order, and takes an available job of the highest priority it can do, usually the nearest. RimWorld's work tab has a standard mode (checkmarks, columns further left more important) and a manual mode with priorities 1 (highest) to 4; all available work at one priority is done before the next, blank cells are never done, incapable work types are excluded, and allowed areas restrict where jobs are taken. Dwarf Fortress uses per-dwarf labor toggles, and Oxygen Not Included combines per-duplicant errand priorities with 1-9 priorities on individual buildings. Inputs: the job queue, skills, distances. Outputs: who does what, and how fast the group responds to new work.
design_levers: granularity of job types
number of priority levels and tie-break rules
global agent-by-type priorities versus per-task or per-building overrides
interaction with distance: nearest job first versus highest priority first
automatic suggestions based on skill
dynamics: Fixing one starved job type exposes the next bottleneck, so the table evolves as the group grows.
Priorities aligned with skills create specialists, which reinforces skill gaps.
Emergencies force temporary reshuffles or direct control, producing spikes of micromanagement.
failure_modes: Priority inversion: an agent hauls a distant item at priority 1 while a patient bleeds, because all priority-1 work is done before the next level.
Large matrices become spreadsheet management that players solve once with a template and stop engaging with.
Poor tie-breaking sends agents across the map for low-value tasks.
Hidden ordering within a job type surprises players.
name: Work priorities
open_questions: Can a manager agent translate high-level intents (keep everyone fed, prioritize medicine) into the priority table and explain its settings?
Does automatic assignment remove the managerial decision or only the spreadsheet tedium?
player_experience: The player acts as a manager, matching people to jobs by skill and interest, then debugging the table when hauling never happens or the doctor is busy cooking. The table is where strategy is expressed without micromanaging each task.
summary: The player sets which agents do which job types in what order, and agents self-assign from that priority table.

definition: The player paints a land-use type, often with density, onto tiles or lots. A zone places nothing by itself. Each update the simulation checks zoned lots and grows, upgrades, downgrades, or abandons buildings based on demand, access, utilities, services, pollution, crime, and nearby uses. In SimCity (1989) players zone residential, commercial, and industrial land, and the Sims choose what to build and upgrade based on traffic, power, crime, and proximity to other buildings, so homes next to a power plant seldom reach the highest grade. Cities: Skylines grows buildings in low- and high-density zones along roads. Games without zoning, such as Anno, have the player place every house directly. State: zone type per tile plus building level per lot.
design_levers: zone categories and density tiers
development rule: growth probability, thresholds, and upgrade conditions
hard requirements such as road access, power, and water
lot size and shape rules
abandonment and decline rules
whether the player can also place specific buildings directly
dynamics: City form emerges from the interaction of zones, transport, and land value rather than from direct design.
Nuisance uses push residential away, producing segregated districts and commute traffic.
Successful zones raise demand and land value, which invites more zoning, a growth loop until services saturate.
failure_modes: Zones fail to develop with no visible reason, forcing players to hunt through overlays and demand meters.
Cheap zoning paint encourages over-zoning, leaving large empty tracts.
Uniform growth rules produce monotonous cities with little local character.
name: Zoning
open_questions: Can LLM-driven developer agents make zoned growth explain itself and vary by local character?
Can generated building assets end the repetition of growable buildings across a large city?
player_experience: Indirect control. Players paint intent and watch a city grow into it, like gardening. The main skill is diagnosing why a zone stalls or decays and fixing the conditions rather than the buildings.
summary: The player paints land-use zones, and the simulation decides whether and what to build, upgrade, or abandon on each zoned lot.
